knowledge_statements.statement_title: Support function of a nonempty set
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(C\subset H\) be nonempty. The supremum is taken in \(( -\infty,+\infty]\), so unboundedness in a direction is permitted.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space support function; no convexity, closedness, or boundedness is required for the definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The support function of \(C\) is the extended-real function \[\sigma_C:H\to(-\infty,+\infty],\qquad \sigma_C(u)=\sup_{x\in C}\langle x,u\rangle.\] Its effective domain is \(\operatorname{dom}\sigma_C=\{u\in H:\sigma_C(u)<+\infty\}\). For each \(u\ne0\) with finite support value, the closed half-space \[H_u=\{x\in H:\langle x,u\rangle\leq\sigma_C(u)\}\] is the smallest closed half-space with outward normal \(u\) containing \(C\). The function depends only on the closed convex hull: \(\sigma_C=\sigma_{\overline{\operatorname{conv}}C}\). Consequently, if \(C\) is closed and convex, it is recovered by \[C=\bigcap_{u\in H}\{x\in H:\langle x,u\rangle\leq\sigma_C(u)\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The support function of a nonempty set \(C\) maps each direction \(u\) to the supremum of the linear functional \(x\mapsto\langle x,u\rangle\) over \(C\). It may be positive infinity. For a finite support value, the corresponding inequality defines the tightest containing half-space with that normal. The support function is unchanged by taking the closed convex hull, and a closed convex set is the intersection of all half-spaces specified by its support function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_C(u)=\sup_{x\in C}\langle x,u\rangle\) for every \(u\in H\), with \(\sigma_C=\sigma_{\overline{\operatorname{conv}}C}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\sigma_C=\sup_{x\in C}\langle x,\cdot\rangle\) pointwise.
If \(C\) is closed and convex, \(x\in C\iff (\forall u\in H)\;\langle x,u\rangle\leq\sigma_C(u)\).
special_cases_latex: \(\sigma_{\{c\}}(u)=\langle c,u\rangle\).
For the closed unit ball \(B\), \(\sigma_B(u)=\|u\|\).
If \(C\) is bounded, then \(\sigma_C\) is finite everywhere.
immediate_consequences_latex: \(\sigma_C(0)=0\), \(\sigma_C(\lambda u)=\lambda\sigma_C(u)\) for \(\lambda>0\), and \(\sigma_C(u+v)\leq\sigma_C(u)+\sigma_C(v)\).
The support function is lower semicontinuous and convex as a pointwise supremum of continuous linear functions.
boundary_notes: If \(C\) is unbounded, \(\sigma_C\) can equal \(+\infty\) in some directions.
The definition for the empty set requires a separate convention and is excluded here.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed Perspective as a Support Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents the closed perspective, including its recession-function value at zero scale and its negative-scale failure boundary, as a support function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be closed, proper, and convex, and define \[k(\lambda,x)=\begin{cases}\lambda f(x/\lambda),&\lambda>0,\\ f^{0+}(x),&\lambda=0,\\ +\infty,&\lambda<0.\end{cases}\] Let \[C=\{(\lambda^*,x^*)\in\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\mid \lambda^*\leq-f^*(x^*)\}.\] Then \(k=\sigma_C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closed perspective of a closed proper convex function equals the support function of the hypograph of the negative conjugate. Its zero-scale value is the recession function, and it is infinite at negative scales.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ is closed, proper, and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: k(\lambda,x)=\begin{cases}\lambda f(x/\lambda),&\lambda>0,\\ f^{0+}(x),&\lambda=0,\\ +\infty,&\lambda<0\end{cases}=\sigma_C(\lambda,x).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Support Value of a Positive-Definite Ellipsoid
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Evaluates the support function of the ellipsoid defined by a positive-definite quadratic form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\succ0\). Then, for every compatible vector \(c\), \[\max_x\left\{\langle c,x\rangle:\langle Ax,x\rangle\le1\right\}=\bigl\langle c,A^{-1}c\bigr\rangle^{1/2}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The support value of the unit ellipsoid induced by a positive-definite matrix A is the square root of the inverse quadratic form in c.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max_{\langle Ax,x\rangle\le1}\langle c,x\rangle=\sqrt{\langle c,A^{-1}c\rangle}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polarity Between the Support-Function Domain and the Asymptotic Cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relates the closed effective domain of a support function to the asymptotic cone of its underlying closed convex set.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Support functions of primal and dual subsets under the canonical dual pairing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty set \(C\subset X\), its support function is \[\sigma_C(\zeta):=\sup_{x\in C}\langle\zeta,x\rangle,\qquad \zeta\in X^*.\] If \(\Sigma\subset X^*\), its support function is defined on \(X^{**}\); under the canonical embedding \(X\hookrightarrow X^{**}\), \[\sigma_\Sigma(x)=\sup_{\zeta\in\Sigma}\langle\zeta,x\rangle,\qquad x\in X.\] Closed convex sets are characterized by their support functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The support function of a nonempty set is the supremum of the dual pairing over that set. A subset of the dual has an analogous support function on the bidual and therefore on the canonically embedded primal space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sigma_C(\zeta)=\sup_{x\in C}\langle\zeta,x\rangle;\qquad \sigma_\Sigma(x)=\sup_{\zeta\in\Sigma}\langle\zeta,x\rangle\text{ under }X\hookrightarrow X^{**}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exposed points characterized by gradients of sublinear set representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes exposed points using a differentiable proper positively homogeneous convex representation; the support function is a canonical admissible choice.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \varnothing\ne C\subseteq\mathbb R^n be closed and convex, and let g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty] be proper, convex, and positively homogeneous, with C=\{z\in\mathbb R^n\mid \langle y,z\rangle\le g(y)\ \forall y\in\mathbb R^n\}. Then z\in C is an exposed point of C if and only if there exists y\in\mathbb R^n such that g is differentiable at y and \nabla g(y)=z. In particular, g may be chosen as the support function of C.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty closed convex set represented by a proper positively homogeneous convex function, a point is exposed exactly when it is the gradient of that representation at some differentiability point. The support function supplies a canonical instance.
assumptions_latex: \varnothing\ne C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is closed and convex}
g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ is proper, convex, and positively homogeneous}
C=\{z\in\mathbb R^n\mid \langle y,z\rangle\le g(y)\ \forall y\in\mathbb R^n\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: z\in\operatorname{Exp}(C)\iff \exists y\in\mathbb R^n:\ g\text{ is differentiable at }y\text{ and }\nabla g(y)=z.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Support-function characterization of closed convex sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order, weak-star compactness, and representation properties of support functions on a normed space and its dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C,D\subset X\) be nonempty closed convex sets and let \(\Sigma,\Delta\subset X^*\) be nonempty weak*-closed convex sets. Then: (i) \(C\subset D\) if and only if \(\sigma_C(\zeta)\le\sigma_D(\zeta)\) for every \(\zeta\in X^*\); (ii) \(\Sigma\subset\Delta\) if and only if \(\sigma_\Sigma(x)\le\sigma_\Delta(x)\) for every \(x\in X\); and (iii) \(\Sigma\) is weak*-compact if and only if \(\sigma_\Sigma\) is finite-valued on \(X\). Moreover, a function \(\sigma:X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is positively homogeneous, subadditive, lower semicontinuous in the strong or weak topology, and not identically \(+\infty\) if and only if \(\sigma=\sigma_\Gamma\) for a unique nonempty weak*-closed convex set \(\Gamma\subset X^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Support functions exactly encode inclusion among nonempty closed convex primal sets and nonempty weak-star closed convex dual sets. A weak-star closed convex dual set is weak-star compact exactly when its support function is finite everywhere. The lower-semicontinuous extended-real sublinear functions that are not identically positive infinity are precisely the support functions of unique nonempty weak-star closed convex dual sets.
assumptions_latex: C,D\subset X\text{ are nonempty, closed, and convex}
\Sigma,\Delta\subset X^*\text{ are nonempty, weak* closed, and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C\subset D\iff\sigma_C(\zeta)\le\sigma_D(\zeta)\ \forall\zeta\in X^*;\quad \Sigma\subset\Delta\iff\sigma_\Sigma(x)\le\sigma_\Delta(x)\ \forall x\in X;\quad \Sigma\text{ is weak* compact}\iff\sigma_\Sigma\text{ is finite-valued on }X;\quad \sigma\text{ is positively homogeneous, subadditive, lsc, and not identically }+\infty\iff\exists!\,\Gamma\subset X^*\text{ nonempty weak* closed convex with }\sigma=\sigma_\Gamma

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The finite nonempty set guarantees attainment of the supremum. No convexity assumption on the set is needed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m\geq1\) and let \(C=\{b_1,\ldots,b_m\}\subseteq\mathbb E\). Then, for every \(y\in\mathbb E^*\), \[\sigma_C(y)=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}\langle b_i,y\rangle.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The support function of a nonempty finite set is the pointwise maximum of the finitely many linear functionals generated by its elements.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sigma_C(y)=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}\langle b_i,y\rangle

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Support function of an intersection via infimal convolution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact attained variational representation for the intersection of two bounded closed convex sets under a nonempty-interior condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q_1,Q_2\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, bounded, closed, and convex. Set \(Q=Q_1\cap Q_2\) and assume \(\operatorname{int}Q\ne\varnothing\). For \(S\subset\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(\xi_S(u)=\sup_{s\in S}\langle s,u\rangle\). Then, for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \(\xi_Q(x)=\min_{y\in\mathbb{R}^n}\{\xi_{Q_1}(x+y)+\xi_{Q_2}(-y)\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For two nonempty bounded closed convex sets whose intersection has nonempty interior, the support function of their intersection is the attained infimal convolution of their support functions in the stated shifted form.
assumptions_latex: Q_1,Q_2\subset\mathbb{R}^n\text{ are nonempty, bounded, closed, and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall x\in\mathbb{R}^n,\qquad \xi_Q(x)=\min_{y\in\mathbb{R}^n}\left\{\xi_{Q_1}(x+y)+\xi_{Q_2}(-y)\right\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Support function of a convex compact-valued mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise support-function encoding of a set-valued mapping together with the induced membership representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $a:X\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^m$ be closed with nonempty convex compact values, where $X$ is an open subset of $\operatorname{dom}a$. Define
\[a(x,\ell)=\max_{z\in a(x)}\langle\ell,z\rangle,\qquad x\in X,\ \ell\in\mathbb R^m.\]
For fixed $x$, this is the support function of $a(x)$. If $\mathcal B=\{\ell\in\mathbb R^m:\|\ell\|\le1\}$, then
\[y\in a(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \langle\ell,y\rangle\le a(x,\ell)\quad\forall\ell\in\mathcal B.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The support function of a convex compact-valued mapping maximizes each linear functional over the corresponding image. A point belongs to an image exactly when it satisfies every resulting support inequality over the unit ball.
assumptions_latex: a(x)\text{ is nonempty, convex, and compact for every }x\in X
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: a(x,\ell)=\max_{z\in a(x)}\langle\ell,z\rangle,\qquad y\in a(x)\Longleftrightarrow(\forall\ell\in\mathcal B)\ \langle\ell,y\rangle\le a(x,\ell).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Support-Function Characterizations of Affine Hull and Relative Interior
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes affine-hull, relative-interior, and interior membership in a nonempty closed convex set through directional support values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(s\in\mathbb{R}^n\). Then: (i) \(s\in\operatorname{aff}S\) if and only if \(\langle s,d\rangle=\sigma_S(d)\) for every \(d\) satisfying \(\sigma_S(d)+\sigma_S(-d)=0\); (ii) \(s\in\operatorname{ri}S\) if and only if \(\langle s,d\rangle<\sigma_S(d)\) for every \(d\) satisfying \(\sigma_S(d)+\sigma_S(-d)>0\); and (iii) \(s\in\operatorname{int}S\) if and only if \(\langle s,d\rangle<\sigma_S(d)\) for every nonzero \(d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty closed convex set, a point lies in its affine hull exactly when it attains the support value in every direction with zero two-sided support sum. It lies in the relative interior exactly when it is strictly below the support value in every direction with positive two-sided support sum. It lies in the interior exactly when this strict inequality holds in every nonzero direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{aligned} s\in\operatorname{aff}S&\iff \forall d\in\mathbb{R}^n,\ \bigl(\sigma_S(d)+\sigma_S(-d)=0\Rightarrow\langle s,d\rangle=\sigma_S(d)\bigr),\\ s\in\operatorname{ri}S&\iff \forall d\in\mathbb{R}^n,\ \bigl(\sigma_S(d)+\sigma_S(-d)>0\Rightarrow\langle s,d\rangle<\sigma_S(d)\bigr),\\ s\in\operatorname{int}S&\iff \forall d\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\},\ \langle s,d\rangle<\sigma_S(d). \end{aligned}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Support function of an intersection as an infimal convolution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact support-function representation for the intersection of two bounded closed convex sets under a nonempty-interior qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Q_1,Q_2\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty bounded closed convex sets, set \(Q=Q_1\cap Q_2\), and assume \(\operatorname{int}Q\ne\varnothing\). For \(S\subset\mathbb R^n\), define \(\xi_S(u)=\sup_{s\in S}\langle s,u\rangle\). Then, for every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\),
\[
\xi_Q(x)=\min_{y\in\mathbb R^n}\left\{\xi_{Q_1}(x+y)+\xi_{Q_2}(-y)\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If two nonempty bounded closed convex sets have an intersection with nonempty interior, then the support function of their intersection equals, in every direction, the attained infimal convolution of their support functions with the stated sign reversal.
assumptions_latex: Q_1,Q_2\subset\mathbb R^n\text{ are nonempty, bounded, closed, and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \xi_{Q_1\cap Q_2}(x)=\min_{y\in\mathbb R^n}\left\{\xi_{Q_1}(x+y)+\xi_{Q_2}(-y)\right\}\quad\forall x\in\mathbb R^n.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order and uniqueness properties of support functions for nonempty closed convex subsets of finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $Q_1,Q_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty closed convex sets, with $\xi_{Q_i}(g)=\sup_{x\in Q_i}\langle g,x\rangle\in(-\infty,+\infty]$ and $\operatorname{dom}\xi_{Q_i}=\{g:\xi_{Q_i}(g)<+\infty\}$. Then
\[
\bigl(\forall g\in\operatorname{dom}\xi_{Q_2},\ \xi_{Q_1}(g)\leq\xi_{Q_2}(g)\bigr)\Longrightarrow Q_1\subseteq Q_2.
\]
Moreover, if $\operatorname{dom}\xi_{Q_1}=\operatorname{dom}\xi_{Q_2}$ and the support functions agree throughout this common domain, then $Q_1=Q_2$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For nonempty closed convex sets, domination of the first support function by the second on the effective domain of the second implies inclusion of the first set in the second. Equality of both effective domains and of the support functions there implies equality of the sets.
assumptions_latex: Q_1,Q_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\text{ are nonempty, closed, and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left[\forall g\in\operatorname{dom}\xi_{Q_2},\ \xi_{Q_1}(g)\leq\xi_{Q_2}(g)\right]\Rightarrow Q_1\subseteq Q_2;\quad \left[\operatorname{dom}\xi_{Q_1}=\operatorname{dom}\xi_{Q_2},\ \xi_{Q_1}=\xi_{Q_2}\text{ on this domain}\right]\Rightarrow Q_1=Q_2

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Support Function and Its Basic Set Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded definition and elementary identities for the support function of a convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), its support function is \(\sigma_C(x^*)=\delta^*(x^*\mid C):=\sup_{x\in C}\langle x,x^*\rangle\). For every \(x^*\in\mathbb R^n\), \(\inf_{x\in C}\langle x,x^*\rangle=-\sigma_C(-x^*)\). For every \(x^*\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(\beta\in\mathbb R\), \(C\subseteq\{x:\langle x,x^*\rangle\leq\beta\}\) if and only if \(\beta\geq\sigma_C(x^*)\). Moreover, \(\operatorname{dom}\sigma_C\) is the barrier cone of \(C\), and \(\sigma_C=\sigma_{\operatorname{cl}C}=\sigma_{\operatorname{ri}C}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The support function records the supremum of each linear functional over a convex set. It recovers linear infima by sign reversal, characterizes containing closed half-spaces, has the barrier cone as its effective domain, and is unchanged by closure or relative interior.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sigma_C(x^*)=\sup_{x\in C}\langle x,x^*\rangle,\quad \inf_{x\in C}\langle x,x^*\rangle=-\sigma_C(-x^*),\quad C\subseteq\{x:\langle x,x^*\rangle\leq\beta\}\iff\beta\geq\sigma_C(x^*),\quad \operatorname{dom}\sigma_C=\operatorname{barrier}(C),\quad \sigma_C=\sigma_{\operatorname{cl}C}=\sigma_{\operatorname{ri}C}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Support-function representation of finite nonnegative sublinear functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set representation, Fenchel conjugacy, linear-optimization access, and the polyhedral specialization for finite nonnegative positively homogeneous convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let h:\mathbb{R}^p\to\mathbb{R} be finite, convex, positively homogeneous, and nonnegative. Then there exists a compact convex set K\subset\mathbb{R}^p with 0\in K such that h(w)=\max_{s\in K}s^\top w for all w\in\mathbb{R}^p, and h^*=I_K. Efficient computation of an element of \arg\max_{s\in K}s^\top w is an additional oracle assumption. If K is polyhedral, then K is the convex hull of finitely many extreme points and h is the maximum of the corresponding finitely many linear functions; the complete extreme-point family may nevertheless have cardinality exponential in p.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite, convex, nonnegative, positively homogeneous function is the support function of a compact convex set containing the origin, and its Fenchel conjugate is the indicator of that set. Efficient linear optimization over the set is a separate computational assumption. When the set is polyhedral, it has finitely many extreme points and the function is a finite maximum of linear functions, although the number of extreme points can be exponential in the dimension.
assumptions_latex: h:\mathbb{R}^p\to\mathbb{R}\text{ is finite, convex, positively homogeneous, and nonnegative}
\text{For the oracle condition, an element of }\arg\max_{s\in K}s^\top w\text{ can be obtained efficiently}
\text{For the finite extreme-point conclusion, }K\text{ is polyhedral}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists K\subset\mathbb{R}^p\text{ compact and convex with }0\in K:\quad h(w)=\max_{s\in K}s^\top w\ (\forall w),\qquad h^*=I_K;\quad K=\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{ext}K)\text{ with }|\operatorname{ext}K|<\infty\text{ if }K\text{ is polyhedral}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Support-function calculus for sums, hulls, and intersections
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set operations correspond to algebraic or lattice operations on extended-real support functions; the intersection formula requires a nonempty intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: (i) If \(S_1,S_2\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) are nonempty closed convex sets and \(t_1,t_2>0\), then \(t_1\sigma_{S_1}+t_2\sigma_{S_2}=\sigma_{\operatorname{cl}(t_1S_1+t_2S_2)}\). (ii) If \(\{S_j\}_{j\in J}\) is a family of nonempty closed convex sets, then \(\sup_{j\in J}\sigma_{S_j}=\sigma_{\overline{\operatorname{co}}(\bigcup_{j\in J}S_j)}\). (iii) If \(\{S_j\}_{j\in J}\) is a family of closed convex sets and \(S:=\bigcap_{j\in J}S_j\ne\varnothing\), then \(\sigma_S=\overline{\operatorname{co}}\!\left(\inf_{j\in J}\sigma_{S_j}\right)\), where \(\overline{\operatorname{co}}\) denotes the closed convex envelope of the pointwise infimum function.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive weighted sums of support functions represent closed weighted Minkowski sums; pointwise suprema represent closed convex hulls of unions; and the support function of a nonempty intersection is the closed convex envelope of the pointwise infimum of the component support functions.
assumptions_latex: S_1,S_2\text{ are nonempty, closed, and convex and }t_1,t_2>0\text{ in (i)}
S_j\text{ is nonempty, closed, and convex for every }j\in J\text{ in (ii)}
S_j\text{ is closed and convex for every }j\in J\text{ and }\bigcap_{j\in J}S_j\ne\varnothing\text{ in (iii)}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: t_1\sigma_{S_1}+t_2\sigma_{S_2}=\sigma_{\operatorname{cl}(t_1S_1+t_2S_2)},\quad \sup_{j\in J}\sigma_{S_j}=\sigma_{\overline{\operatorname{co}}(\bigcup_{j\in J}S_j)},\quad \sigma_{\cap_{j\in J}S_j}=\overline{\operatorname{co}}\!\left(\inf_{j\in J}\sigma_{S_j}\right)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Homogeneity, subadditivity, and set-operation calculus for support functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The assertions at \(\alpha=0\) use the nonnegative extended-real convention \(0\cdot(+\infty)=0\). No closedness, convexity, or boundedness assumption on the generating sets is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every nonempty \(C\subseteq\mathbb E\), every \(y,y_1,y_2\in\mathbb E^*\), and every \(\alpha\geq0\), \[\sigma_C(\alpha y)=\alpha\sigma_C(y),\qquad \sigma_C(y_1+y_2)\leq\sigma_C(y_1)+\sigma_C(y_2),\qquad \sigma_{\alpha C}(y)=\alpha\sigma_C(y).\] Separately, for every pair of nonempty sets \(A,B\subseteq\mathbb E\) and every \(y\in\mathbb E^*\), \[\sigma_{A+B}(y)=\sigma_A(y)+\sigma_B(y).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Support functions are positively homogeneous and subadditive in their dual argument. Nonnegative scaling of a generating set scales its support function, while the support function of a Minkowski sum is the sum of the two support functions.
assumptions_latex: \text{For the first three assertions: }C\subseteq\mathbb E,\ C\neq\varnothing,\ y,y_1,y_2\in\mathbb E^*,\ \alpha\geq0
\text{For the Minkowski-sum assertion: }A,B\subseteq\mathbb E,\ A\neq\varnothing,\ B\neq\varnothing,\ y\in\mathbb E^*

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any \(D\subset\mathbb R^n\), its support function is \(\sigma_D(w):=\sup_{v\in D}\langle v,w\rangle\). For every \(w\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\), \[D\subset\{v:\langle v,w\rangle\leq\alpha\}\iff \sigma_D(w)\leq\alpha.\] If \(D=\varnothing\), then \(\sigma_D\equiv-\infty\); if \(D\neq\varnothing\), then \(\sigma_D(w)>-\infty\) for every \(w\), and \(\sigma_D(0)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The support function is the supremum over the set of the linear functional in a given direction. Its value characterizes the half-spaces with that normal that contain the set. The empty set has support function identically minus infinity; a nonempty set has no minus-infinite support values and has value zero at the origin.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sigma_D(w)=\sup_{v\in D}\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad D\subset\{v:\langle v,w\rangle\leq\alpha\}\iff\sigma_D(w)\leq\alpha

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Support Halfspaces, Support Points, and Supporting Hyperplanes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric interpretation of a finite support value and the additional consequences when that value is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\varnothing\ne C\subseteq\mathcal H\) and \(u\in\mathcal H\setminus\{0\}\). If \(\sigma_C(u)<+\infty\), then \[H_u=\{y\in\mathcal H:\langle y,u\rangle\leq\sigma_C(u)\}\] is the smallest closed half-space with outer normal \(u\) that contains \(C\). If, in addition, \(x\in C\) and \(\sigma_C(u)=\langle x,u\rangle\), then \(x\) is a support point of \(C\), and \[\{y\in\mathcal H:\langle y,u\rangle=\sigma_C(u)\}\] is a supporting hyperplane of \(C\) at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite support value gives the smallest containing closed half-space with the specified nonzero outer normal. If the value is attained at a point of the set, that point is a support point and the corresponding level hyperplane supports the set there.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: H_u=\{y\in\mathcal H:\langle y,u\rangle\leq\sigma_C(u)\}\text{ is the smallest closed half-space with outer normal }u\text{ containing }C;\quad [x\in C\ \wedge\ \sigma_C(u)=\langle x,u\rangle]\Rightarrow x\text{ is a support point and }\{y:\langle y,u\rangle=\sigma_C(u)\}\text{ supports }C\text{ at }x

children.title: Gauge-Minkowski Representation Pair
children.top_down_role: Positive-homogeneous functions generated by absorbing convex sets.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be closed and convex with \(0\in C\). For \(\lambda>0\), write \(\lambda C=\{\lambda c:c\in C\}\), and adopt \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional closed convex gauge representation; the set need not be bounded or absorbing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The gauge, or Minkowski functional, generated by \(C\) is \[\gamma_C(x)=\inf\{\lambda>0:x\in\lambda C\},\qquad x\in\mathbb{R}^n.\] It is a nonnegative, lower-semicontinuous, positively homogeneous convex function. Its radial set representation is \[C=\{x:\gamma_C(x)\leq1\},\qquad rC=\{x:\gamma_C(x)\leq r\}\quad(r>0).\] Conversely, if \(p:\mathbb{R}^n\to[0,+\infty]\) is lower semicontinuous and sublinear and \(C_p=\{x:p(x)\leq1\}\), then \(C_p\) is closed, convex, contains \(0\), and \(p=\gamma_{C_p}\). Thus closed convex sets containing the origin and nonnegative closed sublinear functions form a representation pair under \(C\mapsto\gamma_C\) and \(p\mapsto\{p\leq1\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed convex set \(C\) containing the origin, the gauge of a point is the least positive dilation factor needed to place that point in a dilate of \(C\), with value positive infinity if no dilation works. The original set is the unit sublevel set of its gauge, and every positive sublevel set is the corresponding dilation. Conversely, every nonnegative lower-semicontinuous sublinear function is the gauge of its unit sublevel set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_C(x)=\inf\{\lambda>0:x\in\lambda C\}\) and \(C=\{\gamma_C\leq1\}\); conversely \(p=\gamma_{\{p\leq1\}}\) for every nonnegative closed sublinear \(p\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(t>0\), \(\gamma_C(x)\leq t\iff x\in tC\).
The epigraph of \(\gamma_C\) is the closure of the conical hull generated by \(C\times\{1\}\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is the unit ball of a norm, then \(\gamma_C\) is that norm.
If \(C\) is symmetric and \(0\in\operatorname{int}C\), then \(\gamma_C\) is a norm.
If \(C\) is a closed convex cone, then \(\gamma_C\) is \(0\) on \(C\) and \(+\infty\) outside \(C\).
immediate_consequences_latex: \(\gamma_C\) is finite everywhere exactly when \(0\in\operatorname{int}C\).
The zero set \(\{x:\gamma_C(x)=0\}\) is the recession cone of \(C\).
boundary_notes: Without symmetry, a finite gauge need not be a norm because \(\gamma_C(x)\) and \(\gamma_C(-x)\) may differ.
Closedness is material to the exact identity \(C=\{\gamma_C\leq1\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The gauge generated by \(C\) is the extended-real function \[\gamma_C:X\to[0,+\infty],\qquad \gamma_C(x)=\inf\{t>0:x\in tC\},\] with \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\). It is positively homogeneous: \(\gamma_C(\lambda x)=\lambda\gamma_C(x)\) for every \(\lambda>0\). If \(C\) is convex, then \(\gamma_C\) is subadditive and hence convex. If \(C\) is absorbing, then \(\gamma_C\) is finite everywhere. No symmetry, closedness, or boundedness is required for the definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The gauge of a set is the smallest positive dilation needed to contain a point. Convex sets yield convex gauges, while absorbing sets yield finite gauges.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact degeneracy set for a closed convex gauge generator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty closed convex subset of a finite-dimensional real vector space with \(0\in C\). Then \[\{x:\gamma_C(x)=0\}=\operatorname{rec}C.\] Thus the generated gauge vanishes on a nonzero direction exactly when the generator has a nonzero recession direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed convex generator, the zero set of its gauge is exactly the generator's recession cone.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq X\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_C^{-1}(0)=\operatorname{rec}C\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Domain geometry of an extended-valued gauge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq X\) contain \(0\), and let \(\gamma_C(x)=\inf\{t>0:x\in tC\}\). Then \[\operatorname{dom}\gamma_C=\{x:\gamma_C(x)<+\infty\}=\bigcup_{t>0}tC.\] If \(C\) is convex, this effective domain is a convex cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A gauge is finite exactly on the positive radial hull of its generator; for a convex generator that domain is a convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dom}\gamma_C=\bigcup_{t>0}tC\), which is a convex cone when \(C\) is convex.

If $C$ is convex, then $\gamma_C$ is sublinear and hence convex. If $B$ is the norm unit ball, then $\gamma_B=\|\cdot\|$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The gauge of a nonempty set is the infimum of the nonnegative scaling factors that place a point in the scaled set. Convex generators produce sublinear gauges, and the gauge of the norm unit ball is the norm.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Minkowski functional of \(C\) is its gauge \(p_C=\gamma_C\), defined by \[p_C(x)=\inf\{t>0:x\in tC\},\qquad \inf\varnothing=+\infty.\] Under this convention, \[\{x\in X:p_C(x)<1\}\subseteq C\subseteq\{x\in X:p_C(x)\leq1\}.\] If additionally \(C\) is closed, then \[C=\{x\in X:p_C(x)\leq1\}.\] If instead \(C\) is open, then \[C=\{x\in X:p_C(x)<1\}.\] Thus boundary regularity determines whether the strict or non-strict unit sublevel recovers \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minkowski functional is another name for gauge. A convex set containing the origin lies between its strict and non-strict unit sublevels; a closed or open set is recovered by the corresponding unit sublevel.
knowledge_statements.title: Minkowski Functional Convention

children.title: Absorbing-Set Geometry
children.top_down_role: Set geometry controlling finiteness and domain coverage of gauges.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq X\) is nonempty, convex, and contains \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is absorbing exactly when \(p_C\) is finite-valued on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic absorbing geometry for a convex set containing the origin.

source_refs.locator: 8 Convex Functions p. 139
source_refs.source_title: Convex Analysis and Monotone Operator Theory in Hilbert Spaces

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The set \(C\) is absorbing if, for every \(x\in X\), there exists \(t>0\) such that \(x\in tC\). Its Minkowski functional is \[p_C(x)=\inf\{t>0:x\in tC\},\] with \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\). Thus \(C\) is absorbing if and only if \(p_C(x)<+\infty\) for every \(x\in X\). Moreover, convexity and \(0\in C\) imply that \(p_C\) is positively homogeneous and subadditive wherever it is finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex set containing zero absorbs every vector exactly when its Minkowski functional is finite everywhere; the functional is then sublinear.
knowledge_statements.title: Absorbing-Set Geometry

source_witnesses.locator: 8 Convex Functions p. 139

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic geometric characterization of absorption for convex origin-containing sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a real vector space and let \(C\subseteq X\) be convex with \(0\in C\). Then \(C\) is absorbing if and only if \(0\in\operatorname{core}C\), where \(\operatorname{core}C\) denotes the algebraic interior. If \(X\) is finite-dimensional with its usual vector-space topology, this is further equivalent to \(0\in\operatorname{int}C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex set containing zero, absorption is equivalent to zero being an algebraic interior point; in finite dimensions this is equivalent to ordinary interior membership.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\text{ is absorbing}\iff0\in\operatorname{core}C\), and in finite dimensions this is equivalent to \(0\in\operatorname{int}C\).
knowledge_statements.title: Absorption and Algebraic Interior

children.title: Symmetric Gauge Regimes
children.top_down_role: Balanced or symmetric generating sets leading toward seminorm-like behavior.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Hausdorff real topological vector space.
\(C\subseteq X\) is nonempty, closed, convex, absorbing, and contains \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C=-C\) if and only if \(p_C(-x)=p_C(x)\) for every \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetry and definiteness properties of Minkowski gauges for closed absorbing convex sets.

source_refs.locator: 8 Convex Functions p. 139

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Because \(C\) is closed, convex, absorbing, and contains \(0\), it is recovered from its gauge by \[C=\{x\in X:p_C(x)\leq 1\}.\] Consequently, \[C=-C\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p_C(-x)=p_C(x)\ \text{for every }x\in X.\] In this symmetric regime, sublinearity makes \(p_C\) a seminorm. It is a norm if \(p_C(x)=0\) implies \(x=0\); in particular, this definiteness holds when \(C\) is bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed convex absorbing set containing zero, central symmetry is equivalent to evenness of its gauge. The gauge is then a seminorm, and it is a norm when its zero set is trivial, as occurs when the set is bounded.
knowledge_statements.title: Symmetric Gauge Regimes

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space and let \(C\subseteq X\) be closed, convex, absorbing, centrally symmetric, and contain \(0\). Then its Minkowski functional \(p_C\) is a norm if and only if \(C\) is bounded. In that case \[C=\{x:p_C(x)\le1\}\] is the closed unit ball of \(p_C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, a closed convex absorbing symmetric generator produces a norm exactly when it is bounded, and it is then that norm's closed unit ball.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq X\) is closed, convex, absorbing, and centrally symmetric.

children.title: Set-Distance Function Hierarchy
children.top_down_role: Metric constructions associated with closed convex sets.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(C\subset H\) be nonempty, closed, and convex. Denote by \(P_Cx\) the unique nearest point of \(C\) to \(x\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space metric hierarchy for nonempty closed convex sets, using the norm induced by the Hilbert structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The distance to \(C\) is \[d_C(x)=\inf_{c\in C}\|x-c\|=\min_{c\in C}\|x-c\|=\|x-P_Cx\|.\] For \(p\geq1\), the powered-distance member of the hierarchy is \[D_{C,p}(x)=\frac1p d_C(x)^p.\] The most common smooth member is the half squared distance \[q_C(x)=D_{C,2}(x)=\frac12\|x-P_Cx\|^2.\] Each \(d_C\) and \(D_{C,p}\) is finite and convex; \(d_C\) is \(1\)-Lipschitz. The zero-level set of every member is \(C\): \[C=\{x:d_C(x)=0\}=\{x:D_{C,p}(x)=0\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty closed convex subset \(C\) of a Hilbert space, the distance function is the minimum norm distance from a point to \(C\), attained uniquely at its metric projection. Raising this distance to a power \(p\geq1\) and dividing by \(p\) gives the powered-distance hierarchy. The half squared distance is the standard quadratic member. All members are finite and convex, while the basic distance is globally one-Lipschitz and every member vanishes exactly on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_C(x)=\|x-P_Cx\|\) and \(D_{C,p}(x)=d_C(x)^p/p\) for \(p\geq1\), with \(\operatorname{zer}D_{C,p}=C\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(P_Cx=\operatorname*{argmin}_{c\in C}\|x-c\|\).
\(d_C=\iota_C\mathbin{\square}\|\cdot\|\), where \(\square\) denotes infimal convolution.
\(q_C=\iota_C\mathbin{\square}(\tfrac12\|\cdot\|^2)\).
special_cases_latex: For a closed linear subspace \(V\), \(d_V(x)=\|P_{V^\perp}x\|\).
immediate_consequences_latex: \(|d_C(x)-d_C(y)|\leq\|x-y\|\) for all \(x,y\in H\).
The conjugate satisfies \(d_C^*=\sigma_C+\iota_{B(0,1)}\).
boundary_notes: For a nonclosed set, the distance can vanish outside the set, namely on its closure.
For a nonconvex closed set, nearest points may fail to be unique and the distance need not be convex.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex. Strong convergence is norm convergence; weak convergence is denoted by \(\rightharpoonup\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of a regularity profile for proper convex functions on Hilbert space, separating topological, local, minorization, and recession components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The topological-asymptotic regularity profile of \(f\) is the tuple \[\mathcal R(f)=\bigl(\operatorname{epi}f,\operatorname{cont}f,\mathcal A(f),\operatorname{rec}f\bigr),\] where \(f\) is lower semicontinuous when \(x_n\to x\) implies \(f(x)\leq\liminf_n f(x_n)\); \(\operatorname{cont}f\) is the set of points where \(f\) is finite and continuous; \[\mathcal A(f)=\{(u,\alpha)\in H\times\mathbb R:\langle x,u\rangle+\alpha\leq f(x)\ \forall x\in H\}\] is the family of continuous affine minorants; and the recession function is \[\operatorname{rec}f(d)=\sup_{x\in\operatorname{dom}f}\bigl(f(x+d)-f(x)\bigr).\] For \(f\in\Gamma_0(H)\), the epigraph is closed, \(\mathcal A(f)\ne\varnothing\), and \(f\) is continuous on \(\operatorname{int}\operatorname{dom}f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The topological-asymptotic regularity profile of a proper convex function records four objects: its epigraph, its finite continuity set, its continuous affine lower supports, and its recession function. Lower semicontinuity is the liminf inequality under norm convergence. The affine-minorant family consists of all continuous affine functions lying below the function everywhere. The recession function records the largest increment produced by a fixed displacement. For a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function, the epigraph is closed, at least one continuous affine minorant exists, and the function is continuous throughout the interior of its effective domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal R(f)=(\operatorname{epi}f,\operatorname{cont}f,\mathcal A(f),\operatorname{rec}f)\) defines the topological-asymptotic regularity data of \(f\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Lower semicontinuity is equivalent to closedness of \(\operatorname{epi}f\) and to closedness of every lower level set.
For closed proper convex \(f\), \(f(x)=\sup_{(u,\alpha)\in\mathcal A(f)}(\langle x,u\rangle+\alpha)\).
special_cases_latex: In finite dimensions, every proper convex function is continuous on \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\).
If \(f\) is finite and lower semicontinuous on all of \(H\), it is continuous everywhere.
immediate_consequences_latex: For convex \(f\), strong, weak, sequential, and weak sequential lower semicontinuity coincide.
\(\operatorname{rec}f\) is positively homogeneous and convex when \(f\in\Gamma_0(H)\).
boundary_notes: In infinite-dimensional spaces, an everywhere-finite convex function need not be continuous without lower semicontinuity or local boundedness.
Continuity at boundary points of \(\operatorname{dom}f\) is not guaranteed.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex hull, lower-semicontinuous hull, and closure of a function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epigraphical definitions and associated convexity and closedness properties for extended-real-valued functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), \(\operatorname{conv}f\) is the greatest convex function majorized by \(f\), equivalently
\[
(\operatorname{conv}f)(x)=\inf\{\alpha:(x,\alpha)\in\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f)\}.
\]
The lower-semicontinuous hull is defined by \(\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{lsc}f)=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{epi}f)\), and \(f\) is lower semicontinuous iff \(\operatorname{lsc}f=f\). Define
\[
(\operatorname{cl}f)(x)=\begin{cases}(\operatorname{lsc}f)(x),& (\operatorname{lsc}f)(y)>-\infty\text{ for every }y\in X,\\-\infty,&(\operatorname{lsc}f)(y)=-\infty\text{ for some }y\in X.
\end{cases}
\]
Then \(f\) is closed iff \(\operatorname{cl}f=f\). A proper convex function is closed iff it is lower semicontinuous; if \(f\) is convex, then \(\operatorname{lsc}f\) and \(\operatorname{cl}f\) are convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex hull of a function is its greatest convex minorant and has an epigraphical formula using the convex hull of the original epigraph. The lower-semicontinuous hull has the closed epigraph. The closure equals that hull unless it takes minus infinity somewhere, in which case the closure is identically minus infinity. Proper convex functions are closed exactly when they are lower semicontinuous, and these hull operations preserve convexity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ proper and convex}\implies\bigl(f\text{ closed}\Longleftrightarrow f\text{ lower semicontinuous}\bigr),\qquad f\text{ convex}\implies\operatorname{lsc}f\text{ and }\operatorname{cl}f\text{ are convex}.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\) be a Hausdorff topological space and let \(f:X\to[-\infty,+\infty]\). Equip \(X\times\mathbb R\) with the product topology.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General Hausdorff-space correspondence; sequences suffice in metrizable spaces, while nets express the fully topological definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[\operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,r)\in X\times\mathbb R:f(x)\leq r\},\qquad \operatorname{lev}_{\leq r}f=\{x\in X:f(x)\leq r\}.\] The function \(f\) is lower semicontinuous if, for every net \((x_a)\) converging to \(x\), \[f(x)\leq\liminf_a f(x_a).\] The epigraphical closedness correspondence is the equivalence \[f\text{ is lower semicontinuous}\iff\operatorname{epi}f\text{ is closed in }X\times\mathbb R\iff (\forall r\in\mathbb R)\;\operatorname{lev}_{\leq r}f\text{ is closed in }X.\] In a metric space, the net condition may equivalently be tested on all convergent sequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an extended-real function on a Hausdorff space, lower semicontinuity means that its value at the limit of every convergent net does not exceed the net's lower limiting values. This is equivalent to the epigraph being closed in the product space, and also equivalent to every lower level set being closed. In metric spaces, convergent sequences provide an equivalent test.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is lower semicontinuous if and only if \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is closed, if and only if every \(\operatorname{lev}_{\leq r}f\) is closed.
equivalent_formulations_latex: At \(x\), lower semicontinuity is equivalent to \((\forall \alpha<f(x))(\exists V\in\mathcal V(x))\;f(V)\subset(\alpha,+\infty]\).
In metric spaces, \(f(x)\leq\liminf_n f(x_n)\) for every \(x_n\to x\) is equivalent to lower semicontinuity.
special_cases_latex: The indicator \(\iota_C\) is lower semicontinuous exactly when \(C\) is closed.
For a convex function on a Hilbert space, norm-lower-semicontinuity is equivalent to weak lower semicontinuity.
immediate_consequences_latex: Arbitrary pointwise suprema of lower-semicontinuous functions are lower semicontinuous.
A lower-semicontinuous function has closed sublevel sets at every real height.
boundary_notes: Sequential lower semicontinuity need not imply lower semicontinuity on a nonsequential topological space.
The correspondence itself does not require convexity or properness.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\) be a Hausdorff topological space and let \(f:X\to[-\infty,+\infty]\). The epigraph is a subset of \(X\times\mathbb R\) with the product topology.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topological definition of a closed function through its epigraph; convexity is an independent property.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) is called epigraphically closed, or simply closed, when \[\operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,r)\in X\times\mathbb R:f(x)\leq r\}\] is a closed subset of \(X\times\mathbb R\). Equivalently, for every net \(x_a\to x\), \[f(x)\leq\liminf_a f(x_a),\] or, equivalently, every lower level set \(\{x:f(x)\leq r\}\) is closed for each \(r\in\mathbb R\). If \(X\) is a normed space and \(f\) is convex, the adjective closed therefore means lower semicontinuous in the ambient norm topology, not merely lower semicontinuous relative to \(\operatorname{dom}f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extended-real function is epigraphically closed when its epigraph is a closed subset of the product of its domain space and the real line. This is equivalent to the lower-semicontinuity liminf inequality and to closedness of every lower level set. For a convex function on a normed space, closedness refers to the ambient topology over the whole space, including approaches from outside the effective domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is closed exactly when \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is closed in \(X\times\mathbb R\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(f\) is closed \(\iff (\forall r\in\mathbb R)\;\{f\leq r\}\) is closed.
In a metric space, \(f\) is closed \(\iff (\forall x_n\to x)\;f(x)\leq\liminf_n f(x_n)\).
special_cases_latex: For \(f=\iota_C\), epigraphical closedness is equivalent to closedness of \(C\).
A continuous real-valued function is epigraphically closed.
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(f\) is closed and convex, then \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is a closed convex set.
The pointwise supremum of any family of closed functions is closed.
boundary_notes: Closedness of \(\operatorname{dom}f\) is neither required nor sufficient for epigraphical closedness.
Relative lower semicontinuity on \(\operatorname{dom}f\) does not control approaches to its boundary from the ambient space.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Lower semicontinuity relative to a subset \(D\subseteq X\) means lower semicontinuity for the subspace topology on \(D\). Since the norm topology is metrizable, norm lower semicontinuity is equivalent to \[x_n\to x\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f(x)\leq\liminf_{n\to\infty}f(x_n).\] Weak lower semicontinuity implies norm lower semicontinuity. Conversely, for convex \(f\), every norm-closed sublevel set is convex and therefore weakly closed; hence norm and weak lower semicontinuity are equivalent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lower semicontinuity may be relative or sequential. For convex functions on Banach spaces, norm and weak lower semicontinuity coincide.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Failure of Norm–Weak Equivalence Without Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infinite-dimensional counterexample showing the necessity of convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space, \(S=\{x\in H:\|x\|=1\}\), and \(f=\iota_S\). The set \(S\) is norm closed, so \(f\) is norm-lower-semicontinuous. If \((e_n)\) is orthonormal, then \(e_n\rightharpoonup0\), but \[f(0)=+\infty>0=\liminf_n f(e_n).\] Hence \(f\) is not weakly lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The unit-sphere indicator is norm-lower-semicontinuous but not weakly lower-semicontinuous, showing that convexity is essential.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\iota_S\) is norm-lower-semicontinuous but not weakly lower-semicontinuous.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong, weak, sequential, and relative lower semicontinuity
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(D\subset H\), and let \(f:H\to[-\infty,+\infty]\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space taxonomy distinguishing ambient versus relative topology, strong versus weak topology, and nets versus sequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At \(x\in H\), \(f\) is strongly lower semicontinuous if every net \(x_a\to x\) in norm satisfies \(f(x)\leq\liminf_a f(x_a)\); it is weakly lower semicontinuous if every net \(x_a\rightharpoonup x\) satisfies the same inequality. Replacing nets by sequences defines strong sequential and weak sequential lower semicontinuity. Relative lower semicontinuity on \(D\) means that the corresponding condition is imposed only on nets or sequences contained in \(D\), with convergence in the subspace topology. Global lower semicontinuity means the selected condition holds at every point of \(H\). For convex \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), the four ambient regimes—strong, strong sequential, weak, and weak sequential—are equivalent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lower semicontinuity has several regimes. Strong lower semicontinuity uses norm-convergent nets, while weak lower semicontinuity uses weakly convergent nets. Sequential variants test only sequences. Relative lower semicontinuity restricts the approaching points to a specified subset and uses its subspace topology. A regime is global when it holds at every ambient point. For convex extended-real functions on a Hilbert space that never take negative infinity, all four ambient strong, weak, net, and sequential regimes coincide.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The selected convergence class determines the lower-semicontinuity regime through \(f(x)\leq\liminf f(x_a)\); for convex \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), the four ambient Hilbert-space regimes coincide.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Strong lower semicontinuity is equivalent to norm-closedness of \(\operatorname{epi}f\).
Weak lower semicontinuity is equivalent to weak closedness of \(\operatorname{epi}f\) in \(H\times\mathbb R\).
special_cases_latex: In metric spaces, strong lower semicontinuity and strong sequential lower semicontinuity coincide for arbitrary functions.
For convex functions on Hilbert space, norm-closed convex level sets are also weakly closed.
immediate_consequences_latex: Weak lower semicontinuity implies strong lower semicontinuity because norm convergence implies weak convergence.
For convex Hilbert-space functions, verifying any one of the four ambient regimes verifies them all.
boundary_notes: Relative lower semicontinuity on \(D\) need not imply ambient lower semicontinuity at boundary points of \(D\).
Outside sequential spaces, sequential lower semicontinuity can be strictly weaker than net-based lower semicontinuity.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relative Continuity on the Domain in One Dimension
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The result is specific to extended-real proper closed convex functions on the real line. It asserts sequential continuity relative to the effective domain, including its finite boundary points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper, closed, and convex, and let \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f\). Then, for every sequence \((x_k)\subseteq\operatorname{dom}f\) satisfying \(x_k\to\bar x\),
\[
f(x_k)\to f(\bar x).
\]
Thus \(f\) is continuous at \(\bar x\) relative to \(\operatorname{dom}f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every proper closed convex extended-real function on the real line is continuous relative to its effective domain at every point of that domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(x_k)\to f(\bar x).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lower-semicontinuous convex envelope and affine minorants
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(f:H\to[-\infty,+\infty]\). Pointwise ordering of extended-real functions is used.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space closed convex envelope, including the affine-minorant representation when continuous affine minorants exist.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The lower-semicontinuous convex envelope of \(f\) is \[\breve f=\sup\{g:g\leq f,\ g\text{ is lower semicontinuous and convex}\}.\] It is the greatest lower-semicontinuous convex function majorized by \(f\), and \(\operatorname{epi}\breve f\) is closed and convex. Define the affine-minorant family \[\mathcal A_f=\{(u,\alpha)\in H\times\mathbb R:\langle x,u\rangle+\alpha\leq f(x)\ \forall x\in H\}.\] If \(f\) possesses a continuous affine minorant, then \[\breve f(x)=f^{**}(x)=\sup_{(u,\alpha)\in\mathcal A_f}\bigl(\langle x,u\rangle+\alpha\bigr).\] Thus closed convexification is equivalently the supremal calculus of all continuous affine lower supports.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lower-semicontinuous convex envelope of a function is the pointwise supremum of all lower-semicontinuous convex functions lying below it. It is therefore the largest closed convex minorant. When the original function admits at least one continuous affine minorant, the envelope equals its biconjugate and can be computed as the supremum of all continuous affine functions lying below the original function everywhere.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\breve f=\sup\{g\leq f:g\text{ is lower semicontinuous and convex}\}\), and, when \(\mathcal A_f\ne\varnothing\), \(\breve f=f^{**}=\sup_{(u,\alpha)\in\mathcal A_f}(\langle\cdot,u\rangle+\alpha)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\breve f\) is characterized by \(\breve f\leq f\) and \(g\leq\breve f\) for every lower-semicontinuous convex \(g\leq f\).
When an affine minorant exists, \(\operatorname{epi}\breve f=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(\operatorname{epi}f)\) under the standard properness conditions.
special_cases_latex: If \(f\) is already lower semicontinuous and convex, then \(\breve f=f\).
For a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function, \(f\) is the supremum of its continuous affine minorants.
immediate_consequences_latex: The envelope operator is monotone: \(f\leq h\Rightarrow\breve f\leq\breve h\).
The envelope is idempotent: \(\breve{\breve f}=\breve f\).
boundary_notes: If no continuous affine minorant exists, the affine supremum may degenerate and must not be substituted for the defining envelope without qualification.
The envelope is a minorant of \(f\), despite occasional terminology calling it a hull.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper. Assume that the indicated families of minorants are nonempty.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise hierarchy of convexification and lower-semicontinuous convexification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The convex envelope and lower-semicontinuous convex envelope of \(f\) are respectively \[\operatorname{conv}f=\sup\{g:g\leq f,\ g\text{ convex}\}\] and \[\overline{\operatorname{conv}}f=\sup\{g:g\leq f,\ g\text{ convex and lower semicontinuous}\}.\] They satisfy the hull hierarchy \[\overline{\operatorname{conv}}f\leq\operatorname{conv}f\leq f.\] Epigraphically, under the usual properness and affine-minorization condition, \[\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{conv}f)=\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f),\qquad \operatorname{epi}(\overline{\operatorname{conv}}f)=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(\operatorname{epi}f),\] with vertical completion implicit in the epigraph convention. The closed convex envelope is also \(f^{**}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex envelope of a proper function is the greatest convex function below it. The closed convex envelope is the greatest function below it that is both convex and lower semicontinuous. The closed convex envelope lies below the convex envelope, which lies below the original function. Under the standard affine-minorization condition, their epigraphs are the convex hull and closed convex hull of the original epigraph, and the closed convex envelope equals the Fenchel biconjugate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\overline{\operatorname{conv}}f\leq\operatorname{conv}f\leq f\), with \(\overline{\operatorname{conv}}f=f^{**}\) when \(f\) has a continuous affine minorant.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}f\) is the pointwise supremum of convex minorants of \(f\).
\(\overline{\operatorname{conv}}f\) is the pointwise supremum of lower-semicontinuous convex minorants of \(f\).
special_cases_latex: If \(f\) is convex, then \(\operatorname{conv}f=f\).
If \(f\in\Gamma_0(H)\), then \(\overline{\operatorname{conv}}f=\operatorname{conv}f=f\).
For \(f=\iota_S\), the envelopes correspond to indicators of \(\operatorname{conv}S\) and \(\overline{\operatorname{conv}}S\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Both hull operators are monotone and idempotent on their respective fixed-point classes.
Closed convexification can change boundary values and can enlarge the effective domain to points represented by closed convex epigraph limits.
boundary_notes: The epigraph identities require attention to improper degeneracies and the existence of affine minorants.
Convexification alone need not produce a lower-semicontinuous function.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Whenever the stated hulls remain \((-\infty,+\infty]\)-valued, \[f\le g\Longrightarrow \operatorname{cl}f\le\operatorname{cl}g,\qquad \operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{cl}f)=\operatorname{cl}f.\] Moreover, \(\operatorname{cl}f=f\) if and only if \(f\) is lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lower-semicontinuous hull formation is monotone, idempotent, and fixes exactly the lower-semicontinuous functions.
assumptions_latex: \(f,g:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) have hulls in the stated codomain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Hull formation is monotone and idempotent, with lower-semicontinuous functions as its fixed points.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If the lower-semicontinuous hull does not take the value \(-\infty\), then \[\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{cl}f)=\overline{\operatorname{epi}f}\] in \(X\times\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subject to exclusion of minus-infinity degeneration, the epigraph of the lower-semicontinuous hull is the closure of the original epigraph.
assumptions_latex: The greatest lower-semicontinuous minorant of \(f\) is \((-\infty,+\infty]\)-valued.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure-Operator Laws for the Lower-Semicontinuous Hull
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order-theoretic laws of lower-semicontinuous regularization, without convexification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For extended-real functions \(f,g:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) whose lower-semicontinuous hulls remain in this codomain, \[f\le g\Longrightarrow \operatorname{cl}f\le \operatorname{cl}g,\qquad \operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{cl}f)=\operatorname{cl}f.\] Moreover, \(\operatorname{cl}f=f\) if and only if \(f\) is lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lower-semicontinuous hull formation is monotone and idempotent, and its fixed points are exactly the lower-semicontinuous functions.
assumptions_latex: \(f,g:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) have lower-semicontinuous hulls in the stated codomain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{cl}\) is monotone and idempotent, with lower-semicontinuous functions as its fixed points.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure or Lower-Semicontinuous Hull of a Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General extended-real definition; the hull's codomain permits both infinite values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\), its closure or lower-semicontinuous hull \(\operatorname{cl}f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{\pm\infty\}\) is defined by \[(\operatorname{cl}f)(x):=\liminf_{y\to x}f(y),\qquad x\in\mathbb{R}^n.\] Equivalently, \[\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{cl}f)=\overline{\operatorname{epi}f}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lower-semicontinuous hull is the pointwise lower limit of the function and, equivalently, its epigraph is the closure of the original epigraph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\operatorname{cl}f)(x)=\liminf_{y\to x}f(y),\qquad \operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{cl}f)=\overline{\operatorname{epi}f}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent representations of the closed convex hull
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional closed convexification through closed epigraph hulls, closed convex minorants, and affine minorants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(g:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be not identically \(+\infty\) and admit an affine minorant. Define
\[
\bar f_1(x)=\inf\{r:(x,r)\in\overline{\operatorname{co}}(\operatorname{epi}g)\},
\]
\[
\bar f_2(x)=\sup\{h(x):h\text{ is closed and convex on }\mathbb R^n,\ h\le g\},
\]
and
\[
\bar f_3(x)=\sup\{\langle s,x\rangle-b:\langle s,y\rangle-b\le g(y)\text{ for all }y\in\mathbb R^n\}.
\]
Then \(\bar f_1,\bar f_2,\bar f_3\) are closed and convex, coincide on \(\mathbb R^n\), and equal \(\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{co}g)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper extended-real function with an affine lower bound, its closed convex hull is equivalently obtained from the closed convex hull of its epigraph, as the supremum of its closed convex minorants, or as the supremum of all affine minorants.
assumptions_latex: \exists(s,b)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R\ \forall x\in\mathbb R^n:\ g(x)\ge\langle s,x\rangle-b
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar f_1=\bar f_2=\bar f_3=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{co}g),\qquad \bar f_i\text{ is closed and convex for }i=1,2,3.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: First form the convex envelope \[\operatorname{conv}f(x)=\inf\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{n+1}\lambda_i f(x_i):x_i\in X,\ \lambda_i\geq0,\ \sum_{i=1}^{n+1}\lambda_i=1,\ \sum_{i=1}^{n+1}\lambda_i x_i=x\right\}\qquad(x\in X).\] This is the greatest convex minorant of \(f\), but it need not be lower semicontinuous. Applying lower-semicontinuous closure afterward yields \[\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}f)=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}f=f^{**}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, the convex envelope is represented by finite convex combinations. Taking its lower-semicontinuous hull then gives the closed convex envelope and the Fenchel biconjugate.

Let \(f=\delta_{(0,1)}:\mathbb R\to(-\infty,+\infty]\). Since \((0,1)\) is convex,
\[\operatorname{conv}f=f=\delta_{(0,1)},\]
but \(f\) is not lower semicontinuous and
\[\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}f)=\delta_{[0,1]}.\]

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The closed convex hull \(\operatorname{clconv}f\) is proper if and only if there exist \(a\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(b\in\mathbb{R}\) such that \(\langle a,x\rangle+b\leq f(x)\) for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\). Thus properness of \(f\) alone does not ensure properness of its closed convex hull. For example, if \(f(x)=-x^2\) on \(\mathbb{R}\), then no finite affine function minorizes \(f\) globally, and \(\operatorname{clconv}f\equiv-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper function has a proper closed convex hull exactly when it has a global affine lower bound; the function minus x squared shows failure otherwise.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Continuous affine minorant and exact affine support
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global continuous affine lower bounds, with exactness at a specified point distinguished from mere minorization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A continuous affine function \(a:H\to\mathbb R\) is an affine minorant of \(f\) if there exist \(u\in H\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\) such that \[a(y)=\langle y,u\rangle+\alpha\leq f(y)\qquad(\forall y\in H).\] It is exact at \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\) if additionally \(a(x)=f(x)\), equivalently \[f(y)\geq f(x)+\langle y-x,u\rangle\qquad(\forall y\in H).\] In this case \(u\) is a subgradient of \(f\) at \(x\). Every \(f\in\Gamma_0(H)\) possesses at least one continuous affine minorant, and if \(x\in\operatorname{int}\operatorname{dom}f\), it possesses one exact at \(x\). Moreover, such an \(f\) is the pointwise supremum of all its continuous affine minorants.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous affine minorant of a proper function is a continuous affine function lying below it at every point. It is exact at a point when it also matches the function there. Exact minorization is the subgradient inequality. Every proper lower-semicontinuous convex function on a Hilbert space has at least one continuous affine minorant; at every interior point of its domain it has an exact one. The function itself is the pointwise supremum of all these affine minorants.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a(y)=\langle y,u\rangle+\alpha\) minorizes \(f\) exactly when \(a\leq f\); it is exact at \(x\) exactly when \(f(y)\geq f(x)+\langle y-x,u\rangle\) for all \(y\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(f\) has an affine minorant with slope \(u\) iff \(f-\langle\cdot,u\rangle\) is bounded below.
Exact affine minorization at \(x\) is equivalent to \(u\in\partial f(x)\).
special_cases_latex: A differentiable convex function has the exact affine minorant \(y\mapsto f(x)+\langle y-x,\nabla f(x)\rangle\).
For \(f=\iota_C\), exact affine minorants at \(x\in C\) correspond to normal vectors to \(C\) at \(x\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A proper lower-semicontinuous convex function is bounded below on every bounded subset of \(H\).
For \(f\in\Gamma_0(H)\), \(f=\sup\{a:a\text{ is a continuous affine minorant of }f\}\).
boundary_notes: Exact affine minorants need not exist at arbitrary boundary points of the effective domain.
A discontinuous linear functional on an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space can have no continuous affine minorant.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine-envelope representation of closed proper convex functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation by affine supports, including interior support existence and the linear-support specialization for sublinear functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}} be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. Then f is the pointwise supremum of its affine supports. If \operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\neq\varnothing, an affine support exists at every \bar x\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f). Equivalently, a function g:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}} is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex if and only if g is the pointwise supremum of a nonempty family of affine functions and g\not\equiv+\infty. If f is proper, lower semicontinuous, and sublinear, its supporting affine functions are linear. Conversely, the pointwise supremum of any nonempty family of linear functions is a proper, lower-semicontinuous, sublinear function.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper closed convex function is the pointwise supremum of its affine lower supports and has a support at each interior domain point. Conversely, a nonempty affine envelope that is not everywhere positive infinity is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. For proper closed sublinear functions the supports are linear, and every nonempty supremum of linear functions is proper, lower semicontinuous, and sublinear.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed realization of a convex function operation
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(\Phi\) be an operation producing an extended-real function from inputs \((f_i)_{i\in I}\), and let \(\breve g\) denote the lower-semicontinuous convex envelope of \(g\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of closure calculus as post-operation closed convex regularization; exact commutation laws require operation-specific qualification conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The closed realization of a function operation \(\Phi\) is defined by \[\overline{\Phi}(f_i:i\in I)=\breve{\bigl(\Phi(f_i:i\in I)\bigr)}.\] Thus \(\overline{\Phi}\) is the greatest lower-semicontinuous convex function lying below the raw output \(\Phi(f_i)\). For pointwise supremum, closure is unnecessary when every input is lower semicontinuous and convex: \[\sup_{i\in I}f_i\in\Gamma(H).\] For positive finite sums with compatible proper domains, the sum is likewise closed and convex. For operations involving infima, infimal convolution, linear images, or marginalization, the raw output can fail to be lower semicontinuous; its canonical closed value is therefore its envelope \(\breve{\Phi(f_i)}\), equivalently its biconjugate when a continuous affine minorant exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given any operation on extended-real functions, its closed realization is obtained by applying the lower-semicontinuous convex envelope to the operation's raw output. This produces the largest closed convex function below that output. Pointwise suprema of closed convex functions are already closed and convex, and compatible finite positive sums are also closed. Infimum-type operations, infimal convolutions, images, and marginal functions may lose closedness, so closure must generally be applied unless a qualification condition guarantees exact preservation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\overline{\Phi}(f_i)=\breve{\Phi(f_i)}\) defines the closure calculus for \(\Phi\); when \(\Phi(f_i)\in\Gamma(H)\), \(\overline{\Phi}(f_i)=\Phi(f_i)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(\Phi(f_i)\) has a continuous affine minorant, then \(\overline{\Phi}(f_i)=\Phi(f_i)^{**}\).
Epigraphically, the closed realization replaces the raw epigraph by its closed convex hull under the standard properness conditions.
special_cases_latex: For \(g=\sup_i f_i\) with \(f_i\in\Gamma(H)\), \(\breve g=g\).
For a finite positive sum of lower-semicontinuous convex functions with nonempty common domain, the raw sum is lower semicontinuous and convex.
immediate_consequences_latex: Closed realization is idempotent: \(\breve{\breve g}=\breve g\).
No closure correction occurs precisely when the raw output is already lower semicontinuous and convex.
boundary_notes: Closure does not generally commute with infimum, image, or infimal convolution without additional assumptions.
The definition records the canonical regularized output and does not assert an unconditional algebraic identity between separate closures and the closure of an operation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Epigraphic Closure and Convex Closure of a Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines function closure and closed convex closure epigraphically and records the closedness and domain gaps possible before closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(f:X\to[-\infty,\infty]\). The closure \(\operatorname{cl}f\) is defined by \(\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{cl}f)=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{epi}f)\), equivalently \((\operatorname{cl}f)(x)=\inf\{w\mid (x,w)\in\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{epi}f)\}\). The convex closure \(\overline{\operatorname{co}}f\) is defined by \(\operatorname{epi}(\overline{\operatorname{co}}f)=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f))\). If \(F(x)=\inf\{w\mid (x,w)\in\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f)\}\), then \(F\) is convex and \(\operatorname{cl}F=\overline{\operatorname{co}}f\). The function \(F\) need not be closed, and \(\operatorname{dom}F\) may be strictly contained in \(\operatorname{dom}(\overline{\operatorname{co}}f)\), although their domain closures coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closing an epigraph defines the closure of a function, while closing the convex hull of the epigraph defines its convex closure. The function generated by the unclosed convex hull is convex but may be nonclosed and may have a smaller domain, although the two domain closures coincide.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{cl}f)=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{epi}f),\quad \operatorname{epi}(\overline{\operatorname{co}}f)=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f)),\quad \operatorname{cl}F=\overline{\operatorname{co}}f,\quad \operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{dom}F)=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{dom}(\overline{\operatorname{co}}f)).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines closure by closing the epigraph and convex closure by taking the closed convex hull of the epigraph; it also records the nonclosed intermediate convexification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(f:X\to[-\infty,\infty]\). Define the closure \(\operatorname{cl}f:\mathbb R^n\to[-\infty,\infty]\) by \[(\operatorname{cl}f)(x)=\inf\{w\in\mathbb R:(x,w)\in\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{epi}f)\}.\] Then \(\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{cl}f)=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{epi}f)\); if \(f\) is convex, \(\operatorname{cl}f\) is closed and convex. The convex closure \(\overline{\operatorname{co}}f\) is defined by \[\operatorname{epi}(\overline{\operatorname{co}}f)=\operatorname{cl}\!\left(\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f)\right).\] If \[F(x)=\inf\{w\in\mathbb R:(x,w)\in\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f)\},\] then \(F\) is convex and \(\overline{\operatorname{co}}f=\operatorname{cl}F\). The function \(F\) need not be closed, and \(\operatorname{dom}F\) may be strictly contained in \(\operatorname{dom}(\overline{\operatorname{co}}f)\), although their domain closures coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closing a function's epigraph defines its closure, while closing the convex hull of its epigraph defines its convex closure. The function induced by the unclosed convex hull is convex but may be nonclosed and may have a strictly smaller domain than its closure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{cl}f)=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{epi}f),\qquad \operatorname{epi}(\overline{\operatorname{co}}f)=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f))

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local convex continuity and boundedness regimes
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, and fix \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise Hilbert-space correspondence for proper convex functions; local boundedness means boundedness on a norm neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The following four local regularity conditions at \(x_0\) define the same regime: \[(i)\ f\text{ is locally Lipschitz near }x_0;\qquad (ii)\ f\text{ is continuous at }x_0;\] \[(iii)\ f\text{ is bounded on a neighborhood of }x_0;\qquad (iv)\ f\text{ is bounded above on a neighborhood of }x_0.\] Explicitly, condition (iv) means that there exist \(\rho>0\) and \(M\in\mathbb R\) such that \(f(x)\leq M\) for every \(x\in B(x_0;\rho)\). Local Lipschitz continuity means that there exist \(r>0\) and \(L\geq0\) such that \[|f(x)-f(y)|\leq L\|x-y\|\qquad(x,y\in B(x_0;r)).\] If these equivalent conditions hold at one point, then \(f\) is locally Lipschitz throughout \(\operatorname{int}\operatorname{dom}f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper convex function on a Hilbert space, four pointwise notions coincide: local Lipschitz continuity, continuity, boundedness on a neighborhood, and boundedness above on a neighborhood. Local upper boundedness requires one finite upper bound on some norm ball around the point. Local Lipschitz continuity requires a uniform Lipschitz constant on a possibly smaller ball. Once this regime occurs, the function is locally Lipschitz at every point in the interior of its effective domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At \(x_0\), local Lipschitz continuity, continuity, local boundedness, and local upper boundedness of proper convex \(f\) are equivalent.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x_0\in\operatorname{cont}f\iff(\exists\rho>0)\;\sup_{B(x_0;\rho)}f<+\infty\).
Under any equivalent condition, \(x_0\in\operatorname{int}\operatorname{dom}f\).
special_cases_latex: If \(f\in\Gamma_0(H)\), then \(\operatorname{cont}f=\operatorname{int}\operatorname{dom}f\).
In finite dimensions, every proper convex function is continuous on \(\operatorname{int}\operatorname{dom}f\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A locally upper-bounded convex function is automatically locally bounded below as well.
On compact subsets of the relative interior in finite dimensions, a proper convex function is Lipschitz.
boundary_notes: The correspondence is local and does not imply a global Lipschitz constant.
At boundary points of the effective domain, local boundedness and continuity can fail.
