children.title: Nonconvex-Domain Obstructions
children.top_down_role: Failure of segment and local-to-global reasoning on nonconvex domains.

assumptions_latex: \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) is given by \(f(x)=0\) on \((-2,-1)\) and \(f(x)=1\) on \((1,2)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Although \(f''(x)=0\) throughout \(C\), the global supporting inequality fails for points in different components; hence local curvature does not imply a global first-order criterion on a nonconvex domain.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Disconnected-domain counterexample to local-to-global differential recognition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function is smooth on the open set \(C\) and satisfies \(f''(x)=0\) for every \(x\in C\). Nevertheless, taking \(x\in(1,2)\) and \(y\in(-2,-1)\) gives \[f(y)=0<1=f(x)+f'(x)(y-x).\] Thus the global supporting-affine inequality fails. Convexity of the domain, or an explicit restriction to segments contained in the domain, is indispensable in local-to-global recognition theorems.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A disconnected domain can support zero local curvature everywhere while global supporting inequalities between components fail.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex-Domain Obstructions

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Segment obstruction on a nonconvex domain
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and let \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\). For \(x,y\in D\), write \([x,y]=\{(1-t)x+ty:t\in[0,1]\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Domain-level obstruction to ordinary convexity and to segment-based local-to-global recognition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The segment-obstruction set of \(D\) is
\[
\mathcal{O}(D):=\{(x,y,t)\in D\times D\times(0,1):(1-t)x+ty\notin D\}.
\]
The domain has a nonconvex-domain obstruction exactly when \(\mathcal{O}(D)\neq\varnothing\), equivalently when \(D\) is not convex. For every obstructed triple, the usual convexity inequality
\[
f((1-t)x+ty)\leq(1-t)f(x)+tf(y)
\]
is not even evaluable as an inequality for \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\). Consequently, line-restriction and local-to-global arguments apply only within convex components or to pairs whose entire segment remains in \(D\), unless \(f\) and its domain are extended.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonconvex-domain obstruction is a pair of domain points together with an intermediate weight whose convex combination leaves the domain. Such an obstruction exists exactly when the domain is nonconvex. At that triple, the ordinary convexity inequality cannot be evaluated because the function has no value at the intermediate point. Segment-based recognition therefore cannot compare all pairs without restricting the domain or extending the function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal{O}(D)\neq\varnothing\Longleftrightarrow D\) is nonconvex, and every \((x,y,t)\in\mathcal{O}(D)\) blocks evaluation of the ordinary convexity inequality.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(D\) is convex if and only if \(\mathcal{O}(D)=\varnothing\).
The obstruction is equivalently the existence of \(x,y\in D\) with \([x,y]\nsubseteq D\).
special_cases_latex: If \(D\) is a union of two disjoint convex sets, cross-component pairs ordinarily generate obstructions.
A convex subset \(C\subseteq D\) has no internal segment obstruction even when \(D\) itself is nonconvex.
immediate_consequences_latex: Convexity can be assessed separately on convex subsets of \(D\), but those local assessments do not impose cross-subset inequalities.
A Hessian or gradient condition checked locally on disconnected pieces does not by itself supply a global convex-function structure on \(D\).
boundary_notes: Some authors study functions convex on every segment contained in a nonconvex domain; that is a restricted notion and is not ordinary convexity on a convex domain.
Extending \(f\) by \(+\infty\) does not yield a convex extended-real function unless its effective domain becomes convex.

notation.meaning: The set of triples witnessing failure of segment closure in \(D\).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The function \(f\) is convex but has neither a gradient nor a classical Hessian at \(0\), so classical derivative criteria are inapplicable there.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f(x)=|x|\) is convex on \(\mathbb{R}\), but \(f'(0)\) and \(f''(0)\) do not exist. Consequently, gradient monotonicity and Hessian semidefiniteness cannot be imposed pointwise on the whole domain. Nonsmooth recognition instead uses \[\partial f(0)=[-1,1],\] whose elements generate supporting affine minorants at the nondifferentiable point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex absolute-value function is not differentiable at zero, so gradient and Hessian tests must be replaced by subgradient criteria.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex and let \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\). Derivatives are understood only at points having an appropriate open neighborhood on which \(f\) is defined.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional nonsmooth boundary of gradient- and Hessian-based convexity recognition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the first- and second-derivative failure sets by
\[
N_1(f;C):=\{x\in C:f\text{ is not differentiable at }x\},
\]
\[
N_2(f;C):=\{x\in C:f\text{ is not twice differentiable at }x\}.
\]
The gradient recognition regime applies globally only when \(N_1(f;C)=\varnothing\) and differentiability holds on an open neighborhood of \(C\). The classical Hessian regime applies globally only when \(N_2(f;C)=\varnothing\) under the corresponding open-domain hypothesis. When these sets are nonempty, convexity remains meaningful, but the missing gradient or Hessian cannot be used at those points; subgradient or directional formulations are the appropriate replacements.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The missing-gradient set contains points where the function is not differentiable, and the missing-Hessian set contains points where it is not twice differentiable. A global gradient test requires the first set to be empty, while a global classical Hessian test requires the second set to be empty, together with the relevant open-domain assumptions. Convexity itself does not require either derivative, so nonsmooth points call for subgradients or directional derivatives rather than rejection of convexity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Gradient and Hessian criteria are inapplicable respectively on \(N_1(f;C)\) and \(N_2(f;C)\); these failures do not imply nonconvexity.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x\in N_1(f;C)\) when no single linear map gives the first-order approximation required by differentiability at \(x\).
\(x\in N_2(f;C)\) when the classical Hessian needed by the second-order criterion is undefined at \(x\).
special_cases_latex: For \(f(t)=|t|\), \(0\in N_1(f;\mathbb{R})\), although \(f\) is convex.
A differentiable convex function can still belong to the missing-Hessian regime at points where it is not twice differentiable.
immediate_consequences_latex: At a convex nonsmooth point, \(\partial f(x)\) may replace the missing gradient.
For convex functions, one-sided directional derivatives exist throughout the interior of the effective domain even when the gradient does not.
boundary_notes: Almost-everywhere differentiability does not justify a gradient inequality at exceptional points.
A Hessian condition holding wherever the Hessian exists needs additional regularity before it becomes a global convexity criterion.

notation.meaning: The set of points at which the gradient regime fails.
The set of points at which the classical Hessian regime fails.

children.title: Restricted Convexity-Test Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Insufficient evidence confined to restricted points, directions, or boundary regions.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coverage boundary for restricted convexity tests
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex. Let \(P\subseteq C\times C\) be a set of tested ordered pairs and let \(Q\subseteq C\times\mathbb{R}^n\) be a set of tested point-direction pairs.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formalizes insufficiency caused by checking supporting inequalities or curvature only on restricted points, directions, or boundary regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A pairwise first-order test has complete coverage when \(P=C\times C\); otherwise its coverage gap is
\[
G_P:=(C\times C)\setminus P.
\]
A directional second-order test has complete coverage when, for every \(x\in C\), it includes every direction required by the relevant tangent or affine-hull space \(V_x\); its gap is
\[
G_Q:=\{(x,d):x\in C,\ d\in V_x\}\setminus Q.
\]
The restricted convexity-test failure boundary is reached when \(G_P\neq\varnothing\) or \(G_Q\neq\varnothing\): satisfaction of the certificate on \(P\) or \(Q\) alone is then a restricted certificate, not the universally quantified convexity criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A first-order convexity test is fully covering only when it checks every ordered pair of points required by the criterion. A directional curvature test is fully covering only when it checks every required feasible direction at every point. Any omitted pair or direction forms a coverage gap. Passing a test on a set with a nonempty gap is only restricted evidence and is not, by itself, the standard global convexity certificate.
assumptions_latex: The full first- or second-order criterion being approximated is specified.
\(V_x\) is the ambient direction space on an open domain or the appropriate relative tangent space on a restricted domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A restricted test crosses its failure boundary when \(G_P\neq\varnothing\) or \(G_Q\neq\varnothing\); passing such a test does not equal the full universally quantified certificate.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Complete first-order coverage means every inequality \(f(y)\geq f(x)+\langle g_x,y-x\rangle\) required by the criterion is tested.
Complete Hessian coverage means the quadratic form is nonnegative for every required direction, not merely for a spanning list of directions.
special_cases_latex: Testing only coordinate directions can miss a negative quadratic-form direction with mixed coordinates.
Testing only interior points does not automatically control arbitrary boundary values without a continuity or closure argument.
immediate_consequences_latex: A nonempty coverage gap identifies exactly which universal quantifiers remain uncertified.
Additional structure may close a coverage gap, but that structure must be stated as a separate hypothesis.
boundary_notes: Testing a basis of directions is insufficient for a general quadratic inequality; all directions or an equivalent matrix certificate are required.
Dense-set testing can be sufficient under continuity, but density alone is not the standard certificate.

notation.meaning: The omitted ordered point pairs in a first-order test.
The omitted feasible point-direction pairs in a curvature test.

children.title: Incomplete Local Tests
children.top_down_role: Pointwise or neighborhood evidence too limited to establish global convexity.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Although \(f''(x)>0\) on \(S\), the function is not convex on \(\mathbb{R}\); therefore a curvature test that omits part of the domain is incomplete.

notation.meaning: Subset on which curvature is inspected.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A positive-curvature test on an incomplete region misses nonconvexity elsewhere.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Direct differentiation yields \(f''(x)=12x^2-2\), so \(f''(x)>0\) for every \(x\in S\). However, \(f''(0)=-2<0\). Equivalently, since \(f(-1/2)=f(1/2)=-3/16\), one has \[f(0)=0>\frac{f(-1/2)+f(1/2)}{2}=-\frac{3}{16},\] which violates midpoint convexity. Hence curvature verified only on \(S\) cannot certify global convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive curvature on a tested subset does not certify convexity when an untested region contains negative curvature.
knowledge_statements.title: Incomplete Local Tests

children.title: Boundary-Only Tests
children.top_down_role: Evidence confined to domain boundaries without control of interior chords.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The restriction of \(f\) to \(\partial C\) is constant, but \(f\) is not convex on \(C\); boundary values alone do not certify interior convexity.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constant boundary data conceal strictly concave interior behavior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in\partial C\), one has \(f(x)=0\), so every comparison using only boundary values is compatible with an affine, hence convex, function. Yet \(f(0)=1\), while for any unit vector \(u\), \[f(0)=1>\frac{f(u)+f(-u)}{2}=0.\] Therefore \(f\) violates the midpoint convexity inequality on \(C\), despite its constant boundary restriction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function can be constant on a convex body's boundary yet strictly concave inside, so boundary-only tests cannot certify convexity.
knowledge_statements.title: Boundary-Only Tests

children.title: Restricted-Direction Tests
children.top_down_role: Directional checks that omit portions of the required line geometry.

assumptions_latex: Convexity is tested only along lines parallel to the coordinate axes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every tested line restriction is affine, but \(f\) is not convex on \(\mathbb{R}^2\); the tested directions do not determine full curvature.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate-line convexity does not control mixed curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For fixed \(x\in\mathbb{R}^2\), both maps \(t\mapsto f(x+te_1)\) and \(t\mapsto f(x+te_2)\) are affine, hence convex. However, \[\nabla^2f(x)=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\] has eigenvalues \(1\) and \(-1\). Equivalently, with \(a=(1,-1)\) and \(b=(-1,1)\), \[f((a+b)/2)=0>\frac{f(a)+f(b)}{2}=-1.\] Thus coordinate-direction tests miss nonconvex mixed directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The bilinear function is affine along every coordinate line but nonconvex along diagonal directions.
knowledge_statements.title: Restricted-Direction Tests

children.title: Sparse-Sample Ambiguity
children.top_down_role: Finite observations compatible with both convex and nonconvex extensions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is nonconvex although its restriction to \(S\) is indistinguishable from the convex zero function.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete failure of every convexity test using only finitely many function values.

Choose \(\varepsilon>0\) with \(a-\varepsilon,a+\varepsilon\ne a\). The convexity inequality fails because \[f(a)=1>0=\tfrac12f(a-\varepsilon)+\tfrac12f(a+\varepsilon).\]

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: For each \(i\in I\), let \(f_i:X_i\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be a proper convex function on a finite-dimensional real vector space, and let \(\Phi\) be an operation producing a function \(F=\Phi((f_i)_{i\in I})\) on a specified domain \(X\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract closure notion for operations on extended-real convex functions, including algebraic, supremal, affine-composition, and partial-minimization constructions with their domain qualifications.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An operation \(\Phi\) is convexity preserving on an admissible class \(\mathcal{D}\) when
\[
(f_i)_{i\in I}\in\mathcal{D},\quad f_i\text{ convex for every }i
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
F:=\Phi((f_i)_{i\in I})\text{ is convex}.
\]
Admissibility includes every condition needed for \(F\) to be well-defined and proper, such as a common finite point for a sum or a nonempty effective domain after composition. Standard instances include nonnegative sums, affine precomposition, pointwise suprema, increasing-convex scalar postcomposition, perspectives, and partial minimization of jointly convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function operation is convexity preserving when every admissible tuple of convex input functions is mapped to a convex output function. The admissible class records domain and properness conditions needed to make the result meaningful. Nonnegative sums, affine pullbacks, pointwise suprema, suitable compositions, perspectives, and partial minimization are standard examples, but each carries its own qualifications.
assumptions_latex: Every input \(f_i\) is convex on its stated domain.
The tuple belongs to the operation's admissible class \(\mathcal{D}\).
The output is not identically \(+\infty\) when properness is part of the function class.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Phi\) is convexity preserving exactly when convex admissible inputs always imply convexity of \(\Phi((f_i))\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The class of convex functions is closed under \(\Phi\) on \(\mathcal{D}\).
For every admissible convex input tuple, the epigraph of the output is convex.
special_cases_latex: If \(F=\sum_i\lambda_i f_i\) with \(\lambda_i\geq0\), then \(\Phi\) is convexity preserving subject to properness.
If \(F=f\circ A\) with affine \(A\), then convexity is preserved whenever the image of \(A\) meets \(\operatorname{dom}f\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Preserving operations generate new convex functions from certified convex primitives.
Convexity preservation and closedness preservation are distinct properties and may require different qualifications.
boundary_notes: Negative scalar multiplication is not convexity preserving in general.
An operation may preserve convexity while failing to preserve properness or closedness.

notation.meaning: An operation that maps one or more functions to an output function.
The admissible input class, including domain qualifications.

children.title: Algebraic Operations
children.top_down_role: Scaling, translation, addition, and the boundary of generally nonpreserving algebraic operations.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f_1,\ldots,f_m:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper convex functions, let \(\lambda_i\geq0\), let \(a\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and let \(\beta\in\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite algebraic constructions: nonnegative scaling and addition, together with affine perturbation and translation. Products and negative scaling are excluded from the preserving class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The algebraic convexity-preserving family consists of functions
\[
F(x):=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i f_i(x)+\langle a,x\rangle+\beta,
\qquad \lambda_i\geq0,
\]
provided \(F\) is proper, equivalently its effective domain
\[
\operatorname{dom}F=\bigcap_{i:\lambda_i>0}\operatorname{dom}f_i
\]
is nonempty under the convention that zero-weight terms are omitted. It also includes translated arguments \(x\mapsto f(x-x_0)\). These operations preserve convexity. Negative scalar multiplication reverses curvature, while pointwise products and quotients are not convexity preserving without additional hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An algebraic convex construction is a finite nonnegative weighted sum of convex functions, optionally plus an affine function. The result is required to be proper, so the positively weighted effective domains must intersect. Translations of the argument also preserve convexity. Negative scaling, products, and quotients do not preserve convexity in general and therefore lie outside this basic calculus.
assumptions_latex: The intersection of the domains of positively weighted terms is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(x)=\sum_i\lambda_i f_i(x)+\langle a,x\rangle+\beta\) is proper convex whenever \(\lambda_i\geq0\) and the positively weighted domains intersect.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The epigraph inequality for \(F\) follows from adding the input convexity inequalities with nonnegative coefficients.
Affine addition changes supporting slopes but contributes zero curvature.
special_cases_latex: Positive scaling is obtained with \(m=1\), \(a=0\), and \(\beta=0\).
Addition of two convex functions is obtained with \(m=2\) and \(\lambda_1=\lambda_2=1\).
Adding a constant corresponds to \(a=0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A finite nonnegative weighted average of convex functions is convex.
If one positively weighted term is strongly convex, then the sum inherits an appropriately scaled strong-convexity modulus.
boundary_notes: If a coefficient is negative, the corresponding term is generally concave rather than convex.
Convexity of two nonnegative functions does not by itself guarantee convexity of their pointwise product.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite nonnegative aggregation of convex functions
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), be proper convex functions and let \(\lambda=(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m)\in\mathbb{R}_+^m\) be nonzero.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite additive aggregation preserving the direction of convex curvature. Properness is enforced through a common finite point for positively weighted terms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The nonnegative aggregate of \((f_i)_{i=1}^m\) with weights \(\lambda_i\geq0\) is
\[
F_\lambda(x):=\sum_{i:\lambda_i>0}\lambda_i f_i(x),
\]
with effective domain
\[
\operatorname{dom}F_\lambda=\bigcap_{i:\lambda_i>0}\operatorname{dom}f_i.
\]
The aggregate is admissible when this intersection is nonempty. Every admissible nonnegative aggregate is proper and convex. If \(\sum_i\lambda_i=1\), it is a convex average of functions; normalization is irrelevant to convexity as long as the total weight is positive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative aggregate is the sum of convex functions multiplied by nonnegative weights, with zero-weight terms omitted. It is admissible when all positively weighted functions are finite at some common point. The resulting function is proper and convex. Requiring the weights to sum to one produces an average, but normalization is not needed for preservation of convexity.
assumptions_latex: \(\lambda_i\geq0\) for every \(i\), and at least one weight is positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_\lambda=\sum_{i:\lambda_i>0}\lambda_i f_i\) is a proper convex function with \(\operatorname{dom}F_\lambda=\bigcap_{i:\lambda_i>0}\operatorname{dom}f_i\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: For all \(x,y\in\operatorname{dom}F_\lambda\) and \(t\in[0,1]\), \(F_\lambda(tx+(1-t)y)\leq tF_\lambda(x)+(1-t)F_\lambda(y)\).
If \(s:=\sum_i\lambda_i>0\), then \(F_\lambda=s\sum_i(\lambda_i/s)f_i\), a positive scaling of a convex average.
special_cases_latex: With one positive weight, the construction is nonnegative scalar multiplication.
With all weights equal to one, it is an ordinary finite sum.
With weights summing to one, it is a weighted average.
immediate_consequences_latex: Zero-weight functions impose no domain restriction and do not change the aggregate.
If \(f_i\) is strongly convex with modulus \(c_i\), then the aggregate is strongly convex with modulus \(\sum_i\lambda_i c_i\) whenever that sum is positive.
boundary_notes: A negative weight can reverse a component's curvature and destroys the general preservation rule.
If the positively weighted domains have empty intersection, the extended-real sum is identically \(+\infty\) and is not proper.

notation.meaning: The aggregate formed with the nonnegative weight vector \(\lambda\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extended-Real Domain and Properness of Finite Sums
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Domain and properness of finite nonnegative sums, including zero coefficients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_i:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper convex functions and \(\alpha_i\ge0\), with \(0\cdot(+\infty)=0\). For \(I_+=\{i:\alpha_i>0\}\) and \(F=\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i f_i\), \[\operatorname{dom}F=\bigcap_{i\in I_+}\operatorname{dom}f_i.\] Consequently, \(F\) is proper exactly when this intersection is nonempty; otherwise \(F\equiv+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Only positively weighted component domains constrain an extended-real finite sum, and their intersection exactly determines properness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dom}F=\bigcap_{\alpha_i>0}\operatorname{dom}f_i\), and \(F\) is proper exactly when this set is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.title: Extended-Real Domain and Properness of Finite Sums

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Curvature Aggregation in Finite Nonnegative Sums
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict and strong convexity inherited by finite nonnegative sums.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i f_i\) on a common convex domain, with \(\alpha_i\ge0\). If \(f_j\) is strictly convex and \(\alpha_j>0\) for some \(j\), then \(F\) is strictly convex. If each \(f_i\) is \(\mu_i\)-strongly convex with respect to a common norm, then \(F\) is \(\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i\mu_i\)-strongly convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positively weighted strictly convex summand makes the finite sum strictly convex, while strong-convexity moduli add with the weights.
assumptions_latex: The functions share a common convex domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strict curvature is inherited from any positively weighted strict summand, and the strong-convexity modulus is \(\sum_i\alpha_i\mu_i\).
knowledge_statements.title: Curvature Aggregation in Finite Nonnegative Sums

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A nonnegative affine series whose pointwise sum is extended-valued and discontinuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(C=[0,1]\), let \(f_n(x)=x\) for every \(n\). Each \(f_n:C\to[0,+\infty)\) is affine and convex, but \[\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}f_n(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x=0,\\+\infty,&x>0.\end{cases}\] Hence a nonnegative convex series need not be finite-valued or continuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Summing the affine function x countably many times on [0,1] gives zero at the origin and infinity elsewhere, demonstrating loss of finiteness and continuity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pointwise sum is convex and lower semicontinuous but is neither finite-valued nor continuous at \(0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Loss of Finiteness and Continuity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Curvature Inheritance by a Nonnegative Series
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict and strong convexity inherited by a pointwise-finite nonnegative series.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}f_n\) be finite on a convex set \(D\). If one term \(f_j\) is strictly convex on \(D\), then \(F\) is strictly convex on \(D\). If each \(f_n\) is \(\mu_n\)-strongly convex there with respect to a common norm and \(\sum_n\mu_n<+\infty\), then \(F\) is \(\sum_n\mu_n\)-strongly convex on \(D\). If \(\sum_n\mu_n=+\infty\) and \(D\) contains two distinct points, the series cannot be finite at every point of \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pointwise-finite nonnegative convex series inherits strict convexity from one term and aggregates summable strong-convexity moduli.
assumptions_latex: The stated component curvature assumptions hold on \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strictness is inherited, finite strong-convexity moduli sum, and divergent total modulus is incompatible with finiteness on a nontrivial convex set.
knowledge_statements.title: Curvature Inheritance by a Nonnegative Series

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Domain, Properness, and Closedness of a Nonnegative Series
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effective domain and lower semicontinuity of pointwise nonnegative convex series.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For convex \(f_n:C\to[0,+\infty]\), let \(F=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}f_n=\sup_NS_N\), where \(S_N=\sum_{n=1}^Nf_n\). Then \[\operatorname{dom}F=\left\{x\in C:\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}f_n(x)<+\infty\right\}.\] Thus \(F\) is proper exactly when this set is nonempty. If every \(f_n\) is lower semicontinuous, then every \(S_N\) and their supremum \(F\) are lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convergence set is the effective domain and exactly controls properness; termwise lower semicontinuity passes to the nonnegative series.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed domain and properness characterization holds, and lower semicontinuity of all terms implies lower semicontinuity of the sum.
knowledge_statements.title: Domain, Properness, and Closedness of a Nonnegative Series

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) be given by \(f(x)=x^2\), and define \(g=\alpha f\). Although \(f\) is convex, \(g\) is not convex, since its midpoint inequality at \(-1\) and \(1\) would require \[g(0)\le\tfrac12g(-1)+\tfrac12g(1),\] whereas \(g(0)=0>\alpha=\tfrac12g(-1)+\tfrac12g(1)\). For a convex function on a convex domain, negative scaling is both convex and concave exactly when the original function is affine.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A negative coefficient can destroy convexity: multiplying the convex square function by any negative scalar produces a nonconvex concave function.
knowledge_statements.title: Negative-Weight Failures

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Elementary affine perturbations of a convex function
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\), \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\), \(a\in\mathbb{R}^{m}\), \(d\in\mathbb{R}\), and \(\alpha\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional extended-real convex analysis; the construction permits an affine change of argument, nonnegative output scaling, and addition of an affine function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[g(x):=\alpha f(Ax+b)+a^{T}x+d,\qquad \operatorname{dom}g=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{m}:Ax+b\in\operatorname{dom}f\}.\] The elementary affine-perturbation class generated by \(f\) consists of all such \(g\). If \(f\) is convex, every member of this class is convex. If \(f\) is concave and finite-valued, the analogous construction is concave for \(\alpha\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An elementary affine perturbation is obtained by applying an affine map to the argument of a function, multiplying the resulting value by a nonnegative scalar, and adding an affine function of the new argument. Its domain is the inverse image of the original domain. These operations preserve convexity.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex as an extended-real-valued function.
\(x\mapsto Ax+b\) and \(x\mapsto a^{T}x+d\) are affine maps of the displayed dimensions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g(x)=\alpha f(Ax+b)+a^{T}x+d\) is convex on \(\operatorname{dom}g\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(g=\alpha(f\circ T)+\ell\), where \(T(x)=Ax+b\) and \(\ell(x)=a^{T}x+d\).
\(\operatorname{epi}(f\circ T)=\{(x,t):(Ax+b,t)\in\operatorname{epi}f\}\).
special_cases_latex: For \(A=I\) and \(b=0\), \(g=\alpha f+\ell\).
For \(\alpha=1\), \(a=0\), and \(d=0\), \(g=f\circ T\).
For \(\alpha=0\), \(g=\ell\) is affine.
immediate_consequences_latex: Translations \(x\mapsto f(x+b)\), coordinate changes \(x\mapsto f(Ax)\), and vertical shifts \(f+d\) preserve convexity.
Strict convexity need not survive when \(A\) is noninjective or \(\alpha=0\).
boundary_notes: Negative output scaling generally converts convexity into concavity rather than preserving convexity.
The domain may be empty if the affine image misses the effective domain of \(f\).

notation.meaning: effective domain where the extended-real function is finite

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Scaling of Strict and Strong Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Curvature behavior under strictly positive value scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f\) is strictly convex on \(C\) and \(\alpha>0\), then \(\alpha f\) is strictly convex. If \(f\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex with respect to a norm, then \(\alpha f\) is \(\alpha\mu\)-strongly convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive value scaling preserves strict convexity and multiplies the strong-convexity modulus by the scale factor.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epigraphs, sublevel sets, and minimizers under strictly positive value scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g=\alpha f\) with \(\alpha>0\). Then \[\operatorname{epi}g=\{(x,\alpha t):(x,t)\in\operatorname{epi}f\},\qquad \{x:g(x)\le r\}=\{x:f(x)\le r/\alpha\}.\] Moreover, \(f(x)\le f(y)\iff g(x)\le g(y)\), so \[\inf_C g=\alpha\inf_C f,\qquad \operatorname*{argmin}_C g=\operatorname*{argmin}_C f.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive value scaling vertically rescales the epigraph and level thresholds, scales the infimum, and leaves minimizers unchanged.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed epigraph, sublevel-set, infimum, and argmin identities hold.
knowledge_statements.title: Positive-Scaling Geometry and Minimizers

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Translation Covariance of Domain, Epigraph, and Minimizers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural invariants under a bijective translation of the argument.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(a\in X\) and \(g(x)=f(x+a)\). Then \[\operatorname{dom}g=\operatorname{dom}f-a,\qquad \operatorname{epi}g=\{(x-a,t):(x,t)\in\operatorname{epi}f\}.\] Consequently properness, lower semicontinuity, closedness, strict convexity, and \(\mu\)-strong convexity are preserved in both directions whenever the relevant topology or norm is present. Moreover, \[\inf g=\inf f,\qquad \operatorname*{argmin}g=\operatorname*{argmin}f-a.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Argument translation rigidly translates the domain, epigraph, and minimizer set while preserving values and convex regularity.
assumptions_latex: For lower semicontinuity and strong convexity, \(X\) carries the relevant vector topology and norm.

children.top_down_role: Additive constant shifts of function values.

For all \(x,y\in C\) and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\), \[g(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y)\le\lambda g(x)+(1-\lambda)g(y).\] Moreover, \(\operatorname{dom}g=\operatorname{dom}f\), and strict or strong convexity parameters are unchanged whenever those notions apply.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g=f+b\) with \(b\in\mathbb R\). Then \[\operatorname{epi}g=\{(x,t+b):(x,t)\in\operatorname{epi}f\},\qquad \{x:g(x)\le r\}=\{x:f(x)\le r-b\}.\] Moreover, \(f(x)\le f(y)\iff g(x)\le g(y)\), and hence \[\inf_Cg=\inf_Cf+b,\qquad \operatorname*{argmin}_Cg=\operatorname*{argmin}_Cf.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite constant shift vertically translates the epigraph and optimal value, shifts level thresholds, and leaves minimizers unchanged.

children.title: Affine Perturbations
children.top_down_role: Addition of affine functions without changing convex curvature.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real vector space, \(C\subset X\) is convex, and \(f:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The affine perturbation \(g=f+\ell\) is convex on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Addition of a finite affine functional to a convex function.

source_refs.locator: 8 Convex Functions p. 139
source_refs.source_title: Convex Analysis and Monotone Operator Theory in Hilbert Spaces

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(g:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) by \(g(x)=f(x)+\ell(x)\). Since \(\ell(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y)=\lambda\ell(x)+(1-\lambda)\ell(y)\), the function \(g\) satisfies \[g(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y)\le\lambda g(x)+(1-\lambda)g(y)\] for every \(x,y\in C\) and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\). Its effective domain equals that of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding a finite affine function preserves convexity and the effective domain of a convex function.
knowledge_statements.title: Affine Perturbations

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine Tilts Need Not Preserve Coercivity or Minimizers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimization properties not invariant under affine perturbation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(\mathbb{R}\), let \(f(x)=|x|\) and \(\ell(x)=-2x\). Then \(f\) is proper closed convex, coercive, bounded below, and uniquely minimized at \(0\), whereas \(g(x)=|x|-2x\) satisfies \(g(x)=-x\) for \(x\geq0\), so \(\inf g=-\infty\) and \(g\) has no minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear tilt can turn a coercive convex function with a minimizer into an unbounded-below problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is coercive and has a unique minimizer, while \(f+\ell\) is unbounded below and has no minimizer.
knowledge_statements.title: Affine Tilts Need Not Preserve Coercivity or Minimizers

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine Perturbations Preserve Closedness and Convex Curvature
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural invariants under addition of a continuous finite affine functional.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a normed space, let \(\ell(x)=\langle a^*,x\rangle+\beta\) be continuous affine, and set \(g=f+\ell\). Then \[\operatorname{dom}g=\operatorname{dom}f,\qquad \operatorname{epi}g=\{(x,t+\ell(x)):(x,t)\in\operatorname{epi}f\}.\] Hence properness and lower semicontinuity are preserved in both directions. Convexity, strict convexity, and \(\mu\)-strong convexity are also preserved in both directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding a continuous affine function shears the epigraph without changing the domain, closedness, or convex curvature class.
assumptions_latex: \(\ell(x)=\langle a^*,x\rangle+\beta\) is finite and continuous affine.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Domain, properness, lower semicontinuity, and ordinary, strict, or strong convexity are invariant under \(f\mapsto f+\ell\).

notation.meaning: Continuous linear part of the affine perturbation

knowledge_statements.title: Affine Perturbations Preserve Closedness and Convex Curvature

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine Tilts Need Not Preserve Boundedness or Minimizers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimization properties that are not invariant under affine perturbation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(\mathbb{R}\), let \(f(x)=0\) and \(\ell(x)=-x\). Then \(f\) is proper closed convex, bounded below, and every point minimizes \(f\), whereas \(g(x)=f(x)+\ell(x)=-x\) satisfies \(\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}}g(x)=-\infty\) and has no minimizer. Thus affine perturbation preserves convex curvature but not boundedness below, coercivity, infimum values, or minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine tilt can turn a bounded-below convex function with minimizers into an unbounded problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) has minimizers and is bounded below, while \(f+\ell\) is unbounded below.
knowledge_statements.title: Affine Tilts Need Not Preserve Boundedness or Minimizers

children.title: Nonpreserving Algebraic Operation Boundary
children.top_down_role: Special cases and failures for operations that do not generally preserve convexity.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Boundary of universally convexity-preserving algebraic operations
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \(f,g:C\to\mathbb{R}\) are convex functions on a nonempty convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional real-valued convex functions; the boundary is expressed through algebraic operations that lack a universal convexity-preservation rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[\mathcal{B}(f,g):=\{-f,\ f-g,\ fg,\ f/g\},\] where the quotient is considered only where \(g\neq0\). These operations are called nonpreserving in the universal sense: convexity of the operands alone does not imply convexity of the result on its natural domain. Explicit witnesses are \(-x^{2}\), obtained from the convex function \(x^{2}\); \(x^{2}-2x^{2}=-x^{2}\); and \((x)(x)=x^{2}\) versus \((x^{2}-1)^{2}\), whose second derivative is negative near zero despite both factors being the same convex function \(x^{2}-1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The nonpreserving algebraic boundary consists of operations for which convexity of the input functions alone gives no universal convexity guarantee. It includes negative scaling, subtraction, products, and quotients. Additional sign, monotonicity, domain, or curvature hypotheses can restore convexity in special cases.
assumptions_latex: For \(f/g\), the selected domain is a convex subset of \(\{x\in C:g(x)\neq0\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is no implication \(f,g\text{ convex}\Rightarrow -f,\ f-g,\ fg,\text{ or }f/g\text{ convex}\) without additional hypotheses.
equivalent_formulations_latex: An operation \(\Phi\) lies beyond the universal preservation boundary when there exist convex inputs for which \(\Phi\) is not convex.
For negative scaling, \(\alpha f\) is convex for every convex \(f\) exactly in the universal regime \(\alpha\geq0\).
special_cases_latex: If \(g\) is affine, then \(f+g\) remains convex, although \(f-g\) is then also convex because \(-g\) is affine.
Products can be convex under extra positivity and monotonicity conditions, but not from convexity alone.
immediate_consequences_latex: Difference-of-convex representations do not certify convexity of the represented function.
A proposed algebraic construction must be checked against its signs and attainable domain rather than only the curvature labels of its factors.
boundary_notes: The listed failures are universal failures, not assertions that every particular product, difference, or quotient is nonconvex.
A precise authoritative locator explicitly collecting all four boundary operations was not established from the supplied sources.

notation.meaning: local collection of algebraic constructions lacking universal preservation

review_flags: Exact source support is missing for the combined negative-scaling, subtraction, product, and quotient failure boundary.
knowledge_statements.title: Boundary of universally convexity-preserving algebraic operations

children.title: Product Preservation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Special structural settings where products retain convexity.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite one-dimensional extension of the common-monotonicity product regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(I\subset\mathbb R\) be an interval and let \(f_1,\ldots,f_m:I\to[0,+\infty)\), \(m\geq2\), be convex. If all \(f_i\) are nondecreasing, or all are nonincreasing, then
\[
F(x)=\prod_{i=1}^m f_i(x)
\]
is nonnegative, convex, and has the same monotonicity direction on \(I\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite product of nonnegative convex functions on an interval is convex when all factors share one monotonicity direction.
assumptions_latex: All \(f_i\) are nondecreasing, or all are nonincreasing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\prod_{i=1}^m f_i\) is convex and has the common monotonicity direction on \(I\).
knowledge_statements.title: Finite Products with Common Monotonicity

assumptions_latex: \(I\subset\mathbb{R}\) is an interval and \(f,g:I\to[0,+\infty)\) are convex.
\(f\) and \(g\) are both nondecreasing, or both nonincreasing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pointwise product \(h=fg\) is convex on \(I\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A one-dimensional sufficient regime; products of arbitrary convex functions need not be convex.

source_refs.locator: 8 Convex Functions p. 139
source_refs.source_title: Convex Analysis and Monotone Operator Theory in Hilbert Spaces

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(h:I\to[0,+\infty)\) by \(h(x)=f(x)g(x)\). If the nonnegative convex factors have the same monotonicity direction on \(I\), then for every \(x,y\in I\) and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\), \[h(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y)\le\lambda h(x)+(1-\lambda)h(y).\] Nonnegativity and common monotonicity are sufficient here; convexity of the two factors alone is not a general product-preservation rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On an interval, the product of two nonnegative convex functions is convex when both factors have the same monotonicity direction.
knowledge_statements.title: Product Preservation Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: 8 Convex Functions p. 139

children.title: Quotient Preservation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Restricted settings where quotient constructions remain convex.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Squared-norm affine vector numerator divided by a positive affine denominator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be convex, let \(u:C\to\mathbb R^p\) and \(a:C\to\mathbb R\) be affine, and suppose \(a(x)>0\) on \(C\). Then
\[
q(x)=\frac{\|u(x)\|_2^2}{a(x)}
\]
is convex on \(C\). The scalar quadratic-over-linear function is the case \(p=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A squared Euclidean norm of an affine vector divided by a positive affine function is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\mapsto\|u(x)\|_2^2/a(x)\) is convex on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.title: Vector Quadratic-over-Linear Convexity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epigraph representation on the positive-denominator domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the assumptions above,
\[
\operatorname{epi}q
=\{(x,t)\in C\times\mathbb R:\ \|u(x)\|_2^2\leq t\,a(x)\}.
\]
Because \(a>0\) on \(C\), this is the affine inverse image of a rotated second-order-cone constraint, restricted to \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On its positive-denominator domain, the quadratic-over-linear epigraph has a rotated second-order-cone representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{epi}q=\{(x,t)\in C\times\mathbb R:\|u(x)\|_2^2\leq t a(x)\}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Rotated-Cone Epigraph of Quadratic-over-Linear Functions

assumptions_latex: For the quadratic-over-linear regime, \(u\) and \(a\) are affine and \(a>0\) on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Both \(1/g\) and \(u^2/a\) are convex on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two standard sufficient quotient regimes; arbitrary quotients of convex functions are excluded.

source_refs.locator: 8 Convex Functions p. 139
source_refs.source_title: Convex Analysis and Monotone Operator Theory in Hilbert Spaces

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The reciprocal quotient \(r(x)=1/g(x)\) is convex on \(C\) whenever \(g\) is positive and concave. Independently, if \(u:C\to\mathbb{R}\) and \(a:C\to(0,+\infty)\) are affine, then the quadratic-over-linear function \[q(x)=\frac{u(x)^2}{a(x)}\] is convex on \(C\). These are sufficient structural regimes; positivity of a denominator and convexity of numerator and denominator alone do not ensure convexity of their quotient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reciprocals of positive concave functions and quadratic-over-positive-affine expressions are convex; generic quotients have no such preservation guarantee.
knowledge_statements.title: Quotient Preservation Regimes

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^p\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be convex, let \(C\) be convex, and let \(u:C\to\mathbb R^p\) and \(a:C\to\mathbb R\) be affine with \(a(x)>0\) on \(C\). Then \(q(x)=a(x)f(u(x)/a(x))\) is convex on \(C\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive Linear-Fractional Functions Are Affine Along Their Ratio
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A basic quotient-preservation regime with affine numerator and positive affine denominator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be convex and let \(u,a:C\to\mathbb R\) be affine with \(a(x)>0\) on \(C\). The linear-fractional function
\[
f(x)=\frac{u(x)}{a(x)}
\]
is both quasiconvex and quasiconcave on \(C\). Indeed, for every \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\),
\[
\{x\in C:f(x)\leq\alpha\}=\{x\in C:u(x)-\alpha a(x)\leq0\},
\]
and analogously for superlevel sets. It need not be convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A ratio of affine functions with a positive affine denominator has convex sublevel and superlevel sets, although it is not generally convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u/a\) is quasiconvex and quasiconcave on \(C\), but convexity is not guaranteed.

children.title: Difference-of-Convex Structure
children.top_down_role: Representations built from subtracting one convex component from another.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-valued DC functions on a common convex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(h_1=f_1-g_1\) and \(h_2=f_2-g_2\) are DC on \(C\), then every real linear combination of \(h_1,h_2\), as well as \(\max\{h_1,h_2\}\) and \(\min\{h_1,h_2\}\), is DC. In particular, \[\max\{h_1,h_2\}=\max\{f_1+g_2,f_2+g_1\}-(g_1+g_2),\] and \(\min\{h_1,h_2\}=-\max\{-h_1,-h_2\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite-valued DC functions form a real vector space and are closed under finite pointwise maxima and minima.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Finite linear combinations, maxima, and minima of DC functions are DC.
knowledge_statements.title: Algebraic Closure of DC Functions

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quadratic Compensation for Smooth DC Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient DC decomposition from a uniform lower Hessian bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be open and convex and let \(h\in C^2(U)\). If \(\nabla^2h(x)\succeq-\rho I\) for every \(x\in U\), where \(\rho\ge0\), then \[h(x)=\left(h(x)+\frac{\rho}{2}\|x\|^2\right)-\frac{\rho}{2}\|x\|^2\] is a DC decomposition on \(U\). Consequently, every \(C^2\) function is DC on each compact convex subset of its open domain after restricting to a neighborhood on which its Hessian has a finite lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A uniform lower Hessian bound yields a quadratic DC decomposition, so twice continuously differentiable functions are locally DC.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h=(h+\rho\|\cdot\|^2/2)-\rho\|\cdot\|^2/2\) is a DC decomposition on \(U\).
knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Compensation for Smooth DC Functions

assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a convex subset of a real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A function is DC precisely when it admits a representation \(h=f-g\) with finite convex components on \(C\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the finite-valued difference-of-convex definition is standard and mathematically unambiguous
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-valued DC functions on a fixed convex domain; no uniqueness of decomposition is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(h:C\to\mathbb{R}\) is called difference-of-convex, or DC, on \(C\) if there exist finite-valued convex functions \(f,g:C\to\mathbb{R}\) such that \[h(x)=f(x)-g(x)\qquad\text{for every }x\in C.\] The ordered pair \((f,g)\) is a DC decomposition of \(h\). Such a decomposition is generally nonunique, and the defining condition does not assert that \(h\) itself is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-valued function is difference-of-convex when it can be written as one finite convex function minus another on the same convex domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Difference-of-Convex Structure

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(h=f-g\), choose \(y^k\in\partial g(x^k)\) and then choose \[x^{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_x\{f(x)-\langle y^k,x\rangle\}.\] Whenever both choices exist, \(h(x^{k+1})\le h(x^k)\). A fixed point generated by these choices admits a common subgradient of \(f\) and \(g\).

children.title: Generic Algebraic Failures
children.top_down_role: Counterexample regimes showing the absence of general preservation.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Products, quotients by positive convex denominators, and differences need not preserve convexity.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete one-dimensional counterexamples to three generally nonpreserving algebraic operations.

source_refs.locator: 8 Convex Functions p. 139

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Convexity is not generally preserved by multiplication, division, or subtraction. Indeed, \(f(x)=x^2\) and \(g(x)=(x-2)^2\) are nonnegative and convex, but \((fg)''(1)=-4\). The positive convex denominator \(q(x)=1+x^2\) yields \(r(x)=x^2/q(x)\), whose second derivative is \(r''(x)=2(1-3x^2)/(1+x^2)^3\), so \(r\) is not convex on \(\mathbb{R}\). Finally, the difference of the convex functions \(x\mapsto x^2\) and \(x\mapsto2x^2\) is \(x\mapsto-x^2\), which is not convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even nonnegative products, quotients with positive convex denominators, and differences of convex functions can fail to be convex.

children.title: Pointwise Envelope Calculus
children.top_down_role: Finite and infinite upper envelopes together with lower-envelope failure boundaries.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \(I\neq\varnothing\) is an index set and \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) for \(i\in I\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite- or infinite-indexed extended-real envelopes in finite-dimensional convex analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[U(x):=\sup_{i\in I}f_i(x),\qquad L(x):=\inf_{i\in I}f_i(x).\] The upper-envelope domain is \(\operatorname{dom}U=\{x:\sup_{i\in I}f_i(x)<+\infty\}\). If every \(f_i\) is convex, then \(U\) is convex and \(\operatorname{epi}U=\bigcap_{i\in I}\operatorname{epi}f_i\). In contrast, convexity of all \(f_i\) alone does not guarantee convexity of the lower envelope \(L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The upper envelope is the pointwise supremum of a family of functions, and the lower envelope is its pointwise infimum. Upper envelopes of convex functions are convex because their epigraph is the intersection of the constituent epigraphs. Lower envelopes have no corresponding general convexity rule.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[L(x):=\inf_{i\in I}f_i(x).\] The lower-envelope operation is not universally convexity preserving: there exist finite families of affine, hence convex, functions whose lower envelope is not convex. In particular, with \(f_1(x)=x\) and \(f_2(x)=-x\) on \(\mathbb{R}\), \[L(x)=\min\{x,-x\}=-|x|,\] which is concave and is not convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The pointwise lower envelope takes the infimum of the indexed values. Convexity of every member of the family does not imply convexity of this envelope. Two affine functions already supply a counterexample: the minimum of the identity and its negative is the negative absolute-value function.

Partial minimization is a distinct special construction that does preserve convexity when the minimized function is jointly convex.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_1(x)=x\) and \(f_2(x)=-x\) on \(\mathbb{R}\). Both functions are affine and hence convex, but their pointwise minimum is \[h(x)=\min\{f_1(x),f_2(x)\}=-|x|.\] Since \(h(0)=0\) while \(\tfrac12h(-1)+\tfrac12h(1)=-1\), the convexity inequality fails at the midpoint. Thus even the minimum of two finite continuous convex functions need not be convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimum of the affine functions x and −x is −|x|, which violates the midpoint convexity inequality.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(a\in[-1,1]\), let \(f_a(x)=ax\). Every \(f_a\) is finite, continuous, and convex on \(\mathbb{R}\), whereas their lower envelope is \[h(x)=\inf_{a\in[-1,1]}ax=-|x|.\] Thus \(h\) is not convex. In this example the infimum is attained at every \(x\), so \[\operatorname{epi}h=\bigcup_{a\in[-1,1]}\operatorname{epi}f_a,\] and this union is not convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An arbitrary lower envelope of convex functions need not be convex: the infimum of the affine functions ax over a in [−1,1] is −|x|. In this example the infimum is attained pointwise, so its epigraph is the nonconvex union of the individual epigraphs.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The closed convex envelope of \(h\), defined as the greatest lower-semicontinuous convex function majorized by \(h\), is its Fenchel biconjugate: \[\operatorname{clconv}h=h^{**}.\] Equivalently, \[\operatorname{epi}(h^{**})=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(\operatorname{epi}h).\] In particular, if \(h=\inf_{i\in I}f_i\) is a nonconvex lower envelope, then \(h^{**}\leq h\) supplies its canonical lower-semicontinuous convexification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonconvex lower envelope can be replaced by its biconjugate, the greatest closed convex function below it; its epigraph is the closed convex hull of the original epigraph.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine pullbacks, restrictions, and linear-fiber images
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\), \(T(u)=Au+b\), and \(B:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{p}\) is linear.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional extended-real convex analysis; the calculus groups three constructions induced by affine maps while keeping their domains explicit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The affine pullback is \(T^{*}f(u):=f(Au+b)\). A restriction to an affine slice \(S=x_0+L\) is the function \(f|_S\), equivalently the pullback \(u\mapsto f(x_0+Pu)\) for a linear parametrization \(P\) of \(L\). The linear-image value function is \[(Bf)(y):=\inf\{f(x):Bx=y\},\qquad\inf\varnothing:=+\infty.\] Pullbacks and affine-slice restrictions preserve convexity. The image value function is convex when \(f\) is convex and is bounded below on each fiber.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affine pullback-restriction calculus comprises precomposition by an affine map, restriction to an affine subset through a parametrization, and optimization over fibers of a linear map. The first two always preserve convexity. The fiber value function is convex when it never takes negative infinity.
assumptions_latex: For \(Bf\), \(f\) is bounded below on every fiber \(\{x:Bx=y\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T^{*}f\), every affine-slice restriction of \(f\), and the fiber image \(Bf\) under the stated boundedness condition are convex.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Restriction to \(S=x_0+L\) equals precomposition with any affine parametrization of \(S\).
\(\operatorname{epi}(Bf)\) is the epigraphical image of \(\operatorname{epi}f\) under \((x,t)\mapsto(Bx,t)\).
special_cases_latex: Lines use \(T(t)=x_0+td\).
Coordinate slices arise by fixing selected coordinates.
If \(B\) is invertible, \((Bf)(y)=f(B^{-1}y)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Convexity can be tested by restriction to affine lines.
Indicator functions satisfy \(B\delta_C=\delta_{B(C)}\).
boundary_notes: Linear images of closed convex functions need not be closed without additional hypotheses.
Fiber boundedness excludes the value \(-\infty\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T(x)=Ax+b\) and \(D=T^{-1}(C)=\{x\in X:Ax+b\in C\}\). Then \(D\) is convex, and the pullback \(g:D\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) defined by \(g(x)=f(T(x))\) is convex. If \(X\) and \(Y\) are topological vector spaces, \(A\) is continuous, and \(f\) is lower semicontinuous, then \(g\) is lower semicontinuous. Moreover, \(g\) is proper exactly when \(T(X)\cap\operatorname{dom}f\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Precomposing a convex function with an affine map preserves convexity; properness requires the affine image to meet the function's effective domain.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict-convexity failure along finite-valued kernel segments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g(x)=f(Ax+b)\). If \(x,x+h\in\operatorname{dom}g\) for some \(0\ne h\in\ker A\), then \(g(x+th)=g(x)\) for every \(t\in[0,1]\). Hence \(g\) is not strictly convex on any convex set containing this segment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero kernel direction joining two finite points produces a constant segment and prevents strict convexity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g(x+th)=g(x)\) for all \(t\in[0,1]\), so \(g\) is not strictly convex on a convex set containing the segment.
knowledge_statements.title: Kernel Directions Obstruct Strict Convexity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict and Strong Convexity Under Affine Precomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Curvature transfer through the linear part of an affine map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq X\) be convex, \(T(x)=Ax+b\), and \(g=f\circ T\). If \(T\) is injective on \(D\) and \(f\) is strictly convex on \(T(D)\), then \(g\) is strictly convex on \(D\). If \(X,Y\) are normed spaces, \(f\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex on \(T(D)\), and \(\|Ah\|_Y\geq\alpha\|h\|_X\) for every \(h\in D-D\), then \(g\) is \(\mu\alpha^2\)-strongly convex on \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Injectivity transfers strict convexity, while a uniform lower bound on the linear part transfers strong convexity with the squared factor.
assumptions_latex: The stated strict- or strong-convexity hypothesis holds on \(T(D)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strict convexity transfers under injectivity, and strong convexity transfers with modulus \(\mu\alpha^2\).

notation.meaning: Lower Lipschitz bound for the linear part on feasible differences

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[g(x):=(f\circ T)(x)=f(Ax+b),\qquad \operatorname{dom}g=T^{-1}(\operatorname{dom}f)=\{x:Ax+b\in\operatorname{dom}f\}.\] This \(g\) is the affine precomposition or pullback of \(f\) by \(T(x)=Ax+b\). If \(f\) is convex, then \(g\) is convex; if \(f\) is concave, then \(g\) is concave.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affine precomposition replaces a function's argument by an affine expression. The resulting domain is the inverse image of the original effective domain. Convexity and concavity are preserved without rank assumptions on the affine map.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex for the convexity conclusion, or concave for the concavity conclusion.

Every sublevel set satisfies \(\{x:f(Ax+b)\leq\alpha\}=T^{-1}(\{z:f(z)\leq\alpha\})\).

Linear precomposition: \(g(x)=f(Ax)\).
Restriction to a line: \(g(t)=f(x_0+td)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Convexity along every affine line is necessary for global convexity.
If \(A\) has a nontrivial kernel, \(g\) is constant along its kernel directions.
boundary_notes: Strict convexity is not generally preserved when \(A\) is noninjective.
The pullback may be improper if its effective domain is empty.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Restriction of a convex function to an affine slice
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\), \(S=x_0+L\) with linear subspace \(L\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}\), and \(P:\mathbb{R}^{k}\to L\) linear.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine sets, lines, and coordinate slices in finite-dimensional spaces; the restricted function may be represented intrinsically or by coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The intrinsic restriction is \[f|_S:S\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\},\qquad (f|_S)(x)=f(x),\qquad\operatorname{dom}(f|_S)=S\cap\operatorname{dom}f.\] A parametrized restriction is \[g(u)=f(x_0+Pu),\qquad\operatorname{dom}g=\{u:x_0+Pu\in\operatorname{dom}f\}.\] If \(f\) is convex, both restrictions are convex on their respective affine domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restricting a function to an affine slice means retaining its values only on that affine set. After choosing coordinates for the slice, this is exactly affine precomposition. A convex function remains convex on every affine set, line, or coordinate slice intersecting its domain.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is linear with range contained in \(L\); for a full parametrization, \(\operatorname{range}P=L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f|_S\) and \(u\mapsto f(x_0+Pu)\) are convex.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For a line \(S=x_0+\mathbb{R}d\), the restriction is \(t\mapsto f(x_0+td)\).
Fixing coordinates is precomposition by the affine embedding of the remaining coordinates.
special_cases_latex: Line restrictions use \(k=1\).
Coordinate slices fix a subset of components and vary the others.
Restriction to a singleton is a zero-dimensional convex function.
immediate_consequences_latex: A function is convex if and only if its restriction to every line intersecting its domain is convex, provided its domain is convex.
Affine feasibility constraints can be incorporated by restricting the objective to their solution set.
boundary_notes: Restriction can conceal nonconvexity in directions transverse to the slice.
A slice disjoint from \(\operatorname{dom}f\) yields an improper restriction.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(g:M\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) by \(g(x)=f(x)\). For every \(x,y\in M\) and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\), the point \((1-\lambda)x+\lambda y\) belongs to \(M\), and \[g((1-\lambda)x+\lambda y)\leq(1-\lambda)g(x)+\lambda g(y).\] Hence \(g=f|_M\) is convex on the affine space \(M\). Its effective domain is \(M\cap\operatorname{dom}f\), so the restriction is proper exactly when this intersection is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restricting a convex function to an affine set preserves relative convexity, and the restricted function is proper exactly when the set meets its effective domain.

\(g=f|_M\) is proper for the curvature assertions.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a normed space, \(d\ne0\), and \(\varphi(t)=f(x_0+td)\) on its effective interval \(I\). Lower semicontinuity of \(f\) also passes to \(\varphi\).

assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is a proper convex function on a real vector space.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the restriction \(g=f|_M\), one has \[\operatorname{dom}g=M\cap\operatorname{dom}f.\] This intersection is convex because both \(M\) and \(\operatorname{dom}f\) are convex. Since \(f\) never takes \(-\infty\), the restricted function \(g\) is proper if and only if \(M\cap\operatorname{dom}f\neq\varnothing\). Thus affine restriction preserves convexity but can destroy properness when the affine set misses the effective domain; it can also reduce the domain's affine dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affine restriction intersects the effective domain with the affine set; convexity survives, but properness is lost exactly when that intersection is empty.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty convex subset of a finite-dimensional real vector space and let \(M\) be affine. If \(M\cap\operatorname{ri}C\ne\varnothing\), then \[\operatorname{ri}(C\cap M)=\operatorname{ri}C\cap M,\qquad \operatorname{cl}(C\cap M)=\operatorname{cl}C\cap M.\] Without this relative-interior intersection hypothesis, neither identity is guaranteed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If an affine set meets the relative interior of a convex domain, restriction commutes with relative interior and closure.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is nonempty and convex in a finite-dimensional real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{ri}(C\cap M)=\operatorname{ri}C\cap M\) and \(\operatorname{cl}(C\cap M)=\operatorname{cl}C\cap M\).

children.top_down_role: Functions obtained by optimization over fibers of linear mappings.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are real vector spaces, \(C\subseteq X\) is convex, and \(A:X\to Y\) is linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g\) is convex on \(Y\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(y\in Y\), define \[g(y)=\inf\{f(x):x\in C,\ Ax=y\},\qquad \inf\varnothing=+\infty.\] Then, for all \(y_0,y_1\in Y\) and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\), \[g((1-\lambda)y_0+\lambda y_1)\leq (1-\lambda)g(y_0)+\lambda g(y_1).\] Thus optimization over the affine fibers of a linear mapping preserves convexity, although the infimum need not be attained and \(g\) need not be lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The infimum of a convex function over each fiber of a linear map is a convex value function, without guaranteeing attainment or lower semicontinuity.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unbounded-Below Fibers Can Produce Minus Infinity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Codomain and properness boundary for fiber infima.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A proper convex source function need not have a proper linear-image value function: if \(F\) is unbounded below on a nonempty fiber \(A^{-1}(y)\), then \(g(y)=-\infty\). For example, with \(A:\mathbb{R}\to\{0\}\) the zero map and \(F(x)=x\), one has \(g(0)=-\infty\). Thus exclusion of unbounded-below fibers is necessary when \(g\) is required to take values only in \(( -\infty,+\infty]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper source function may yield minus infinity after fiber minimization if a fiber is unbounded below.
assumptions_latex: Some nonempty fiber is unbounded below for \(F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The corresponding value is \(-\infty\), so the value function is not proper in the usual extended-real convex class.
knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded-Below Fibers Can Produce Minus Infinity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Feasible Image, Domain, and Epigraph Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Image representation distinguishing feasibility, finite values, and attained boundary points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), let \(A:X\to Y\) be linear, and define \(g(y)=\inf\{F(x):Ax=y\}\). The set of parameters having a feasible finite-valued point is \(A(\operatorname{dom}F)\). If no such fiber is unbounded below, then \(\operatorname{dom}g=A(\operatorname{dom}F)\). Every strict epigraph point \((y,t)\) with \(g(y)<t\) equals \((Ax,t)\) for some \((x,t)\in\operatorname{epi}F\), while a finite boundary point \((y,g(y))\) has such a lift exactly when the fiber infimum is attained. Consequently \((A\times\operatorname{id})(\operatorname{epi}F)=\operatorname{epi}g\) exactly when every finite fiber value is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Feasible parameters form the image of the original domain; strict epigraph points always lift, while finite boundary points lift exactly at attained fiber minima.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility is represented by \(A(\operatorname{dom}F)\), and epigraph-image equality is equivalent to attainment of every finite fiber value.
knowledge_statements.title: Feasible Image, Domain, and Epigraph Boundary

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Inf-Compactness Ensures Closed Attained Fiber Values
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional sufficient condition for lower semicontinuity and attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X,Y\) be finite-dimensional, let \(F:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper lower-semicontinuous convex, and let \(A:X\to Y\) be linear. Suppose that for every compact \(K\subseteq Y\) and every \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\), the set \[\{x\in X:Ax\in K,\ F(x)\leq\alpha\}\] is compact. Then \(g(y)=\inf\{F(x):Ax=y\}\) is a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function, and every finite value \(g(y)\) is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform level-boundedness over compact parameter sets makes fiber minima attained and the value function proper and closed.
assumptions_latex: The displayed parameterized sublevel sets are compact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g\) is proper lower-semicontinuous convex and attains every finite value.
knowledge_statements.title: Inf-Compactness Ensures Closed Attained Fiber Values

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Value function over fibers of a linear mapping
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \(A:\mathbb{R}^{m}\to\mathbb{R}^{n}\) is linear and \(g:\mathbb{R}^{m}\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional extended-real convex analysis; values are obtained by infimizing over equality-constrained linear fibers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The linear image of \(g\) under \(A\) is \[(Ag)(x):=\inf\{g(y):Ay=x\},\qquad \inf\varnothing:=+\infty.\] Its effective domain is \(A(\operatorname{dom}g)\) when all nonempty fibers have finite infimum. If \(g\) is convex and bounded below on every fiber \(A^{-1}(x)\), then \(Ag\) is convex and nowhere equals \(-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear-image value function assigns to each target point the infimum of the original function over all points mapped to that target. Empty fibers have value positive infinity. Convexity passes to this value function when the original function is convex and its value is bounded below on every fiber.
assumptions_latex: For every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\), \(g\) is bounded below on \(\{y:Ay=x\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Ag\) is an extended-real convex function on \(\mathbb{R}^{n}\), with \(\operatorname{dom}(Ag)=A(\operatorname{dom}g)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: For an indicator \(g=\delta_C\), \(Ag=\delta_{A(C)}\).
special_cases_latex: If \(A\) is invertible, \((Ag)(x)=g(A^{-1}x)\).
If \(A(x,y)=x\), then \((Ag)(x)=\inf_y g(x,y)\), the marginal function.
immediate_consequences_latex: Linear images of convex sets are convex through the indicator-function specialization.
Equality-constrained optimal values inherit convexity in their right-hand side.
boundary_notes: The infimum need not be attained.
Closedness is not guaranteed by convexity alone under a linear image.
Without fiberwise lower boundedness, the value may equal \(-\infty\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Domain and Epigraph of a Linear-Image Value Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact image representation, including the distinction between strict epigraph points and attained boundary points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(A:X\to Y\) be linear, and define \(g(y)=\inf\{F(x):Ax=y\}\). For every \(y\) with \(g(y)>-\infty\), \(g(y)<t\) holds exactly when there exists \(x\) with \(Ax=y\) and \(F(x)<t\). Moreover, \[(y,g(y))\in\{(Ax,t):(x,t)\in\operatorname{epi}F\}\] exactly when the fiber infimum is attained. Thus the linear image of \(\operatorname{epi}F\) contains every strict epigraph point of \(g\), and it equals \(\operatorname{epi}g\) precisely when every finite fiber value is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epigraph of a fiber value function is the linear image of the original epigraph except that an unattained finite infimum can omit its boundary point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strict epigraph points always lift through \((x,t)\mapsto(Ax,t)\), and a finite boundary point lifts exactly when its fiber infimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.title: Domain and Epigraph of a Linear-Image Value Function

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity of four infimal combination constructions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The operation (f_i\lambda_i) is retained with the source's previously established functional-scaling convention, including its interpretation at \lambda_i=0. The last infimum ranges over every convex-combination representation of x.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f_1,\ldots,f_m be proper convex functions on \mathbb{R}^n. Then the following functions are convex:\quad f(x)=\inf_{x_1+\cdots+x_m=x}\max_{1\le i\le m}f_i(x_i),\quad g(x)=\inf_{\substack{\lambda_i\ge 0\\\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1}}\sum_{i=1}^m(f_i\lambda_i)(x),\quad h(x)=\inf_{\substack{\lambda_i\ge 0\\\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1}}\max_{1\le i\le m}(f_i\lambda_i)(x),\quad k(x)=\inf_{\substack{\lambda_i\ge 0,\ \sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1\\x=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i x_i}}\max_{1\le i\le m}\lambda_i f_i(x_i).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For finitely many proper convex functions, four value-function constructions remain convex: minimizing a maximum over additive decompositions; minimizing a sum or maximum of the source-defined scaled-function terms over simplex weights; and minimizing a weighted maximum over convex-combination representations. The formulas allow zero weights and therefore depend on the source's scaling convention at zero.
assumptions_latex: f_i\text{ is a proper convex function on }\mathbb{R}^n\text{ for }i=1,\ldots,m
(f_i\lambda_i)\text{ is interpreted using the source's functional-scaling convention, including }\lambda_i=0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f,\ g,\ h,\text{ and }k\text{ defined above are convex functions on }\mathbb{R}^n.
