knowledge_statements.statement_title: Global Lipschitz Bound for Max-Affine Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean Lipschitz regularity determined by the finitely many component slopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=\max_i(a_i^{\mathsf T}x+b_i)\), \[|f(x)-f(y)|\le L\|x-y\|\qquad(x,y\in\mathbb R^n),\quad L=\max_i\|a_i\|.\] Thus every finite max-affine function is globally Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite max-affine function is globally Lipschitz, with the largest component-slope norm as a valid constant.
assumptions_latex: The domain carries the Euclidean norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|f(x)-f(y)|\le(\max_i\|a_i\|)\|x-y\|\) for all \(x,y\).
knowledge_statements.title: Global Lipschitz Bound for Max-Affine Functions

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is convex piecewise-linear if there exist \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\in\mathbb R^n\) such that
\[
f(x)=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}a_i^{\mathsf T}x.
\]
Equivalently, \(f\) is finite, convex, polyhedral, and positively homogeneous. Its domains of linearity are the polyhedral cones on which a fixed subset of the linear forms is active, and its epigraph is a polyhedral cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite convex piecewise-linear function is a maximum of finitely many linear forms and is therefore polyhedral and positively homogeneous.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b\}\) be a nonempty polyhedron, and let \(a_i\in\mathbb R^n\), \(\beta_i\in\mathbb R\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), where \(m\ge1\). Extended-real values encode the domain.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional extended-real convex analysis; the definition permits a polyhedral effective domain and finitely many affine pieces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A proper function \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is piecewise-linear convex, equivalently polyhedral convex, when
\[f(x)=\begin{cases}\max_{1\le i\le m}(a_i^{\mathsf T}x+\beta_i),&x\in C,\\+\infty,&x\notin C.\end{cases}\]
Thus its finite-valued restriction is the pointwise maximum of finitely many affine functions on a polyhedral domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper extended-real function on Euclidean space is piecewise-linear convex when its domain is a nonempty polyhedron and, on that domain, it is the maximum of finitely many affine functions; it equals positive infinity outside the domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f(x)=\max_i(a_i^{\mathsf T}x+\beta_i)+\delta_C(x),\qquad C\text{ polyhedral}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(f\) is piecewise-linear convex if and only if its epigraph \(\operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,r):r\ge f(x)\}\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}\) is a nonempty polyhedral convex set containing no vertical line.
The representation may be written as \(f=h+\delta_C\), where \(h=\max_{1\le i\le m}(a_i^{\mathsf T}\cdot+\beta_i)\) and \(\delta_C\) is the convex indicator of \(C\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C=\mathbb R^n\), then \(f\) is finite everywhere and is exactly a finite maximum of affine functions.
The functions \(x\mapsto\|x\|_1\) and \(x\mapsto\|x\|_\infty\) are finite-valued piecewise-linear convex functions.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every proper piecewise-linear convex function is closed and convex.
Each sublevel set \(\{x:f(x)\le\alpha\}\) is polyhedral.
boundary_notes: This finite-piece definition is specific to finite-dimensional spaces.
A general continuous piecewise-linear function need not be convex; convexity is encoded here by the finite-maximum representation.
The term does not include piecewise linear–quadratic functions unless their quadratic terms vanish.

notation.meaning: Convex indicator: zero on C and positive infinity outside C.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Piecewise-Affine Proximal Map and PLQ Moreau Envelope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: PLQ-specific regularization structure for a proper closed convex PLQ function in Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be proper, lower-semicontinuous, convex, and PLQ, and let \(\lambda>0\). Then \[\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{y}\left\{f(y)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\|y-x\|^2\right\}\] is single-valued, nonexpansive, and piecewise affine. The Moreau envelope \[e_\lambda f(x)=\min_y\left\{f(y)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\|y-x\|^2\right\}\] is finite, continuously differentiable, and PLQ, with \[\nabla e_\lambda f(x)=\lambda^{-1}\bigl(x-\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)\bigr).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex PLQ function has a piecewise-affine proximal mapping and a continuously differentiable PLQ Moreau envelope.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower-semicontinuous, convex, and PLQ.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}\) is nonexpansive and piecewise affine, while \(e_\lambda f\) is continuously differentiable PLQ with \(\nabla e_\lambda f=\lambda^{-1}(I-\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f})\).
knowledge_statements.title: Piecewise-Affine Proximal Map and PLQ Moreau Envelope

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower-semicontinuous, and convex.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subdifferential of a Finite Max-Affine Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded representation for the convex piecewise-linear subclass of piecewise linear–quadratic functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(m\ge 1\), let \(a_i\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(b_i\in\mathbb{R}\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), and define
\[
f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le m}\{a_i^Tx+b_i\},\qquad I(x)=\{i:f(x)=a_i^Tx+b_i\}.
\]
Then, for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\),
\[
\partial f(x)=\operatorname{conv}\{a_i:i\in I(x)\}
=\left\{\sum_{i\in I(x)}\lambda_i a_i:\lambda_i\ge0,\ \sum_{i\in I(x)}\lambda_i=1\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex piecewise-linear function expressed as the maximum of finitely many affine functions, the subdifferential at any point is the convex hull of the slopes of the active affine pieces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial f(x)=\operatorname{conv}\{a_i:i\in I(x)\}=\left\{\sum_{i\in I(x)}\lambda_i a_i:\lambda_i\ge0,\ \sum_{i\in I(x)}\lambda_i=1\right\}.

children.title: Log-Domain Entropic Function Family
children.top_down_role: Function families underlying log-domain modeling, probability, and barrier geometry.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(n\ge1\), \(\Delta_n=\{p\in\mathbb R_+^n:\sum_i p_i=1\}\), and \(\tau>0\). Adopt \(0\log0=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional scalar-valued entropic family on the probability simplex and its full-domain Fenchel conjugate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The log-domain entropic pair at temperature \(\tau\) consists of the extended negative entropy
\[H_\tau(p)=\begin{cases}\tau\sum_{i=1}^n p_i\log p_i,&p\in\Delta_n,\\+\infty,&p\notin\Delta_n,\end{cases}\]
and its log-partition conjugate
\[L_\tau(y)=\tau\log\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^n e^{y_i/\tau}\right),\qquad y\in\mathbb R^n.\]
The family is \(\mathcal E_n=\{(H_\tau,L_\tau):\tau>0\}\), with \(L_\tau=H_\tau^*\) and \(H_\tau=L_\tau^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For each positive temperature, the log-domain entropic family pairs negative Shannon entropy on the probability simplex with the temperature-scaled log-sum-exp function on all of Euclidean space. The two functions are Fenchel conjugates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal E_n=\{(H_\tau,L_\tau):\tau>0,\ L_\tau=H_\tau^*,\ H_\tau=L_\tau^*\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[L_\tau(y)=\sup_{p\in\Delta_n}\left\{\langle p,y\rangle-\tau\sum_i p_i\log p_i\right\}.\]
The gradient coordinates are the Gibbs probabilities \(\nabla_iL_\tau(y)=e^{y_i/\tau}/\sum_j e^{y_j/\tau}\).
special_cases_latex: At \(\tau=1\), \(L_1(y)=\log\sum_i e^{y_i}\) and \(H_1(p)=\sum_i p_i\log p_i+\delta_{\Delta_n}(p)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: \(H_\tau\) and \(L_\tau\) are proper closed convex functions.
Translation along the all-ones direction satisfies \(L_\tau(y+c\mathbf1)=L_\tau(y)+c\).
boundary_notes: This record defines the entropy/log-partition core of the umbrella family; logarithmic barriers and relative-entropy divergences are represented by their own sibling nodes.
The sign convention is negative entropy, which is convex; Shannon entropy itself is its negative and is concave.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Log-sum-exp soft maximum of affine scores
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(m\ge1\), \(a_i\in\mathbb R^n\), \(b_i\in\mathbb R\), and \(\tau>0\). Define affine scores \(s_i(x)=a_i^{\mathsf T}x+b_i\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite smooth convex aggregation of affine functions on Euclidean space, with positive smoothing temperature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The exponential soft-max aggregation generated by \((s_i)_{i=1}^m\) at temperature \(\tau\) is
\[\operatorname{smax}_\tau(s_1(x),\ldots,s_m(x))=\tau\log\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^m e^{s_i(x)/\tau}\right),\qquad x\in\mathbb R^n.\]
Its normalized exponential weights are
\[w_i(x)=\frac{e^{s_i(x)/\tau}}{\sum_{j=1}^m e^{s_j(x)/\tau}},\qquad w(x)\in\Delta_m.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given finitely many affine scores and a positive temperature, their exponential soft maximum is the temperature times the logarithm of the sum of their exponentials after temperature scaling. Its associated weights are the normalized exponentials of those scores.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[F_\tau(x)=\tau\log\sum_{i=1}^m\exp\!\left((a_i^{\mathsf T}x+b_i)/\tau\right).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[F_\tau(x)=\sup_{p\in\Delta_m}\left\{\sum_i p_i s_i(x)-\tau\sum_i p_i\log p_i\right\}.\]
\[\nabla F_\tau(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m w_i(x)a_i.\]
special_cases_latex: For coordinate scores \(s_i(x)=x_i\), this becomes \(\tau\log\sum_i e^{x_i/\tau}\).
For \(m=1\), the aggregation equals the sole affine score.
immediate_consequences_latex: \[\max_i s_i(x)\le F_\tau(x)\le\max_i s_i(x)+\tau\log m.\]
\(F_\tau\) is finite, smooth, and convex on \(\mathbb R^n\).
boundary_notes: The parameter must satisfy \(\tau>0\); the hard maximum is obtained only as the limiting case \(\tau\downarrow0\).
Replacing affine scores by arbitrary functions preserves convexity only under additional hypotheses, such as convexity of every score.

notation.meaning: Normalized exponential weight of score i.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(f(x)=\exp(a^{\mathsf T}x+b)\). The function is positive and smooth on \(\mathbb R^n\), with
\[
\nabla f(x)=f(x)a,
\qquad
\nabla^2f(x)=f(x)aa^{\mathsf T}\succeq0.
\]
It is convex on \(\mathbb R^n\). For every \(x,d\in\mathbb R^n\), the restriction \(t\mapsto f(x+td)\) is strictly convex when \(a^{\mathsf T}d\neq0\) and constant when \(a^{\mathsf T}d=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exponential of an affine form is smooth and convex; along a line it is strictly convex unless the direction is orthogonal to the affine slope, in which case it is constant.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The temperature-scaled log-sum-exp is a smooth convex approximation of \(\max_i z_i\) with additive error at most \(\tau\log m\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The log-sum-exp aggregator is
\[
L_\tau(z)=\tau\log\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^m e^{z_i/\tau}\right).
\]
It is finite, smooth, and convex on \(\mathbb R^m\). For \(M=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}z_i\),
\[
M\leq L_\tau(z)\leq M+\tau\log m.
\]
Consequently, \(L_\tau(z)\to\max_{1\leq i\leq m}z_i\) as \(\tau\downarrow0\), with an error bound uniform over \(z\in\mathbb R^m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Temperature-scaled log-sum-exp smoothly approximates the maximum, with error between zero and temperature times the logarithm of the number of terms.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subtracting the largest coordinate gives an exact overflow-resistant evaluation of log-sum-exp.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_\tau(z)=M+\tau\log\sum_i e^{(z_i-M)/\tau}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: With \(\Delta_m=\{p\geq0:\sum_i p_i=1\}\) and \(0\log0=0\), \[L_\tau(z)=\max_{p\in\Delta_m}\left\{\langle p,z\rangle-\tau\sum_i p_i\log p_i\right\}.\] The unique maximizer is \(p_i=e^{z_i/\tau}/\sum_j e^{z_j/\tau}\); equivalently, \(L_\tau=(\tau\sum_i p_i\log p_i+\delta_{\Delta_m})^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Log-sum-exp is the conjugate of scaled negative entropy on the simplex, with soft-max as its unique optimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_\tau(z)=\max_{p\in\Delta_m}\{\langle p,z\rangle-\tau\sum_i p_i\log p_i\}\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonnegative weighted finite log-sum-exp aggregation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(w_i\geq0\) and not all \(w_i\) vanish, then \[\tau\log\sum_i w_i e^{z_i/\tau}=\tau\log\sum_{i:w_i>0}\exp\!\left(\frac{z_i+\tau\log w_i}{\tau}\right).\] Thus positive weights are affine coordinate offsets, while zero weights delete terms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted log-sum-exp reduces to ordinary log-sum-exp after offsetting coordinates by temperature times log weight.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Weighted log-sum-exp is ordinary log-sum-exp over the positive-weight indices after the offsets \(z_i\mapsto z_i+\tau\log w_i\).
knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Log-Sum-Exp Reduction

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel conjugate of log-sum-exp, including its simplex effective domain and boundary convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be defined by \(g(x)=\log(\sum_{j=1}^n e^{x_j})\), and let \(\Delta_n=\{y\in\mathbb{R}_+^n:\sum_{i=1}^n y_i=1\}\). With \(0\log0=0\), for every \(y\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \[g^*(y)=\begin{cases}\sum_{i=1}^n y_i\log y_i,&y\in\Delta_n,\\+\infty,&y\notin\Delta_n.\end{cases}\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conjugate of log-sum-exp is negative entropy on the probability simplex, using the standard boundary convention, and is infinite outside the simplex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g^*(y)=\begin{cases}\sum_{i=1}^n y_i\log y_i,&y\in\Delta_n,\\+\infty,&y\notin\Delta_n.\end{cases}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(L_\tau(z)=\tau\log\bigl(\sum_j e^{z_j/\tau}\bigr)\), define
\[
p_i(z)=\frac{e^{z_i/\tau}}{\sum_j e^{z_j/\tau}}.
\]
Then \(p(z)\) lies in the relative interior of the probability simplex and
\[
\nabla L_\tau(z)=p(z),
\qquad
\nabla^2L_\tau(z)=\tau^{-1}\bigl(\operatorname{Diag}(p)-pp^{\mathsf T}\bigr)\succeq0.
\]
Moreover, \(p(z+c\mathbf1)=p(z)\), and the Hessian annihilates \(\mathbf1\), expressing translation invariance along the all-ones direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Soft-max is the simplex-valued gradient of log-sum-exp; its Hessian is a scaled categorical covariance and ignores common shifts of all coordinates.
knowledge_statements.title: Soft-Max Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(z\), \[0\preceq\nabla^2L_\tau(z)\preceq\frac1{2\tau}I.\] Hence soft-max is globally \(1/(2\tau)\)-Lipschitz in Euclidean norm. For \(m\geq2\), the constant is the sharp supremum, approached when probability is split equally between two coordinates and tends to zero on the others.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The soft-max Jacobian has operator norm at most one over twice the temperature, and the bound is globally sharp.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Soft-max coordinates on the relative interior of the simplex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Soft-max is constant exactly on cosets \(z+\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf1\}\) and induces a bijection \[\mathbb R^m/\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf1\}\longrightarrow\operatorname{ri}\Delta_m.\] For \(p\in\operatorname{ri}\Delta_m\), all representing logits satisfy \(z_i=\tau\log p_i+c\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Modulo a common shift, logits correspond bijectively to strictly positive probability vectors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Soft-max induces a bijection from \(\mathbb R^m/\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf1\}\) onto \(\operatorname{ri}\Delta_m\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concentration of soft-max around a unique maximizing coordinate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose \(i_*\) uniquely maximizes \(z_i\), and let \(\delta=z_{i_*}-\max_{j\ne i_*}z_j>0\). Then
\[
1-p_{i_*}(z)\leq (m-1)e^{-\delta/\tau}.
\]
Consequently \(p(z)\to e_{i_*}\) as \(\tau\downarrow0\), at an exponential rate controlled by the logit gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With a unique largest logit, soft-max concentrates exponentially fast on its index as temperature decreases.
assumptions_latex: \(m\geq2\), \(\tau>0\), and \(z\) has a unique maximizing coordinate with gap \(\delta>0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Scalar and positive-definite logarithmic barrier atoms
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(n\ge1\). Write \(\mathbb R_{++}^n\) for the positive orthant and \(\mathbb S_{++}^n\) for the cone of real symmetric positive-definite matrices.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional scalar and spectral barrier atoms with extended-real domain enforcement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The logarithmic barrier atom family contains the scalar atom
\[\ell(t)=\begin{cases}-\log t,&t>0,\\+\infty,&t\le0,\end{cases}\]
its positive-orthant sum \(B_+(x)=-\sum_{i=1}^n\log x_i\) for \(x\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\), and the matrix atom
\[B_{\det}(X)=\begin{cases}-\log\det X,&X\in\mathbb S_{++}^n,\\+\infty,&X\notin\mathbb S_{++}^n.\end{cases}\]
Both extended-real barriers diverge when an interior sequence approaches the corresponding domain boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The basic logarithmic barrier is negative logarithm on the positive ray and positive infinity elsewhere. Summing this atom gives the positive-orthant barrier, while applying it spectrally gives negative log determinant on the positive-definite cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[B_+(x)=-\sum_i\log x_i,\qquad B_{\det}(X)=-\log\det X=-\sum_i\log\lambda_i(X).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(X\in\mathbb S_{++}^n\), \(B_{\det}(X)=B_+(\lambda(X))\).
For positive affine slacks \(s_i(x)>0\), a weighted scalar barrier has the form \(-\sum_i\mu_i\log s_i(x)\) with \(\mu_i>0\).
special_cases_latex: For \(n=1\), the matrix and scalar atoms coincide.
For a diagonal positive-definite matrix \(X=\operatorname{diag}(x)\), \(-\log\det X=-\sum_i\log x_i\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The scalar, orthant, and log-determinant atoms are proper closed convex functions.
If \(x^k\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\) approaches a point with a zero coordinate, then \(B_+(x^k)\to+\infty\); analogously, \(\lambda_{\min}(X^k)\downarrow0\) implies \(B_{\det}(X^k)\to+\infty\).
boundary_notes: The atom is finite only in the strict interior of its positive domain.
General self-concordant barriers are a larger class and need not be logarithmic sums or log determinants.

notation.meaning: Cone of symmetric positive-definite n by n matrices.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The scalar negative-log atom is the extended-real function
\[
f(x)=
\begin{cases}
-\log x,&x>0,\\
+\infty,&x\leq0.
\end{cases}
\]
On \((0,+\infty)\), it is smooth and strictly convex, with
\[
f'(x)=-x^{-1},
\qquad
f''(x)=x^{-2}>0.
\]
It satisfies \(f(x)\to+\infty\) as \(x\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The extended-real negative logarithm is smooth and strictly convex on the positive half-line and diverges to positive infinity at zero.

children.top_down_role: Barrier atoms on positive-definite matrix domains.

assumptions_latex: \(n\geq1\), and \(\mathbb S_{++}^n\) is the cone of real symmetric positive-definite matrices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The atom \(F(X)=-\log\det X\) is strictly convex on \(\mathbb S_{++}^n\) and diverges to \(+\infty\) as \(X\) approaches a singular positive-semidefinite matrix.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Log-determinant barrier on the symmetric positive-definite cone.

source_refs.locator: 8 Convex Functions p. 139

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The log-determinant barrier atom is
\[
F(X)=
\begin{cases}
-\log\det X,&X\in\mathbb S_{++}^n,\\
+\infty,&X\notin\mathbb S_{++}^n.
\end{cases}
\]
For every \(X\in\mathbb S_{++}^n\) and symmetric \(H\), its first and second directional derivatives are
\[
DF(X)[H]=-\operatorname{tr}(X^{-1}H),
\qquad
D^2F(X)[H,H]=\operatorname{tr}(X^{-1}HX^{-1}H).
\]
The second derivative is positive for every nonzero symmetric \(H\), so \(F\) is strictly convex. Moreover, \(F(X_k)\to+\infty\) whenever \(X_k\in\mathbb S_{++}^n\) converges to a singular matrix in \(\mathbb S_+^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negative log-determinant is strictly convex on the positive-definite cone and diverges as a positive-definite matrix converges to a singular positive-semidefinite boundary point.
knowledge_statements.title: Log-Determinant Barrier Atoms

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under \(\langle X,Y\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(XY)\), \[F^*(Y)=\begin{cases}-n-\log\det(-Y),&Y\in\mathbb S_{--}^n,\\+\infty,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}\] For \(Y\prec0\), the unique maximizing matrix is \(X=-Y^{-1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conjugate is a shifted negative log-determinant on the negative-definite cone, with optimizer given by inversion.
assumptions_latex: The trace inner product is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F^*(Y)=-n-\log\det(-Y)\) for \(Y\prec0\), and \(+\infty\) otherwise.
knowledge_statements.title: Fenchel Conjugate of Negative Log-Determinant

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transformation laws for negative log-determinant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(X\succ0\), invertible \(A\), and \(t>0\), \[F(AXA^{\mathsf T})=F(X)-2\log|\det A|,\qquad F(tX)=F(X)-n\log t.\] Thus orthogonal conjugation leaves \(F\) invariant and \(F\) is logarithmically homogeneous with parameter \(n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negative log-determinant is orthogonally invariant and logarithmically homogeneous, with an exact congruence transformation law.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(AXA^{\mathsf T})=F(X)-2\log|\det A|\) and \(F(tX)=F(X)-n\log t\).
knowledge_statements.title: Congruence and Logarithmic Homogeneity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Differential Calculus of the Log-Determinant Barrier
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Records convexity and the first three differential formulas for the negative log-determinant on the positive-definite cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $F:\operatorname{int}(\mathbb{S}_+^n)\to\mathbb{R}$ be $F(X)=-\ln\det X$. Then $F$ is convex and continuously differentiable, $\nabla F(X)=-X^{-1}$, and for every $X\in\operatorname{int}(\mathbb{S}_+^n)$ and $\Delta\in\mathbb{S}^n$, $\langle\nabla^2F(X)\Delta,\Delta\rangle_F=\|X^{-1/2}\Delta X^{-1/2}\|_F^2=\langle X^{-1}\Delta X^{-1},\Delta\rangle_F=\operatorname{Trace}([X^{-1/2}\Delta X^{-1/2}]^2)$ and $D^3F(X)[\Delta,\Delta,\Delta]=-2\langle I_n,[X^{-1/2}\Delta X^{-1/2}]^3\rangle_F=-2\operatorname{Trace}([X^{-1/2}\Delta X^{-1/2}]^3)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The negative log-determinant is convex on the positive-definite cone, has gradient minus the matrix inverse, has a Hessian quadratic form equal to the squared Frobenius norm of the symmetrically scaled direction, and has the stated cubic trace formula for its third directional derivative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is convex and continuously differentiable},\quad \nabla F(X)=-X^{-1},\quad \langle\nabla^2F(X)\Delta,\Delta\rangle_F=\|X^{-1/2}\Delta X^{-1/2}\|_F^2=\langle X^{-1}\Delta X^{-1},\Delta\rangle_F=\operatorname{Trace}([X^{-1/2}\Delta X^{-1/2}]^2),\quad D^3F(X)[\Delta,\Delta,\Delta]=-2\langle I_n,[X^{-1/2}\Delta X^{-1/2}]^3\rangle_F=-2\operatorname{Trace}([X^{-1/2}\Delta X^{-1/2}]^3)

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A convex function \(F:C\to\mathbb{R}\) has domain-boundary blowup if, for every sequence \((x_k)_{k\geq1}\subset C\) converging to a boundary point \(\bar x\in\partial C\), one has \[\lim_{k\to\infty}F(x_k)=+\infty.\] Equivalently, the extension \(\bar F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\), defined by \(\bar F=F\) on \(C\) and \(\bar F=+\infty\) outside \(C\), cannot be approached with bounded values from within \(C\) at any finite boundary point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex barrier blows up at its domain boundary when every interior sequence approaching any boundary point has function values tending to positive infinity.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite boundary divergence versus escape along unbounded sequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Boundary blowup controls approaches to finite points of \(\partial C\), not escape to infinity. For \(F(x)=-\log x\) on \(C=(0,+\infty)\), \(F(x)\to+\infty\) as \(x\downarrow0\), whereas \(F(x)\to-\infty\) as \(x\to+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Boundary divergence does not imply coercivity or boundedness below.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Domain-boundary blowup does not imply coercivity or a finite lower bound.

children.title: Entropic Divergence Function Family
children.top_down_role: Convex information-theoretic function families.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(N\ge1\), \(x=(x_i)\), \(y=(y_i)\in\mathbb R^N\), and let \(\phi:\mathbb R\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper convex with an effective domain containing \(\mathbb R_{++}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional positive-vector divergences; the primary definition uses a strictly positive reference vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Csiszár entropic divergence generated by \(\phi\) is
\[D_\phi(x,y)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^N y_i\phi(x_i/y_i),&y\in\mathbb R_{++}^N,\\+\infty,&y\notin\mathbb R_{++}^N.\end{cases}\]
For \(\phi(t)=t\log t\) on \(t>0\) and \(+\infty\) otherwise, this becomes the Kullback–Leibler divergence
\[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(x\|y)=\sum_{i=1}^N x_i\log(x_i/y_i)\]
when \(x,y\in\mathbb R_{++}^N\), and \(+\infty\) otherwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An entropic divergence is obtained by summing the perspective terms of a convex scalar generator. Choosing the generator t log t yields the Kullback–Leibler divergence between strictly positive vectors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[D_\phi(x,y)=\sum_i y_i\phi(x_i/y_i),\qquad D_{\mathrm{KL}}(x\|y)=\sum_i x_i\log(x_i/y_i).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(x,y\in\Delta_N\cap\mathbb R_{++}^N\), then \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(x\|y)\) is the Bregman divergence of \(h(x)=\sum_i x_i\log x_i\).
Each summand \(y_i\phi(x_i/y_i)\) is the perspective of \(\phi\).
special_cases_latex: For \(x=y\in\mathbb R_{++}^N\), \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(x\|x)=0\).
On the probability simplex, the definition is the usual discrete relative entropy.
immediate_consequences_latex: \(D_\phi\) is jointly convex in \((x,y)\) under the stated perspective convention.
For positive probability vectors, \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(x\|y)\ge0\).
boundary_notes: The displayed source convention assigns positive infinity unless both arguments of the KL specialization are strictly positive.
The divergence is generally asymmetric: \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(x\|y)\neq D_{\mathrm{KL}}(y\|x)\).
This is not a metric and does not generally satisfy the triangle inequality.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Entropy generators for φ-divergences, including the superlinear-growth boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(\varphi:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is an entropy function if it is lower semicontinuous and convex, \(\operatorname{dom}\varphi\subseteq[0,+\infty)\), and \(\operatorname{dom}\varphi\cap(0,+\infty)\neq\varnothing\). Its asymptotic slope is \(\varphi'_{\infty}=\lim_{x\to+\infty}\varphi(x)/x\in\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\). If \(\varphi'_{\infty}=+\infty\), then \(\varphi\) is called superlinear.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An entropy function is a lower-semicontinuous convex extended-real function whose domain lies in the nonnegative half-line and contains a positive point. Its asymptotic slope is the limit of φ(x)/x at positive infinity; it is called superlinear when this slope is infinite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\varphi\text{ is an entropy function}\iff \varphi\text{ is lower semicontinuous and convex},\ \operatorname{dom}\varphi\subseteq[0,+\infty),\ \operatorname{dom}\varphi\cap(0,+\infty)\neq\varnothing;\quad \varphi'_{\infty}=+\infty\Rightarrow\varphi\text{ is superlinear}.\)

children.title: Negative-Entropy Functions
children.top_down_role: Convex negative-entropy families on probability or positive domains.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n h(x_i)\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex on \(\mathbb{R}^n\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the extended scalar negative-entropy atom by \[h(t)=\begin{cases}t\log t,&t>0,\\0,&t=0,\\+\infty,&t<0.\end{cases}\] The separable negative-entropy function on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is \[H(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n h(x_i).\] Its effective domain is \(\mathbb{R}_+^n\); on \(\mathbb{R}_{++}^n\), it equals \(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\log x_i\). The boundary value uses the continuous convention \(0\log0=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negative entropy is the separable convex function summing each coordinate times its logarithm, continuously extended by zero at zero and by infinity on negative coordinates.
knowledge_statements.title: Negative-Entropy Functions

knowledge_statements.statement_title: No Finite Subgradient at a Zero Coordinate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order boundary singularity of the lower-semicontinuous entropy extension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the closed entropy atom \(h(t)=t\log t\) for \(t>0\), \(h(0)=0\), and \(h(t)=+\infty\) for \(t<0\), one has \(\partial h(0)=\varnothing\). Consequently, if \(H(x)=\sum_i h(x_i)\), then \(\partial H(x)=\varnothing\) whenever some \(x_i=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negative entropy is finite at zero, but its slope tends to negative infinity, so no finite subgradient exists at a zero coordinate.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is the lower-semicontinuous extension of \(t\log t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial h(0)=\varnothing,\qquad x\in\mathbb R_+^n\setminus\mathbb R_{++}^n\Longrightarrow\partial H(x)=\varnothing.
knowledge_statements.title: No Finite Subgradient at a Zero Coordinate

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Interior Differential Geometry of Negative Entropy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gradient, Hessian, and strict convexity of separable negative entropy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(H(x)=\sum_i x_i\log x_i\) on \(\mathbb R_{++}^n\), \[\nabla H(x)_i=1+\log x_i,\qquad \nabla^2H(x)=\operatorname{Diag}(x_1^{-1},\ldots,x_n^{-1})\succ0.\] The closed extended function is strictly convex on \(\mathbb R_+^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negative entropy has logarithmic gradient, positive diagonal Hessian, and is strictly convex on its effective domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \nabla H(x)=\mathbf1+\log x,\qquad \nabla^2H(x)=\operatorname{Diag}(1/x_i)\succ0.
knowledge_statements.title: Interior Differential Geometry of Negative Entropy

children.title: Relative-Entropy Functions
children.top_down_role: Convex divergence-like functions comparing positive arguments.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D(x,y)=\sum_{i=1}^n d(x_i,y_i)\) is a jointly convex, nonnegative extended-real function, and \(D(x,y)=0\) exactly when \(x=y\) on its finite domain.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generalized relative entropy for nonnegative, not necessarily normalized, vectors.

source_refs.locator: 8 Convex Functions p. 139
source_refs.source_title: Convex Analysis and Monotone Operator Theory in Hilbert Spaces

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(a,b\in\mathbb{R}\), define \[d(a,b)=\begin{cases}a\log(a/b)-a+b,&a>0,\ b>0,\\b,&a=0,\ b\geq0,\\+\infty,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\] For \(x,y\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the generalized relative-entropy function is \[D(x,y)=\sum_{i=1}^n d(x_i,y_i).\] It is the lower-semicontinuous perspective extension of negative entropy, is jointly convex, and satisfies \(D(x,y)\geq0\), with equality precisely when \(x=y\) wherever it is finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Generalized relative entropy sums scalar perspective terms, includes their lower-semicontinuous boundary values, and is jointly convex and nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.title: Relative-Entropy Functions

knowledge_statements.scope_note: First- and second-order structure on strictly positive arguments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x,y\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\), \[\nabla_xD(x,y)_i=\log\frac{x_i}{y_i},\qquad \nabla_yD(x,y)_i=1-\frac{x_i}{y_i}.\] The Hessian is block diagonal by coordinates, with blocks \[\begin{pmatrix}1/x_i&-1/y_i\\-1/y_i&x_i/y_i^2\end{pmatrix}\succeq0,\] whose null direction is \((x_i,y_i)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative entropy has explicit interior gradients and positive-semidefinite rank-one coordinate Hessian blocks.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
abla_xD=\log(x/y),\qquad
abla_yD=\mathbf1-x/y,\qquad
abla^2D\succeq0.
knowledge_statements.title: Interior Derivatives of Relative Entropy

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive Homogeneity and Failure of Joint Strict Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Common-scaling ray structure of generalized relative entropy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(\lambda\ge0\) and every \((x,y)\) in the effective domain, \[D(\lambda x,\lambda y)=\lambda D(x,y).\] Thus \(D\) is affine along common positive-scaling rays and is not jointly strictly convex on any convex set containing two distinct points of such a ray.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Generalized relative entropy is jointly one-homogeneous and therefore cannot be jointly strictly convex along common-scaling rays.
assumptions_latex: \((x,y)\) lies in the effective domain of \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D(\lambda x,\lambda y)=\lambda D(x,y)\quad(\lambda\ge0).
knowledge_statements.title: Positive Homogeneity and Failure of Joint Strict Convexity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Log-Sum Inequality for Generalized Relative Entropy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Aggregate lower bound with the closed support convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x,y\in\mathbb R_+^n\) satisfy \(x_i>0\Rightarrow y_i>0\), and set \(s=\sum_i x_i\), \(t=\sum_i y_i\). Then \[\sum_i x_i\log\frac{x_i}{y_i}\ge s\log\frac{s}{t},\qquad D(x,y)\ge d(s,t),\] with the closed zero conventions. If \(s,t>0\), equality holds exactly when \(x_i/y_i=s/t\) for every index with \(x_i+y_i>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The log-sum inequality bounds coordinatewise relative entropy by the relative entropy of the total masses, with equality for proportional vectors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D(x,y)\ge d\!\left(\sum_i x_i,\sum_i y_i\right).
knowledge_statements.title: Log-Sum Inequality for Generalized Relative Entropy

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The lower-semicontinuous convex extension of \(t\mapsto t\log t\) from \((0,+\infty)\) is \(h(0)=0\) and \(h(t)=+\infty\) for \(t<0\). The closed perspective extension of \(r(a,b)=a\log(a/b)\) from \(a>0\), \(b>0\), is \[\bar r(a,b)=\begin{cases}a\log(a/b),&a>0,\ b>0,\\0,&a=0,\ b\geq0,\\+\infty,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\] Thus limits at admissible zero coordinates are retained, while impossible support configurations receive \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Entropic atoms extend convexly to zero by their limiting values and take infinity on incompatible signs or support configurations.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathbb S^n\) be the real symmetric matrices and let \(\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) be rectangular matrices. Write \(\lambda(X)\in\mathbb R^n\) for ordered eigenvalues and \(\sigma(Y)\in\mathbb R^r\), \(r=\min\{m,n\}\), for ordered singular values.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional orthogonally invariant extended-real matrix functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A spectral matrix function is a proper function obtained by applying a proper vector function to a matrix spectrum. On symmetric matrices it has the form
\[F(X)=\varphi(\lambda(X)),\qquad X\in\mathbb S^n.\]
On rectangular matrices it has the form
\[G(Y)=\psi(\sigma(Y)),\qquad Y\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}.\]
The symmetric spectral subclass requires \(\varphi\) to be permutation invariant and \(\psi\) to be invariant under permutations and sign changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Spectral matrix calculus constructs proper matrix functions by applying a vector function to the ordered eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix or to the ordered singular values of a rectangular matrix. Orthogonal invariance corresponds to permutation symmetry, or absolute permutation symmetry, of the associated vector function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[F=\varphi\circ\lambda\quad\text{or}\quad G=\psi\circ\sigma.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Permutation invariance of \(\varphi\) gives \(F(UXU^{\mathsf T})=F(X)\) for every orthogonal \(U\).
Absolute permutation invariance of \(\psi\) gives \(G(UYV^{\mathsf T})=G(Y)\) for compatible orthogonal \(U,V\).
special_cases_latex: \(\varphi(z)=\max_i z_i\) yields \(F(X)=\lambda_{\max}(X)\).
\(\psi(z)=\|z\|_p\) yields the Schatten \(p\)-norm \(\|Y\|_{S_p}\).
\(\varphi(z)=-\sum_i\log z_i\) on \(\mathbb R_{++}^n\) yields \(-\log\det X\).
immediate_consequences_latex: If the associated symmetric vector function is proper, closed, and convex, then its spectral lift is proper, closed, and convex.
The matrix function depends only on the spectrum, not on the chosen eigenvectors or singular vectors.
boundary_notes: For nonsymmetric square matrices, arbitrary eigenvalue compositions are not covered.
Permutation symmetry alone suffices for eigenvalues; singular-value constructions require absolute permutation symmetry when the associated function is defined on all of \(\mathbb R^r\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Analytic trace spectral function and its domain
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded definition of a spectral matrix function induced by a scalar power series.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(\tau)=a_0+\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}a_k\tau^k\) have radius of convergence \(R>0\), with \(a_k\ge 0\) for every \(k\ge 2\). For \(X\in S_n\), define \(F(X)=\sum_{i=1}^n f(\lambda^{(i)}(X))\), where \(\lambda^{(1)}(X)\ge\cdots\ge\lambda^{(n)}(X)\). Then \(\operatorname{dom}F=\{X\in S_n:\lambda^{(1)}(X)<R,\ \lambda^{(n)}(X)>-R\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scalar power series of radius R, with nonnegative coefficients from degree two onward, defines a spectral function by summing over the eigenvalues. Its domain consists of the symmetric matrices whose eigenvalues all lie strictly between -R and R.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F(X):=\sum_{i=1}^n f(\lambda^{(i)}(X)),\qquad \operatorname{dom}F=\{X\in S_n:\lambda^{(1)}(X)<R,\ \lambda^{(n)}(X)>-R\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Ky Fan trace variational formulas and spectral-sum curvature
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variational representations and curvature of sums of the smallest or largest eigenvalues of a real symmetric matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ be symmetric with $\lambda_1(A)\leq\cdots\leq\lambda_n(A)$. For every $r\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$, $$\sum_{i=1}^{r}\lambda_i(A)=\min_{\substack{U\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r}\\ U^\top U=I_r}}\operatorname{tr}(U^\top AU),$$ and $$\sum_{i=n-r+1}^{n}\lambda_i(A)=\max_{\substack{U\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r}\\ U^\top U=I_r}}\operatorname{tr}(U^\top AU).$$ Consequently, the sum of the $r$ smallest eigenvalues is concave in $A$, whereas the sum of the $r$ largest eigenvalues is convex in $A$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a real symmetric matrix, the sum of its r smallest eigenvalues is the minimum compressed trace over matrices with r orthonormal columns, while the sum of its r largest eigenvalues is the corresponding maximum. Hence the smallest-eigenvalue sum is concave and the largest-eigenvalue sum is convex as functions of the matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sum_{i=1}^{r}\lambda_i(A)=\min_{U^\top U=I_r}\operatorname{tr}(U^\top AU),\quad \sum_{i=n-r+1}^{n}\lambda_i(A)=\max_{U^\top U=I_r}\operatorname{tr}(U^\top AU);\quad A\mapsto\sum_{i=1}^{r}\lambda_i(A)\text{ is concave, and }A\mapsto\sum_{i=n-r+1}^{n}\lambda_i(A)\text{ is convex}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variational characterizations of the ordered eigenvalues of a real symmetric matrix, including convexity and concavity of its extreme-eigenvalue functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let A\in\mathbb{S}^n have eigenvalues \lambda_1(A)\le\cdots\le\lambda_n(A). For every k\in\{1,\ldots,n\}, \lambda_k(A)=\min_{\dim S=n-k+1}\max_{0\ne x\in S}\frac{x^\top Ax}{x^\top x}=\max_{\dim S=k}\min_{0\ne x\in S}\frac{x^\top Ax}{x^\top x}. In particular, \lambda_{\max}(A)=\max_{\|x\|_2=1}x^\top Ax and \lambda_{\min}(A)=\min_{\|x\|_2=1}x^\top Ax. Consequently, A\mapsto\lambda_{\max}(A) is convex and A\mapsto\lambda_{\min}(A) is concave on \mathbb{S}^n.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each ordered eigenvalue of a real symmetric matrix has equivalent min–max and max–min Rayleigh-quotient characterizations. The largest eigenvalue is convex as a function of the matrix, while the smallest eigenvalue is concave.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lambda_k(A)=\min_{\dim S=n-k+1}\max_{0\ne x\in S}\frac{x^\top Ax}{x^\top x}=\max_{\dim S=k}\min_{0\ne x\in S}\frac{x^\top Ax}{x^\top x},\quad \lambda_{\max}\text{ is convex and }\lambda_{\min}\text{ is concave on }\mathbb{S}^n.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the Ky Fan norms of real rectangular matrices through an absolutely permutation-symmetric vector generator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r=\min\{m,n\}\) and \(1\leq k\leq r\). For \(x\in\mathbb R^r\), order the components so that \(|x_{\langle1\rangle}|\geq\cdots\geq|x_{\langle r\rangle}|\), and define \(f_k(x)=\sum_{i=1}^k|x_{\langle i\rangle}|\). For \(X\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), the Ky Fan \(k\)-norm is \[\|X\|_{\langle k\rangle}=f_k(\sigma(X))=\sum_{i=1}^k\sigma_i(X).\] In particular, \(\|\cdot\|_{\langle1\rangle}\) is the spectral, or Schatten-\(\infty\), norm, and \(\|\cdot\|_{\langle r\rangle}\) is the trace, or Schatten-\(1\), norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Ky Fan k-norm of a real matrix is the sum of its k largest singular values. Its endpoint cases are the spectral norm for k=1 and the trace norm when k equals the number of singular values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \|X\|_{\langle k\rangle}=\sum_{i=1}^k\sigma_i(X),\qquad \|X\|_{\langle1\rangle}=\|X\|_{S_\infty},\qquad \|X\|_{\langle r\rangle}=\|X\|_{S_1}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex spectral functions of symmetric matrices
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\lambda:\mathbb S^n\to\mathbb R^n\) list eigenvalues in nonincreasing order. Let \(\varphi:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, closed, convex, and permutation invariant.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Real symmetric matrices and extended-real orthogonally invariant convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The eigenvalue-based convex function generated by \(\varphi\) is
\[F:\mathbb S^n\to(-\infty,+\infty],\qquad F(X)=\varphi(\lambda(X)).\]
Permutation invariance means \(\varphi(Pz)=\varphi(z)\) for every permutation matrix \(P\). The resulting \(F\) is a proper closed convex function and is invariant under orthogonal similarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex eigenvalue-based matrix function is formed by composing the ordered eigenvalue map on symmetric matrices with a proper closed convex permutation-invariant vector function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[F(X)=\varphi(\lambda(X)),\qquad F(UXU^{\mathsf T})=F(X).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: A proper orthogonally invariant \(F\) has this representation with \(\varphi(z)=F(\operatorname{diag}z)\), which is permutation invariant.
Closedness and convexity of \(F=\varphi\circ\lambda\) are equivalent to closedness and convexity of its proper permutation-symmetric associated function \(\varphi\).
special_cases_latex: \(\varphi(z)=\max_i z_i\) gives the maximum-eigenvalue function.
\(\varphi(z)=\sum_i z_i\) gives \(\operatorname{tr}X\).
\(\varphi(z)=\|z\|_p\) gives the corresponding symmetric-matrix Schatten norm.
immediate_consequences_latex: The effective domain is \(\{X\in\mathbb S^n:\lambda(X)\in\operatorname{dom}\varphi\}\).
The value is independent of the ordering convention because \(\varphi\) is permutation invariant.
boundary_notes: The requirement that \(X\) be symmetric is essential for a real ordered eigenvalue vector.
Without permutation invariance, the composition can depend on the arbitrary ordering convention and need not describe an orthogonally invariant function.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(X\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), let \(\sigma(X)\in\mathbb{R}^r\) be its singular values in nonincreasing order, where \(r=\min\{m,n\}\). Define \[G(X)=g(\sigma(X)).\] If \(g\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, convex, and absolutely symmetric, meaning invariant under all signed coordinate permutations, then \(G\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. For orthogonal \(U\) and \(V\), it satisfies \(G(UXV)=G(X)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An absolutely symmetric convex function of a matrix's singular values yields a convex function invariant under orthogonal changes of row and column coordinates.
knowledge_statements.title: Singular-Value-Based Convex Functions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The singular-value representation and absolute-symmetry hypothesis are appropriate, but no source supports the theorem-level convexity assertion.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex spectral functions of rectangular matrices
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(r=\min\{m,n\}\), and let \(\sigma:\mathbb R^{m\times n}\to\mathbb R_+^r\) list singular values nonincreasingly. Let \(\psi:\mathbb R^r\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, closed, convex, and absolutely permutation invariant.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Real rectangular matrices and extended-real unitarily invariant convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The singular-value-based convex function generated by \(\psi\) is
\[G:\mathbb R^{m\times n}\to(-\infty,+\infty],\qquad G(X)=\psi(\sigma(X)).\]
Absolute permutation invariance means \(\psi(PDz)=\psi(z)\) for every permutation matrix \(P\) and every diagonal sign matrix \(D\). The resulting \(G\) is proper, closed, convex, and invariant under left and right orthogonal transformations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex singular-value-based function is the composition of the singular-value vector of a rectangular matrix with a proper closed convex vector function invariant under coordinate permutations and sign changes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[G(X)=\psi(\sigma(X)),\qquad G(UXV^{\mathsf T})=G(X).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: A proper orthogonally invariant rectangular-matrix function has an absolutely permutation-symmetric associated vector function.
Closedness and convexity of \(G=\psi\circ\sigma\) are equivalent to closedness and convexity of its proper absolutely permutation-symmetric associated function.
special_cases_latex: \(\psi(z)=\|z\|_1\) gives the nuclear norm \(\|X\|_*\).
\(\psi(z)=\|z\|_\infty\) gives the operator norm \(\sigma_1(X)\).
\(\psi(z)=\|z\|_2\) gives the Frobenius norm.
immediate_consequences_latex: The effective domain is \(\{X:\sigma(X)\in\operatorname{dom}\psi\}\).
Every Schatten \(p\)-norm with \(1\le p\le\infty\) belongs to this family.
boundary_notes: Singular values are nonnegative, but absolute symmetry provides the canonical extension of the associated function to all of \(\mathbb R^r\).
Functions depending on singular vectors as well as singular values are outside this family.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operator-convex interpretation of matrix-order convexity on an interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A continuous function \(h:I\to\mathbb{R}\) is matrix-order convex on an interval \(I\) if, for every \(n\geq1\), all \(A,B\in\mathbb{S}^n\) with spectra contained in \(I\), and every \(\theta\in[0,1]\), \[h(\theta A+(1-\theta)B)\preceq\theta h(A)+(1-\theta)h(B).\] Here \(h(A)\) is defined by spectral functional calculus and \(C\preceq D\) means that \(D-C\) is positive semidefinite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scalar function is matrix-order convex when its spectral functional calculus satisfies the convexity inequality in Loewner order at every matrix size.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Scalar and Hessian characterizations of matrix convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Collects scalarization, second-order, block-Hessian sufficient, and largest-eigenvalue consequences of semidefinite-order convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G:\mathbb R^n\to\mathcal S^p\). (i) The map \(G\) is matrix convex if and only if \(x\mapsto z^TG(x)z\) is convex for every \(z\in\mathbb R^p\). (ii) If every entry \(g_{ij}\) is twice continuously differentiable, matrix convexity is equivalent to \[\sum_{i,j=1}^p z_i z_j\nabla^2 g_{ij}(x)\succeq0\quad\text{for every }x\in\mathbb R^n\text{ and }z\in\mathbb R^p.\] (iii) If \(G\) is twice continuously differentiable and \(H(x)=[\nabla^2g_{ij}(x)]_{i,j=1}^p\succeq0\) for every \(x\), then \(G\) is matrix convex. (iv) If \(G\) is matrix convex, then \(x\mapsto\lambda_{\max}(G(x))\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetric-matrix-valued map is matrix convex exactly when every quadratic scalarization is convex. For twice continuously differentiable entries, this is equivalent to positive semidefiniteness of every scalarized Hessian. Positive semidefiniteness of the full block Hessian is sufficient for matrix convexity, and matrix convexity implies convexity of the largest-eigenvalue function.
assumptions_latex: \text{Parts (ii) and (iii) assume the stated twice-continuous differentiability}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ is matrix convex}\iff\forall z\in\mathbb R^p,\ z^TG(\cdot)z\text{ is convex};\quad G\text{ matrix convex}\Rightarrow\lambda_{\max}(G(\cdot))\text{ is convex}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed convex spectral domains under the trace inner product.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be closed, convex, permutation invariant, and contain \(0\), and let \(D_C=\{X:\lambda(X)\in C\}\). Then \[h_{D_C}(Y)=h_C(\lambda(Y)),\qquad D_C^\circ=D_{C^\circ},\] where the matrix polar uses \(\operatorname{tr}(XY)\) and the vector polar uses the Euclidean inner product.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Support functions and polars of invariant matrix domains reduce exactly to those of their symmetric eigenvalue sets.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is closed, convex, permutation invariant, and contains \(0\).
Matrix duality uses the trace inner product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h_{D_C}=h_C\circ\lambda\) and \(D_C^\circ=D_{C^\circ}\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orthogonally invariant convex subsets of real symmetric matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is convex and permutation invariant, then \[D_C=\{X\in\mathbb S^n:\lambda(X)\in C\}\] is convex and orthogonally invariant. Conversely, if \(D\subseteq\mathbb S^n\) is convex and orthogonally invariant, then \(C_D=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\operatorname{Diag}(x)\in D\}\) is convex and permutation invariant and \(D=D_{C_D}\). The ordered section \(\lambda(D)\) lies in the Weyl chamber and need not itself be permutation invariant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Invariant convex matrix domains correspond exactly to permutation-invariant convex diagonal sets; ordered eigenvalue sections must not be confused with those symmetric sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\mapsto D_C\) and \(D\mapsto C_D\) give inverse correspondences between permutation-invariant convex vector sets and orthogonally invariant convex symmetric-matrix sets.

notation.meaning: diagonal eigenvalue set associated with D

knowledge_statements.title: Invariant Convex Domain Characterization

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(C\) is convex, then \(D\) is convex and invariant under orthogonal conjugation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Eigenvalue representation of orthogonally invariant convex matrix domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex and invariant under coordinate permutations. Its spectral lift is \[D=\{X\in\mathbb{S}^n:\lambda(X)\in C\}.\] Then \(D\) is convex and orthogonally invariant: \(QXQ^{\mathsf T}\in D\) whenever \(X\in D\) and \(Q\) is orthogonal. Conversely, every orthogonally invariant convex set \(D\subseteq\mathbb{S}^n\) is determined by the permutation-invariant convex set \(C=\{\lambda(X):X\in D\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Permutation-invariant convex eigenvalue sets lift exactly to orthogonally invariant convex domains of symmetric matrices.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty convex subset of a real vector space and let \(f:C\to I\), where \(I\subseteq\mathbb R\) is an interval. For each \(t\in(0,1)\), let \(M_t:I\times I\to I\) be a prescribed two-point aggregator.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A taxonomic scalar framework covering the principal Jensen, level-set, and multiplicative convexity variants represented by descendant nodes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Relative to an aggregator family \(M=(M_t)_{0<t<1}\), a function \(f\) is \(M\)-convex when
\[f(tx+(1-t)y)\le M_t(f(x),f(y))\quad\text{for all }x,y\in C,\ t\in(0,1).\]
The canonical convexity variants arise from \(M_t(u,v)=tu+(1-t)v\) (ordinary convexity), \(M_t(u,v)=\max\{u,v\}\) (quasiconvexity), and, for positive-valued functions, \(M_t(u,v)=u^tv^{1-t}\) (log-convexity). Strict variants replace the inequality by a strict one for distinct endpoints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scalar convexity variant can be specified by choosing the two-point comparison used on the right side of a Jensen-type inequality. Arithmetic averaging gives ordinary convexity, the maximum gives quasiconvexity, and geometric averaging gives log-convexity for positive functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f(tx+(1-t)y)\le M_t(f(x),f(y)),\qquad x,y\in C,\ 0<t<1.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(M_t(u,v)=\max\{u,v\}\), the condition is equivalent to convexity of every sublevel set of \(f\).
For positive \(f\) and \(M_t(u,v)=u^tv^{1-t}\), the condition is equivalent to convexity of \(\log f\).
special_cases_latex: Choosing arithmetic means recovers the usual convex-function class.
Choosing maximum aggregation retains convex minimizer and sublevel-set geometry without requiring a convex epigraph.
immediate_consequences_latex: Ordinary convexity implies quasiconvexity because \(tu+(1-t)v\le\max\{u,v\}\).
Log-convexity implies ordinary convexity for positive functions.
boundary_notes: This record formalizes a taxonomic umbrella rather than asserting that every named generalized-convexity notion is generated by a scalar aggregator.
Cone-ordered vector-valued convexity requires replacing the scalar inequality by an order relation and is not included in the displayed scalar definition.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict, uniform, and strong convexity regimes
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(f:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper. Let \(x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and \(t\in(0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Qualitative and quantitative convexity regimes on a Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is strictly convex when, for every \(x\ne y\),
\[f(tx+(1-t)y)<tf(x)+(1-t)f(y).\]
It is uniformly convex with modulus \(\phi:\mathbb R_+\to[0,+\infty]\), where \(\phi\) is increasing and vanishes only at zero, when
\[f(tx+(1-t)y)+t(1-t)\phi(\|x-y\|)\le tf(x)+(1-t)f(y).\]
It is \(\mu\)-strongly convex when the latter holds with \(\phi(r)=\mu r^2/2\) for some \(\mu>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict convexity requires a strict Jensen inequality between distinct domain points. Uniform convexity adds a positive distance-dependent deficit, and strong convexity is the quadratic-modulus specialization with a positive parameter.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\text{strong convexity}\Longrightarrow\text{uniform convexity}\Longrightarrow\text{strict convexity}\Longrightarrow\text{convexity}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(f\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex if and only if \(x\mapsto f(x)-\frac\mu2\|x\|^2\) is convex.
Strict convexity is equivalent to the absence of equality in the convex Jensen inequality at every interior point of every nondegenerate domain segment.
special_cases_latex: On a Hilbert space, \(x\mapsto\|x\|^2\) is strongly convex with parameter \(2\) under this normalization.
Affine functions are convex but are not strictly convex on any domain containing a nondegenerate segment.
immediate_consequences_latex: A strictly convex function has at most one minimizer on any convex subset of its domain.
A positive uniform modulus rules out affine behavior on every nondegenerate segment.
boundary_notes: The reverse implications in the displayed hierarchy generally fail.
Positive-definite Hessians are sufficient in smooth finite-dimensional settings but are not part of the general definition.
Strict convexity depends on the effective domain; vacuous cases can occur when the domain contains no distinct points.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strictly Convex Lower-Semicontinuous Extension from Positive Second Derivative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constructs an extended-real strictly convex function on the closure of an open interval by radial boundary limits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(h:\mathbb R\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) have effective domain \(D=\operatorname{dom}h\), where \(D\) is a nonempty open interval. Suppose \(h\) is twice differentiable on \(D\) and \(h''(x)>0\) for every \(x\in D\). Fix \(y\in D\), and define
\[
f(x)=\begin{cases}
h(x),&x\in D,\\
\displaystyle\lim_{\alpha\downarrow0}h((1-\alpha)x+\alpha y),&x\in\operatorname{bdry}D,\\
+\infty,&x\notin\overline D.
\end{cases}
\]
Then \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathbb R)\), \(f|_D=h|_D\), \(D\subset\operatorname{dom}f\subset\overline D\), and \(f\) is strictly convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If an extended-real function has a nonempty open interval as its effective domain, is twice differentiable there, and has positive second derivative everywhere, then retaining its interior values, assigning radial limits at boundary points, and assigning positive infinity outside the closed interval produces a proper lower-semicontinuous strictly convex function. It agrees with the original function on the interval, and its effective domain lies between the interval and its closure.
assumptions_latex: D=\operatorname{dom}h\text{ is a nonempty open interval}
f\text{ is defined by the stated interior, radial-boundary-limit, and exterior clauses}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\in\Gamma_0(\mathbb R),\quad f|_D=h|_D,\quad D\subset\operatorname{dom}f\subset\overline D,\quad f\text{ is strictly convex}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Flat segments witnessing failure of strict convexity
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\) be convex and let \(f:C\to\mathbb R\) be convex. For \(x,y\in C\), write \([x,y]=\{tx+(1-t)y:0\le t\le1\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-valued convex functions on a convex domain; the object records equality segments rather than a topological boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The facial-flatness set of \(f\) is
\[\operatorname{Flat}(f)=\left\{(x,y,t):x,y\in C,\ x\ne y,\ 0<t<1,\ f(tx+(1-t)y)=tf(x)+(1-t)f(y)\right\}.\]
A nonempty \(\operatorname{Flat}(f)\) is a certificate that strict convexity fails. Equivalently, the graph of \(f\) contains a nondegenerate line segment, or the lower boundary of \(\operatorname{epi}f\) contains a nontrivial flat segment joining \((x,f(x))\) and \((y,f(y))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The facial-flatness set consists of distinct domain endpoints and an interior interpolation parameter at which the convex Jensen inequality is an equality. Its nonemptiness is exactly the failure of strict convexity and identifies a flat segment on the lower epigraph boundary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f\text{ is strictly convex on }C\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\operatorname{Flat}(f)=\varnothing.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For convex \(f\), equality at one interior point of \([x,y]\) identifies affine behavior along the corresponding graph segment.
The points \((x,f(x))\) and \((y,f(y))\) belong to a common nontrivial lower flat portion of \(\operatorname{epi}f\).
special_cases_latex: Every affine function on a domain containing a nondegenerate segment has a nonempty facial-flatness set.
A polyhedral convex function usually has flat regions on cells where one affine piece is active.
immediate_consequences_latex: If two distinct minimizers exist, their entire connecting segment consists of minimizers and supplies facial flatness.
A strictly convex function cannot have a nontrivial segment contained in one finite level set at its minimum value.
boundary_notes: The word “boundary” here refers to the transition from strict Jensen inequality to equality, not to the topological boundary of the effective domain.
Domain geometry alone may make strictness vacuous when the domain contains no nondegenerate segment.
Essential strict convexity uses a different localization through the conjugate subdifferential domain.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a convex face \(F\) of \(C\) contains distinct points \(x,y\) and the restriction \(f|_F\) is affine. Then, for every \(\theta\in(0,1)\), \[f(\theta x+(1-\theta)y)=\theta f(x)+(1-\theta)f(y).\] Hence the strict convexity inequality fails on the segment \([x,y]\). More generally, any nonconstant line segment contained in a face on which \(f\) is affine is a certificate that \(f\) is not globally strictly convex.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quasiconvex function via the max-Jensen inequality
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty convex subset of a real vector space and let \(f:C\to[-\infty,+\infty]\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar extended-real quasiconvexity on a convex domain; no continuity or ordinary convexity is assumed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is quasiconvex on \(C\) when
\[f(tx+(1-t)y)\le\max\{f(x),f(y)\}\]
for every \(x,y\in C\) and every \(t\in(0,1)\). Thus values at interior points of a segment cannot exceed the larger endpoint value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function on a convex domain is quasiconvex when its value at every interior convex combination of two points is at most the maximum of its two endpoint values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\forall x,y\in C\ \forall t\in(0,1):\quad f(tx+(1-t)y)\le\max\{f(x),f(y)\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For every \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\), the sublevel set \(\{x\in C:f(x)\le\alpha\}\) is convex.
Every restriction of \(f\) to a line segment is a one-dimensional quasiconvex function.
special_cases_latex: Every convex function is quasiconvex.
Every monotone real-valued function on an interval is quasiconvex, even when it is not convex.
immediate_consequences_latex: The minimizer set \(\operatorname{argmin}_C f\), when nonempty, is convex.
Quasiconvexity is preserved under increasing scalar reparameterizations and pointwise suprema under the standard domain conditions.
boundary_notes: Quasiconvexity does not require a convex epigraph.
A sum of quasiconvex functions need not be quasiconvex.
Quasiconvexity is distinct from quasiconcavity; satisfying both gives quasilinearity.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Level-set definitions and their immediate relationships for real-valued functions on Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), let \(S_\alpha=\{x\in\operatorname{dom}f\mid f(x)\leq\alpha\}\). The function \(f\) is quasiconvex iff \(\operatorname{dom}f\) and every \(S_\alpha\), \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\), are convex. It is quasiconcave iff \(-f\) is quasiconvex, equivalently iff every superlevel set \(\{x\in\operatorname{dom}f\mid f(x)\geq\alpha\}\) is convex. It is quasilinear iff it is both quasiconvex and quasiconcave; then its domain and every level set \(\{x\in\operatorname{dom}f\mid f(x)=\alpha\}\) are convex. Every convex function is quasiconvex, but the converse is false.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is quasiconvex when its domain and every sublevel set are convex. It is quasiconcave when every superlevel set is convex and quasilinear when it is both. Quasilinear functions have convex domains and level sets. Convexity implies quasiconvexity, but not conversely.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ quasiconvex}\iff \operatorname{dom}f\text{ and all }S_\alpha\text{ are convex};\quad f\text{ quasiconcave}\iff -f\text{ is quasiconvex};\quad f\text{ quasilinear}\Rightarrow \operatorname{dom}f\text{ and every }\{f=\alpha\}\text{ are convex}.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(f:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, and let \(\phi:\mathbb R_+\to[0,+\infty]\) be increasing and vanish only at zero.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global strict and uniform quasiconvexity on the effective domain of a proper scalar function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is strictly quasiconvex when, for all distinct \(x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and all \(t\in(0,1)\),
\[f(tx+(1-t)y)<\max\{f(x),f(y)\}.\]
It is uniformly quasiconvex with modulus \(\phi\) when
\[f(tx+(1-t)y)+t(1-t)\phi(\|x-y\|)\le\max\{f(x),f(y)\}\]
for all \(x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and \(t\in(0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict quasiconvexity replaces the quasiconvex max inequality by a strict inequality between distinct endpoints. Uniform quasiconvexity strengthens it by a positive deficit controlled by the endpoint distance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\text{uniform quasiconvexity}\Longrightarrow\text{strict quasiconvexity}\Longrightarrow\text{quasiconvexity}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Strict quasiconvexity says every open segment between distinct domain points lies strictly below the larger endpoint value.
Uniform quasiconvexity quantifies this decrease through \(t(1-t)\phi(\|x-y\|)\).
special_cases_latex: Every strictly convex function is strictly quasiconvex.
A strictly monotone proper function on an interval is strictly quasiconvex, although it need not be strictly convex.
immediate_consequences_latex: A strictly quasiconvex function has at most one global minimizer.
Uniform quasiconvexity excludes nontrivial constant segments in the effective domain.
boundary_notes: Strict quasiconvexity is weaker than strict convexity.
Strict convexity of every sublevel set is not, without qualifications, interchangeable with the displayed strict max inequality.
The local-on-\(C\) versions quantify only over endpoints in a specified subset \(C\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict and Uniform Quasiconvexity, Globally and on a Subset
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proper extended-real-valued functions on a Hilbert space, including global and subset-restricted strengthened quasiconvexity; extraction-grounded evidence without verified full-text span alignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, let \(\varnothing\neq C\subset\operatorname{dom}f\), and let \(\phi:\mathbb R_+\to[0,+\infty]\) be increasing and vanish only at \(0\). For \(z_\alpha=\alpha x+(1-\alpha)y\): (i) \(f\) is strictly quasiconvex if \(f(z_\alpha)<\max\{f(x),f(y)\}\) for all distinct \(x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and \(\alpha\in(0,1)\); (ii) \(f\) is uniformly quasiconvex with modulus \(\phi\) if \(f(z_\alpha)+\alpha(1-\alpha)\phi(\|x-y\|)\leq\max\{f(x),f(y)\}\) for all \(x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and \(\alpha\in(0,1)\); (iii) and (iv) strict and uniform quasiconvexity on \(C\) are defined by the respective conditions with \(x,y\in C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict quasiconvexity imposes a strict segment maximum inequality for distinct points. Uniform quasiconvexity strengthens the non-strict inequality by a modulus term. The corresponding notions on a nonempty subset restrict the endpoint quantifiers to that subset.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\begin{aligned}f\text{ strictly quasiconvex}&\iff(\forall x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f)(\forall\alpha\in(0,1))\,[x\neq y\Rightarrow f(z_\alpha)<\max\{f(x),f(y)\}],\\f\text{ uniformly quasiconvex with modulus }\phi&\iff(\forall x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f)(\forall\alpha\in(0,1))\;f(z_\alpha)+\alpha(1-\alpha)\phi(\|x-y\|)\leq\max\{f(x),f(y)\},\end{aligned}\) with the corresponding definitions on \(C\) obtained by restricting \(x,y\) to \(C\).

children.top_down_role: Strict quasiconvex regimes relevant to minimizer structure.

assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a convex subset of a real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is strictly quasiconvex precisely when the strict endpoint-maximum inequality holds on every nontrivial segment.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) is strictly quasiconvex on \(C\) if, for every pair of distinct points \(x,y\in C\) and every \(t\in(0,1)\), \[f((1-t)x+ty)<\max\{f(x),f(y)\}.\] In particular, strict quasiconvexity implies quasiconvexity, but it does not require the convex interpolation bound \(f((1-t)x+ty)\leq(1-t)f(x)+tf(y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict quasiconvexity requires every interior point of a nontrivial segment to have value strictly below the larger endpoint value.
knowledge_statements.title: Strict Quasiconvexity

source_witnesses.locator: 10 Convex Functions: Variants p. 177

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduction of the strict segment condition to one-dimensional restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A real-valued function \(f\) on a convex set \(C\) is strictly quasiconvex if and only if its restriction to every affine line is strictly quasiconvex on the interval where that line meets \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict quasiconvexity can be checked on every affine-line restriction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ is strictly quasiconvex}\iff\text{ every affine-line restriction is strictly quasiconvex}.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Linewise Characterization of Strict Quasiconvexity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp converse failure for the strict-convexity implication.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f(x)=x^3\) is strictly increasing and therefore strictly quasiconvex on \(\mathbb R\), although it is not convex on \(\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The cubic is strictly quasiconvex but not convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ is strictly quasiconvex but not convex}.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Strict Quasiconvexity Without Convexity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Places strict quasiconvexity below the stronger chord inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f\) is strictly convex, then for distinct \(x,y\) and \(t\in(0,1)\), \[f((1-t)x+ty)<(1-t)f(x)+tf(y)\le\max\{f(x),f(y)\},\] so \(f\) is strictly quasiconvex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict convexity implies strict quasiconvexity, but the converse fails.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ is strictly quasiconvex}.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Strict Convexity Implies Strict Quasiconvexity

children.title: Semistrict Quasiconvexity
children.top_down_role: Semistrict quasiconvex regimes between ordinary or strict variants.

assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a convex subset of a real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is semistrictly quasiconvex precisely when unequal endpoint values imply strict decrease from the larger value at every interior point.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the unequal-endpoint convention; some sources call this semistrict quasiconvexity.

source_refs.locator: 10 Convex Functions: Variants p. 177

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) is semistrictly quasiconvex on \(C\) if, whenever \(x,y\in C\), \(f(x)<f(y)\), and \(t\in(0,1)\), one has \[f((1-t)x+ty)<f(y).\] Equivalently, whenever \(f(x)\neq f(y)\), every interior point of \([x,y]\) has value strictly below \(\max\{f(x),f(y)\}\). No strict inequality is imposed when the endpoint values are equal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Semistrict quasiconvexity enforces strict improvement from the worse endpoint only when the two endpoint values differ.
knowledge_statements.title: Semistrict Quasiconvexity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Semistrictness Alone Need Not Imply Quasiconvexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Terminology-sensitive boundary for the seed's unequal-endpoint-only convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) by \(f(0)=1\) and \(f(x)=0\) for \(x\ne0\). It satisfies the unequal-endpoint semistrict condition but is not quasiconvex because \(f(-1)=f(1)=0<f(0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the unequal-endpoint-only definition, semistrict quasiconvexity does not imply ordinary quasiconvexity.
assumptions_latex: Semistrictness uses the packet's unequal-endpoint convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ is semistrictly quasiconvex but not quasiconvex}.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Semistrictness Alone Need Not Imply Quasiconvexity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relation between the two strictness regimes under the packet's conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every strictly quasiconvex function is semistrictly quasiconvex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict quasiconvexity implies semistrict quasiconvexity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ is semistrictly quasiconvex}.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m=\min_{x\in C}f(x)\) be finite and let \(M=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\). If \(f\) is quasiconvex, then \(M\) is convex. If \(f\) is strictly quasiconvex, then \(M\) contains exactly one point. Semistrict quasiconvexity alone does not imply uniqueness of an attained minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The attained minimizer set of a quasiconvex function is convex. Strict quasiconvexity makes it a singleton, whereas semistrict quasiconvexity alone need not imply uniqueness.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a semistrictly quasiconvex function, a local minimum cannot be nonglobal.
assumptions_latex: \(\bar x\in C\) is a local minimizer relative to \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(\bar x)=\inf_{x\in C}f(x).\)

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper strictly convex function on a Hilbert space has at most one minimizer; existence is not asserted.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{card}(\operatorname{Argmin}f)\le 1\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniqueness of a Constrained Quasiconvex Minimizer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two alternative sufficient-condition regimes for at-most-one minimizer over a convex subset of a Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a Hilbert space, let \(f:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be quasiconvex, and let \(C\subseteq\mathcal H\) be convex with \(C\cap\operatorname{dom}f\neq\varnothing\). Suppose either (i) \(f+\iota_C\) is strictly quasiconvex, or (ii) \(f\) is convex, \(\operatorname{int}C\cap\operatorname{Argmin}f=\varnothing\), and \(C\) is strictly convex in the sense that \(x,y\in C\) and \(x\neq y\) imply \((x+y)/2\in\operatorname{int}C\). Then \(f\) has at most one minimizer over \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quasiconvex function has at most one minimizer over a convex feasible set meeting its domain if either the extended objective is strictly quasiconvex, or the objective is convex, no global minimizer lies in the feasible set's interior, and the feasible set is strictly convex.
assumptions_latex: Either \(f+\iota_C\) is strictly quasiconvex, or \(f\) is convex, \(\operatorname{int}C\cap\operatorname{Argmin}f=\varnothing\), and \((\forall x,y\in C)[x\neq y\Rightarrow (x+y)/2\in\operatorname{int}C]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{card}(\operatorname{Argmin}_{x\in C}f(x))\le 1\).
