children.title: Bregman Projection Well-Posedness Regimes
children.top_down_role: Generator and set geometries supporting well-posed projections.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Attained, unique, and strongly well-posed Bregman projection regimes
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(h:E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) generate \(D_h\), let \(C\subseteq E\), let \(y\) be an admissible base point, and define \(F_y(x)=\iota_C(x)+D_h(x,y)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional left-projection problem. The terms classify properties of a fixed triple \((h,C,y)\), rather than asserting that a broad class automatically possesses them.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The left Bregman projection problem for \((h,C,y)\) is called attained if \(\operatorname*{argmin}F_y\neq\varnothing\), uniquely attained if \(\operatorname*{argmin}F_y=\{p\}\), and strongly well posed if it is uniquely attained and every sequence \((x_k)\subseteq C\cap\operatorname{dom}h\) satisfying \(D_h(x_k,y)\to\inf_{x\in C}D_h(x,y)\) converges to \(p\). A standard compact-level regime is characterized by lower semicontinuity of \(F_y\), nonempty domain, and compactness of one nonempty sublevel set \(\{x:F_y(x)\leq\alpha\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Bregman projection problem is attained when its argmin is nonempty, uniquely attained when that argmin is a singleton, and strongly well posed when every minimizing sequence converges to the unique minimizer. A compact-level regime records lower semicontinuity, feasibility, and compactness of a nonempty sublevel set.
assumptions_latex: \(F_y(x)=\iota_C(x)+D_h(x,y)\) is defined on a finite-dimensional space.
\(C\cap\operatorname{dom}h\neq\varnothing\), and \(y\) is an admissible second argument of \(D_h\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strong well-posedness means \(\operatorname*{argmin}F_y=\{p\}\) and \(F_y(x_k)\downarrow\inf F_y\Rightarrow x_k\to p\) for every minimizing sequence \((x_k)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Unique attainment is equivalent to \(P_C^{h,L}(y)=\{p\}\).
Level-boundedness means that every sublevel set \(\{x:F_y(x)\leq\alpha\}\) is bounded; together with lower semicontinuity in finite dimensions, its nonempty finite sublevels are compact.
special_cases_latex: A proper lower-semicontinuous coercive projection objective lies in the compact-level regime.
Strict convexity of \(F_y\) on its convex feasible domain is a uniqueness condition, not an attainment condition.
immediate_consequences_latex: Strong well-posedness includes both existence and uniqueness.
Compact-level and strict-convexity conditions address different components of well-posedness: attainment and uniqueness, respectively.
boundary_notes: A unique formal stationary point does not by itself establish attainment.
In infinite-dimensional spaces, bounded sublevels need not be compact, so the compact-level formulation must be changed.
Right-oriented projections require a separate analysis because their objective may be nonconvex.

notation.meaning: The unique projected point when it exists.

review_flags: A source supporting this exact hierarchy of Bregman projection well-posedness notions was not identified among the inspected hints.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports the proposed hierarchy, and the conclusion uses monotone decrease to the infimum whereas the main definition only requires convergence of objective values.

children.title: Projection Existence Regimes
children.top_down_role: Generator or set geometries supporting attainment of Bregman projections.

assumptions_latex: \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is open and \(f:U\to\mathbb{R}\) is continuously differentiable
\(C\subseteq U\) is nonempty and closed in \(\mathbb{R}^n\)
\(x\mapsto D_f(x,y)\) is level-bounded on \(C\) for fixed \(y\in U\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P^{\mathrm L}_{C,f}(y)\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional direct-method regime for left projection attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(y\in U\). Suppose \(C\) is nonempty and closed in \(\mathbb{R}^n\), and suppose every sublevel set \[\{x\in C:D_f(x,y)\leq\alpha\}\] is bounded for each \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\). Since \(x\mapsto D_f(x,y)\) is continuous on \(C\), every nonempty sublevel set is compact. A minimizing sequence therefore has a convergent subsequence with limit in \(C\), and the minimum is attained. Equivalently, \(P^{\mathrm L}_{C,f}(y)\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous left-divergence objective attains its minimum on a nonempty closed constraint set when its constrained sublevel sets are bounded.
knowledge_statements.title: Projection Existence Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-dimensional attainment claim is mathematically sound and theorem fits the existence-regimes leaf, but no source is cited. The statement_latex field also contains a proof-style minimizing-sequence argument, which must be removed when a sourced replacement is prepared.

children.title: Projection Uniqueness Regimes
children.top_down_role: Curvature or constraint geometries supporting unique projections.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constraint-geometry boundary for strict-generator uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strictly convex generator need not give a unique projection onto a nonconvex set.
knowledge_statements.title: Failure Without Constraint Convexity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generator-curvature boundary for uniqueness of an attained left projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(U=\mathbb R\), \(f\equiv0\), and \(C=[0,1]\), one has \(D_f(x,y)=0\) for all \(x,y\in U\), and hence \(P^{\mathrm L}_{C,f}(y)=[0,1]\) for every \(y\in U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convexity without strict convexity does not ensure uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P^{\mathrm L}_{C,f}(y)=[0,1]\) for every \(y\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.title: Failure Without Strict Convexity

assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable and strictly convex on an open convex set \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P^{\mathrm L}_{C,f}(y)\) is a singleton.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict-convexity uniqueness regime for attained left projections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For fixed \(y\in U\), the left objective has the form \[D_f(x,y)=f(x)-\langle\nabla f(y),x\rangle+\text{a constant independent of }x.\] Hence \(x\mapsto D_f(x,y)\) is strictly convex whenever \(f\) is strictly convex. Its restriction to the convex set \(C\) consequently has at most one minimizer. If the left projection is attained, then there exists a unique \(p\in C\) such that \(P^{\mathrm L}_{C,f}(y)=\{p\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict convexity of the generator and convexity of the constraint set make every attained left Bregman projection unique.
knowledge_statements.title: Projection Uniqueness Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The uniqueness theorem is correct for an attained left projection over a convex set, but it has no cited source with a specific locator. The statement_latex field includes derivational proof text that should not appear in the knowledge statement.

children.title: Generator-Coercivity Interface
children.top_down_role: Role of generator growth in projection well-posedness.

assumptions_latex: \(f:U\to\mathbb{R}\) is differentiable and convex on open \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_f(\cdot,y)\) is level-bounded on \(C\) if and only if \(f(\cdot)-\langle\nabla f(y),\cdot\rangle\) is level-bounded on \(C\).

notation.meaning: tilted generator for the base point y

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Left-projection coercivity is coercivity of a linearly tilted generator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For fixed \(y\in U\), \[D_f(x,y)=f(x)-\langle
abla f(y),xangle+\langle
abla f(y),yangle-f(y).\] The final two terms are independent of \(x\). Therefore \(D_f(\cdot,y)\) is coercive, or level-bounded, on \(C\) exactly when the tilted generator \(x\mapsto f(x)-\langle
abla f(y),xangle\) has the corresponding property on \(C\). In particular, if \(f\) is supercoercive on \(\mathbb{R}^n\), then \(D_f(\cdot,y)\) is coercive for every fixed \(y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coercivity of a left Bregman objective is exactly coercivity of the generator after subtracting the linear term determined by the base point.
knowledge_statements.title: Generator-Coercivity Interface

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The constant-shift equivalence of level-boundedness is correct, and condition is a reasonable kind for this interface leaf. No supporting citation is supplied, and statement_latex contains explanatory derivation rather than only the mathematical statement.

children.title: Constraint-Set Geometry
children.top_down_role: Geometric features of target sets relevant to projection behavior.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constraint-set characterization of a left Bregman projection; existence is not asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(h\) be differentiable and convex on an open convex set \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), let \(C\subseteq U\) be nonempty and convex, and let \(y\in U\). For \(p\in C\), the following are equivalent: \[p\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}D_h(x,y),\] \[\langle
abla h(p)-
abla h(y),x-pangle\ge0\quad( orall x\in C),\] \[
abla h(y)-
abla h(p)\in N_C(p),\] and \[D_h(x,y)\ge D_h(x,p)+D_h(p,y)\quad( orall x\in C).\] If \(C\) is affine, the variational inner product vanishes for every \(x\in C\), and the Pythagorean inequality becomes equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a convex target, projection optimality is equivalent to a gradient variational inequality, a normal-cone condition, and the generalized Pythagorean inequality; affine targets give equality.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is differentiable and convex on an open convex set \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Projection optimality, the variational inequality, normal-cone membership, and the Bregman Pythagorean inequality are equivalent; for affine \(C\), the last relation is equality.

notation.meaning: convex normal cone with convention \(\langle v,x-p\rangle\le0\) for every x in C

knowledge_statements.title: Bregman Variational and Pythagorean Characterization

assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable and strictly convex on open convex \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\)
\(C\subseteq U\) is nonempty, closed in \(\mathbb{R}^n\), and convex
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P^{\mathrm L}_{C,f}(y)=\{p\}\) and \(\langle\nabla f(p)-\nabla f(y),z-p\rangle\geq0\) for all \(z\in C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closedness supports attainment; convexity supports uniqueness and the variational inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the stated hypotheses, continuity and level-boundedness give an attained minimum, while strict convexity of \(f\) gives uniqueness. Thus \(P^{\mathrm L}_{C,f}(y)=\{p\}\) for some \(p\in C\). Since the differentiable objective \(x\mapsto D_f(x,y)\) is convex, its minimizer over \(C\) satisfies \[\langle\nabla f(p)-\nabla f(y),z-p\rangle\geq0\qquad\text{for every }z\in C.\] Conversely, this variational inequality is sufficient for \(p\) to minimize \(D_f(\cdot,y)\) over \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closedness, convexity, and level-boundedness yield an attained unique left projection characterized by a first-order variational inequality.
knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-Set Geometry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The result is fundamentally a theorem or optimality characterization, not merely a condition. The assumptions do not explicitly introduce y as an element of U, the record has no source citation, and statement_latex contains proof-style justification. A sourced revision must correct all three issues without weakening the result.

children.title: Bregman Pythagorean Family
children.top_down_role: Projection inequalities and affine-set equality regimes.

assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable and convex on open convex \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_f(z,y)\geq D_f(z,p)+D_f(p,y)\) for every \(z\in C\), with equality when \(C\) is affine.

notation.meaning: an attained left Bregman projection of y

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Left-projection inequality, with the affine-constraint equality regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The projection optimality condition gives \(\langle
abla f(p)-
abla f(y),z-pangle\geq0\) for every \(z\in C\). The three-point identity then yields \[D_f(z,y)=D_f(z,p)+D_f(p,y)+\langle z-p,
abla f(p)-
abla f(y)angle,\] and hence \[D_f(z,y)\geq D_f(z,p)+D_f(p,y)\qquad(z\in C).\] If \(C\) is affine, both feasible directions \(z-p\) and \(p-z\) are available, so the inner product vanishes and the displayed inequality becomes equality for every \(z\in C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A left Bregman projection gives a Pythagorean inequality on convex constraints and an exact identity on affine constraints.
knowledge_statements.title: Bregman Pythagorean Family

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Pythagorean inequality and affine-set equality regime are correct under the stated attained left-projection assumptions, and theorem matches the topic role. No source is cited, and statement_latex includes the optimality and three-point-identity derivation, which is proof text.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bregman Pythagorean inequality and equality relations
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(h\) be differentiable and convex on an open convex set \(U\), let \(C\subseteq U\), let \(y\in U\), and let \(p\in C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The record defines the Pythagorean relations for a candidate projection point. It does not assert that every projection satisfies them without appropriate convexity and optimality hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The triple \((C,p,y)\) satisfies the left Bregman Pythagorean inequality if
\[D_h(x,y)\geq D_h(x,p)+D_h(p,y)\qquad\text{for every }x\in C.\]
It satisfies the Pythagorean equality if equality holds for every \(x\in C\). By the three-point identity, these relations are equivalently specified by
\[\langle\nabla h(p)-\nabla h(y),x-p\rangle\geq0\quad\text{or}\quad
\langle\nabla h(p)-\nabla h(y),x-p\rangle=0,\]
respectively, for every \(x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point p satisfies the Bregman Pythagorean inequality relative to C and y when every feasible x has direct divergence to y at least equal to the sum of its divergence to p and p's divergence to y. Equality is the corresponding exact decomposition. The inequality and equality are equivalently expressed by a dual-gradient pairing condition.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is convex and differentiable on an open convex set \(U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Pythagorean inequality is \(D_h(x,y)\geq D_h(x,p)+D_h(p,y)\) for all \(x\in C\), and the equality regime replaces \(\geq\) by \(=\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The inequality is equivalent to \(\langle\nabla h(p)-\nabla h(y),x-p\rangle\geq0\) for every \(x\in C\).
The equality is equivalent to \(\nabla h(p)-\nabla h(y)\in(\operatorname{par}C)^{\perp}\) when \(C\) is affine, where \(\operatorname{par}C=C-C\).
special_cases_latex: For a quadratic generator, the equality reduces to the usual orthogonal Pythagorean identity.
For a convex feasible set and a left Bregman projection satisfying the first-order variational inequality, the inequality relation applies.
immediate_consequences_latex: The inequality implies \(D_h(x,y)\geq D_h(p,y)\) for every \(x\in C\).
The equality regime decomposes every feasible direct divergence into two directed legs through \(p\).
boundary_notes: For a general convex set, equality need not hold; the usual projection relation is an inequality.
The displayed orientation is tied to minimizing \(D_h(\cdot,y)\); reversing the divergence requires a different relation.

notation.meaning: The direction space of an affine set C.

review_flags: No inspected source locator was available for the Bregman Pythagorean inequality together with its affine equality regime and orientation.
knowledge_statements.title: Bregman Pythagorean inequality and equality relations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Pythagorean relations and pairing formulation are plausible with the stated orientation, but no source supports the exact inequality and affine-equality regimes.

children.title: Bregman Projection Attainment Boundary
children.top_down_role: Projection failures caused by open domains, orientation, or insufficient coercivity.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Attainment and nonattainment boundary for a Bregman projection
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(h:E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be differentiable on \(U=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\), let \(C\subseteq E\), fix \(y\in U\), and put \(\alpha=\u200b\inf_{x\in C\cap\operatorname{dom}h}D_h(x,y)\), with \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional left-oriented projection. The classification separates feasibility, finite nonattainment, and attainment without prescribing sufficient conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The projection datum \((h,C,y)\) is attained if there exists \(p\in C\cap\operatorname{dom}h\) with \(D_h(p,y)=\alpha\). It is finitely unattained if \(\alpha<+\infty\) but no such \(p\) exists. It is infeasible if \(C\cap\operatorname{dom}h=\varnothing\). A finite nonattainment sequence is any \((x_k)\subseteq C\cap\operatorname{dom}h\) such that \(D_h(x_k,y)\to\alpha\) while \((x_k)\) has no cluster point in \(C\cap\operatorname{dom}h\). The attainment boundary is the distinction among these three cases.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Bregman projection is attained when a feasible point realizes the divergence infimum. It is finitely unattained when the infimum is finite but no feasible point realizes it, and infeasible when the effective feasible set is empty. Nonattainment can be witnessed by a minimizing sequence having no feasible cluster point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Attainment is \(P_C^{h,L}(y)\neq\varnothing\); finite nonattainment is \(\alpha<+\infty\) and \(P_C^{h,L}(y)=\varnothing\); infeasibility is \(C\cap\operatorname{dom}h=\varnothing\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Finite nonattainment means that minimizing sequences exist but no point of the effective feasible set has objective value \(\alpha\).
Attainment is equivalent to \(\alpha\in\{D_h(x,y):x\in C\cap\operatorname{dom}h\}\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C\cap\operatorname{dom}h\) is compact and \(D_h(\cdot,y)\) is lower semicontinuous there, the datum is attained.
If feasible points approach an excluded boundary point at which the limiting divergence is finite, finite nonattainment may occur.
immediate_consequences_latex: A finite projection value does not imply that a projection point exists.
Strict convexity can ensure at most one minimizer but cannot alone prevent nonattainment.
boundary_notes: Open generator domains can exclude the limit of a minimizing sequence.
For right-oriented projection, the effective feasible set is normally \(C\cap U\), so its attainment boundary may differ.
Failure of coercivity can permit minimizing sequences to escape to infinity.
review_flags: No inspected source supported this exact formal classification of Bregman projection attainment failures.
knowledge_statements.title: Attainment and nonattainment boundary for a Bregman projection

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The attainment classification lacks a source; the ambient-context formula contains the invalid command \u200b, and without lower semicontinuity finite nonattainment need not admit a minimizing sequence with no feasible cluster point.

children.title: Open-Domain Boundary Failure
children.top_down_role: Projection obstruction caused by inaccessible domain boundaries.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in C}D_f(x,y)=\tfrac12\) but \(P^{\mathrm L}_{C,f}(y)=\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: Bregman divergence generated by the quadratic f
constraint curve approaching the excluded boundary of U

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative closedness inside an open domain does not prevent escape to its boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The set \(C\) is closed relative to \(U\), but its Euclidean closure contains the excluded boundary point \((0,0)\). For \(x_t=(t,t^4)\in C\), \[D_f(x_t,y)=\tfrac12\bigl(t^2+(t^4-1)^2\bigr)=\tfrac12\bigl(1+t^2-2t^4+t^8\bigr).\] For \(0<t\leq\tfrac12\), this value is strictly greater than \(\tfrac12\), while it converges to \(\tfrac12\) as \(t\downarrow0\). Hence the infimum is not attained, despite relative closedness of \(C\) in the open domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A relatively closed constraint curve can approach an excluded domain boundary, causing a quadratic Bregman projection infimum to remain unattained.
knowledge_statements.title: Open-Domain Boundary Failure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The constructed curve is closed relative to the open domain, the displayed values approach one half from above, and the example correctly shows nonattainment at an excluded boundary. Counterexample fits the failure leaf, but the record has no inspectable source and statement_latex includes verification-style proof text.

children.title: Projection Nonattainment
children.top_down_role: Infimal projection values lacking an attaining point.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}D_h(x,y)=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A one-dimensional open-set counterexample to Bregman projection attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h(x)=-\log x\) for \(x>0\), let \(C=(0,1)\), and fix \(y>1\). Then \[D_h(x,y)=\frac{x}{y}-\log\!\left(\frac{x}{y}\right)-1.\] The infimum over \(C\) is the finite value \(D_h(1,y)\), but it is not attained because \(1\notin C\). Hence \[\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}D_h(x,y)=\varnothing.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For negative-logarithmic geometry, projection of a point above one onto the open interval (0,1) has a finite infimum at the excluded endpoint and therefore no minimizer.
knowledge_statements.title: Projection Nonattainment

children.title: Orientation-Specific Failure
children.top_down_role: Projection failures occurring for only one divergence orientation.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\arg\min_{x\in C}D_h(x,y)=\{0\}\), whereas \(D_h(y,0)\) is not classically defined.

notation.meaning: entropy-generated Bregman divergence with gradient taken at the second argument

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure caused by exchanging the differentiated and nondifferentiated Bregman arguments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h(x)=x\log x-x\) on \((0,\infty)\), with \(h(0)=0\), and let \(C=\{0\}\). For every \(y>0\), the forward divergence extends finitely to the first-argument boundary and satisfies \(D_h(0,y)=y\), so the forward projection onto \(C\) exists. In the reversed orientation, evaluating \(D_h(y,0)\) requires \(h'(0)\), but \(h'(x)=\log x\to-\infty\) as \(x\downarrow0\). Thus exchanging the arguments destroys classical feasibility even though the forward problem is well defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Entropy divergence permits a boundary point as its first argument, but not as its differentiated second argument, so reversing orientation can destroy feasibility.
knowledge_statements.title: Orientation-Specific Failure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The entropy example correctly distinguishes the differentiated second argument from the nondifferentiated first argument, and failure_boundary fits the leaf. No source with a specific locator is supplied, so the record cannot pass evidence review.

children.top_down_role: Nonattainment associated with insufficient growth of the generator.

Let \(h:\mathbb R^n	o(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, closed, and convex, let \(y\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\) be a differentiability point, and let \(C\) be nonempty, closed, and convex with \(C\cap\operatorname{dom}h
e\varnothing\). Put \[F_y(x)=D_h(x,y)+\delta_C(x).\] Then \(F_y\) is level-bounded if and only if \[h^\infty(d)+\delta_C^\infty(d)-\langle
abla h(y),dangle>0\qquad	ext{for every }d
e0.\] Thus a nonzero direction with nonpositive displayed recession value certifies failure of level-boundedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constrained left Bregman objective is level-bounded exactly when its recession growth is positive in every nonzero direction.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is proper, closed, and convex on \(\mathbb R^n\).
\(C\) is nonempty, closed, convex, and intersects \(\operatorname{dom}h\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_h(\cdot,y)+\delta_C\) is level-bounded iff \(h^\infty(d)+\delta_C^\infty(d)-\langle\nabla h(y),d\rangle>0\) for every \(d\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Recession-Direction Test for Bregman Level-Boundedness

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional normed space, \(h:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is differentiable at \(y\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\), and \(C\subseteq\operatorname{dom}h\).
There exists \((x_n)\subset C\) such that \(\|x_n\|\to\infty\) and \(\sup_nD_h(x_n,y)<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sublevel sets of \(D_h(\cdot,y)\) need not be compact, so the finite-dimensional compact-sublevel attainment criterion is unavailable.

notation.meaning: Bregman objective at the fixed reference point y

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies the compactness mechanism lost when the Bregman objective is not level-bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\), \(h\), \(y\), and \(C\) satisfy the stated assumptions. If \((x_n)\subset C\) obeys \(\|x_n\|\to\infty\) and \(\sup_nD_h(x_n,y)<\infty\), then every sublevel set \(L_\alpha\) with \(\alpha\geq\sup_nD_h(x_n,y)\) is unbounded and therefore noncompact. Thus lower semicontinuity cannot establish attainment through the finite-dimensional compact-sublevel criterion. This condition identifies failure of that sufficient criterion; it does not by itself imply nonattainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unbounded feasible sequence with bounded Bregman values makes sufficiently high sublevel sets noncompact, so the compact-sublevel existence criterion is unavailable, although nonattainment does not follow by itself.
knowledge_statements.title: Coercivity Breakdown

children.top_down_role: Gradient and conjugate-gradient coordinate systems induced by Legendre generators.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Mirror-coordinate duality induced by a Legendre generator
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space and let \(h:E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be Legendre. Set \(U=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\) and \(U^*=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h^*)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Legendre duality. Coordinates are restricted to the primal and conjugate interior domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Mirror-coordinate duality assigns to each \(x\in U\) the dual coordinate \(\eta=
abla h(x)\in U^*\), and to each \(\eta\in U^*\) the primal coordinate \(x=
abla h^*(\eta)\in U\). The coordinate relations are
\[\eta=
abla h(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x=
abla h^*(\eta)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad h(x)+h^*(\eta)=\langle x,\eta\rangle.\]
Thus primal and dual coordinates are paired by mutually inverse gradient maps and Fenchel equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Legendre generator equips the interior of its domain with mirror coordinates. The dual coordinate of x is ∇h(x), and the primal coordinate of η is ∇h*(η). These assignments are inverse, and a paired coordinate pair satisfies Fenchel equality.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is a Legendre convex function on a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\(\eta=
abla h(x)\iff x=
abla h^*(\eta)\iff h(x)+h^*(\eta)=\langle x,\eta\rangle\).
equivalent_formulations_latex:
\(\eta=
abla h(x)\) is equivalent to \(\eta\in\partial h(x)\), and \(x=
abla h^*(\eta)\) is equivalent to \(x\in\partial h^*(\eta)\).

In paired coordinates \(x=
abla h^*(\eta)\), one has \(D_h(x',x)=D_{h^*}(\eta,
abla h(x'))\).
special_cases_latex: For \(h(x)=\tfrac12\|x\|^2\), primal and dual coordinates coincide.
For negative entropy on the positive orthant, the dual coordinates are componentwise logarithmic up to an additive constant determined by the chosen generator.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every point of \(U\) has a unique dual coordinate in \(U^*\), and every point of \(U^*\) has a unique primal coordinate in \(U\).
Divergence orientation reverses when expressed through conjugate coordinates.
boundary_notes: For a non-Legendre generator, the gradient may fail to be injective, surjective onto \(U^*\), or differentiably invertible.
Boundary points outside \(U\) or \(U^*\) are not assigned coordinates by these gradient maps.

notation.meaning: Interior of the effective domain of the Fenchel conjugate.

abla h(x)\) lies in \(\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h^*)\). Conversely, every \(u\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h^*)\) has the unique primal coordinate \(x=

abla h^*(
abla h(x))=x,\qquad 
abla h(

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Loss of Surjectivity Without Essential Smoothness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the interior-to-interior coordinate correspondence for a closed strictly convex generator lacking essential smoothness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(h(x)=x^2\) for \(x\ge0\) and \(h(x)=+\infty\) for \(x<0\). Then \(h\) is proper, closed, convex, and strictly convex on \((0,\infty)\), but it is not essentially smooth. Its conjugate is \[h^*(u)=\begin{cases}0,&u\le0,\\u^2/4,&u>0,\end{cases}\] so \(\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h^*)=\mathbb R\), whereas \(\nabla h((0,\infty))=(0,\infty)\). Therefore the gradient map is not onto the conjugate-domain interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A half-line quadratic lacks boundary-gradient blow-up, and its gradient misses nonpositive dual coordinates although its conjugate is finite everywhere.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla h(\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h))=(0,\infty)\subsetneq\mathbb R=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h^*)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Loss of Surjectivity Without Essential Smoothness

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Loss of Injectivity Without Essential Strict Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the primal-to-dual coordinate bijection when the generator is differentiable but not essentially strictly convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(h(x)=0\) on \(\mathbb R\), \(h\) is proper, closed, convex, and differentiable, but \(\nabla h(x)=0\) for every \(x\). Thus the gradient coordinate map is not injective, showing that differentiability alone cannot replace the essential-strict-convexity part of the Legendre hypothesis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constant convex generator sends every primal point to the same dual coordinate, so essential strict convexity is needed for invertibility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla h\equiv0\) is not injective.
knowledge_statements.title: Loss of Injectivity Without Essential Strict Convexity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Attainable dual coordinates and boundary escape
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(h:E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex and differentiable on \(U=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional geometry of the range of the mirror map. Legendre and essential-smoothness properties are stated as distinguished regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The attainable dual-coordinate set of \(h\) is
\[\mathcal A_h=
abla h(U)=\{\eta\in E:\exists x\in U,\eta=
abla h(x)\}.\]
A dual coordinate \(\eta\) is attainable precisely when \(\eta\in\mathcal A_h\). The mirror map is globally attainable if \(\mathcal A_h=E\). It is boundary steep if every sequence \(x_k\in U\) converging to a boundary point of \(\operatorname{dom}h\) satisfies \(\|\nabla h(x_k)\|\to+\infty\). For Legendre \(h\), \(\mathcal A_h=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h^*)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The attainable dual coordinates are exactly the range of the mirror map ∇h on the interior of the primal domain. Global attainability means that this range is the entire dual space. Boundary steepness means that gradients become unbounded along every interior sequence converging to the domain boundary. For a Legendre generator, the attainable set is the interior of the conjugate domain.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is proper and convex and differentiable on \(U=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\neq\varnothing\).
The norm in the boundary-steepness condition is any fixed norm on the finite-dimensional dual space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\(\mathcal A_h=
abla h(U)\); for Legendre \(h\), \(\mathcal A_h=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h^*)\), and global attainability is equivalent to \(\operatorname{dom}h^*=E\) up to its interior-domain convention.
equivalent_formulations_latex:
\(\eta\in\mathcal A_h\iff\exists x\in U\) such that \(\eta=
abla h(x)\).

Under Legendre duality, \(\eta\in\mathcal A_h\iff
abla h^*(\eta)\in U\).
special_cases_latex: For a positive-definite quadratic generator on \(E\), \(\mathcal A_h=E\).
For negative entropy on the positive orthant, componentwise logarithmic coordinates range over all of \(\mathbb R^n\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A dual vector outside \(\mathcal A_h\) has no primal interior preimage under the mirror map.
Boundary steepness prevents a bounded sequence of dual coordinates from corresponding to primal points approaching a finite domain boundary.
boundary_notes: Essential smoothness also includes differentiability on the domain interior; boundary steepness is only its gradient blow-up component.
If \(\operatorname{dom}h\) has no boundary in the ambient space, the boundary-steepness condition is vacuous.
Surjectivity onto \(E\) is stronger than surjectivity onto \(\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h^*)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Formal operator interfaces induced by Bregman geometry
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(h:E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be a differentiable convex generator with Bregman divergence \(D_h\), let \(g:E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, and let \(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A taxonomy of static mathematical operators linking Bregman geometry to optimization methods. It contains no iteration rule, convergence assertion, or rate statement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The principal Bregman method interfaces are the mirror-response map
\[Q_h(\eta)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in E}\{\langle\eta,x\rangle-h(x)\},\]
the Bregman proximal map
\[\operatorname{prox}^{h}_{\lambda g}(y)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in E}\{g(x)+\lambda^{-1}D_h(x,y)\},\]
and the Bregman projection map
\[P_C^h(y)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}D_h(x,y)=\operatorname{prox}^{h}_{\lambda\iota_C}(y).\]
The taxonomy classifies an interface by whether its input is a dual coordinate, a primal base point with a penalty, or a primal base point with a feasibility indicator.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bregman geometry exposes three static interfaces: mirror response converts a dual coordinate into maximizers of a linear functional minus the generator; the Bregman proximal map minimizes a penalty plus a scaled divergence; and Bregman projection is the indicator-penalty specialization. These are set-valued operator definitions, not algorithms or convergence claims.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is a proper convex generator differentiable at every base point used by \(D_h\).
Each argmax or argmin is interpreted as a possibly empty set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_C^h=\operatorname{prox}^{h}_{\lambda\iota_C}\), while \(Q_h\), \(\operatorname{prox}^{h}_{\lambda g}\), and \(P_C^h\) form the dual-response, penalized-primal, and constrained-primal interface classes.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Where \(h^*\) is differentiable and the supremum is attained, \(Q_h(\eta)=\{\nabla h^*(\eta)\}\).
The proximal objective is equivalently \(g(x)+\lambda^{-1}h(x)-\lambda^{-1}\langle\nabla h(y),x\rangle\), up to constants independent of \(x\).
special_cases_latex: If \(g=\iota_C\), the proximal interface is the Bregman projection interface.
If \(h(x)=\tfrac12\|x\|^2\), the interfaces become ordinary Euclidean response, proximal, and projection maps.
immediate_consequences_latex: The projection interface is a specialization of the proximal interface.
Mirror response accepts a dual-coordinate input, whereas the proximal and projection interfaces accept a primal base point.
boundary_notes: The taxonomy does not define an iterative method or prescribe how an operator is evaluated.
Existence, uniqueness, numerical solvability, and convergence are separate properties.
Alternative right-oriented proximal constructions are not included.
review_flags: The node is a synthetic interface taxonomy; no inspected source was available that supports the exact three-class definition and conventions.
knowledge_statements.title: Formal operator interfaces induced by Bregman geometry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The three operator interfaces are formally defined, but the asserted taxonomy is synthetic and has no source supporting its exact scope and conventions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unconstrained mirror descent as an attainable dual translation followed by Legendre coordinate inversion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(h\) be Legendre, \(x_k\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\), \(g_k\in\mathbb R^d\), and \(\eta_k>0\). Form \[u_{k+1}=
abla h(x_k)-\eta_kg_k.\] If \(u_{k+1}\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h^*)\), then the unconstrained mirror step is uniquely defined by \[x_{k+1}=
abla h^*(u_{k+1}),\qquad 
abla h(x_{k+1})=u_{k+1}.\] If the translated coordinate lies outside \(\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h^*)\), this unconstrained interface produces no primal iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unconstrained mirror step translates the current dual coordinate and maps it back through the conjugate gradient; the step exists exactly when the translated coordinate is attainable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The mirror step exists uniquely exactly when \(u_{k+1}\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h^*)\), and then equals \(\nabla h^*(u_{k+1})\).

children.title: Cross-Method Correspondences

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Euclidean Specialization of the Three Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical Euclidean specialization of the mirror, proximal, and projection correspondence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(h(x)=\tfrac12\|x\|_2^2\), one has \(D_h(x,y)=\tfrac12\|x-y\|_2^2\) and \(\nabla h=\nabla h^*=\operatorname{Id}\). Hence \(y_{k+1}=x_k-\eta_kg_k\). If \(C\subset\mathbb R^d\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, then \[\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\left\{\eta_k\langle g_k,x\rangle+\tfrac12\|x-x_k\|_2^2\right\}=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\tfrac12\|x-y_{k+1}\|_2^2=P_C(y_{k+1}).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the squared Euclidean generator, mirror translation is an ordinary gradient step and the constrained proximal and projection forms reduce to Euclidean projected gradient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: All three interfaces reduce to the displayed Euclidean gradient and projected-gradient formulas.
knowledge_statements.title: Euclidean Specialization of the Three Interfaces

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact correspondence among attainable mirror, linearized Bregman-proximal, and left-projection updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h:\mathbb R^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be Legendre, \(x_k\in U=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\), \(\eta_k>0\), and \(g_k\in\mathbb R^d\). Suppose \(u_{k+1}=\nabla h(x_k)-\eta_kg_k\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h^*)\), and set \(y_{k+1}=\nabla h^*(u_{k+1})\). Then \[y_{k+1}=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in U}\{\eta_k\langle g_k,x\rangle+D_h(x,x_k)\}.\] If \(C\subseteq U\) is nonempty and convex and the constrained minimum is attained, then \[\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\{\eta_k\langle g_k,x\rangle+D_h(x,x_k)\}=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}D_h(x,y_{k+1})=P_C^h(y_{k+1}).\]

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The mirror trial point is the unique unconstrained linearized Bregman proximal point, and the constrained update is its left Bregman projection onto \(C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact correspondence among attainable mirror, Bregman proximal, and left-projection updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The attainable mirror trial point satisfies \[y_{k+1}=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in U}\bigl\{\eta_k\langle g_k,x\rangle+D_h(x,x_k)\bigr\}=\nabla h^*\bigl(\nabla h(x_k)-\eta_kg_k\bigr).\] If the constrained minimum is attained, then \[x_{k+1}=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\bigl\{\eta_k\langle g_k,x\rangle+D_h(x,x_k)\bigr\}=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}D_h(x,y_{k+1})=P_C^h(y_{k+1}).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An attainable mirror trial point is the unconstrained linearized Bregman proximal point, and the attained constrained update is the left Bregman projection of that trial point.
knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Method Correspondences

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Euclidean Specialization of Mirror, Proximal, and Projection Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact common Euclidean specialization of the three Bregman method interfaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h(x)=\tfrac12\|x\|_2^2\), so \(D_h(x,y)=\tfrac12\|x-y\|_2^2\) and \(\nabla h=\nabla h^*=\operatorname{Id}\). Then the unconstrained mirror update driven by \(g_k\) is \[y_{k+1}=x_k-\eta_kg_k.\] For every nonempty closed convex set \(C\subset\mathbb R^d\), the constrained linearized Bregman-proximal update and the left Bregman projection coincide with the Euclidean projected-gradient update: \[x_{k+1}=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\left\{\eta_k\langle g_k,x\rangle+\tfrac12\|x-x_k\|_2^2\right\}=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\tfrac12\|x-y_{k+1}\|_2^2=P_C(y_{k+1}).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With the squared Euclidean generator, mirror translation is an ordinary gradient step and the constrained Bregman-proximal and Bregman-projection formulations both reduce to Euclidean projected gradient.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^d\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The mirror, linearized Bregman-proximal, and left Bregman-projection interfaces reduce to the displayed Euclidean gradient and projected-gradient formulas.
knowledge_statements.title: Euclidean Specialization of Mirror, Proximal, and Projection Interfaces

children.title: Canonical Bregman Geometries
children.top_down_role: Representative geometries generated by standard convex kernels.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: For a finite-dimensional space \(E\), a Bregman geometry is specified by a convex domain \(\Omega\subseteq E\), a differentiable convex generator \(h\), and its divergence \(D_h\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A representative finite-dimensional taxonomy defined by standard kernels. Matrix cases use the trace inner product and positive-definite domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A canonical Bregman geometry is a triple \((\Omega,h,D_h)\) belonging to the following standard families: quadratic geometry, with \(h(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx\), \(Q\succ0\); entropic geometry, with \(h(x)=\sum_i x_i\log x_i\) on the positive orthant or simplex interior; Burg geometry, with \(h(x)=-\sum_i\log x_i\) on \(\mathbb R_{++}^n\); and spectral matrix geometry, with \(h(X)=\operatorname{tr}(\phi(X))\) on a spectral domain. In every family,
\[D_h(x,y)=h(x)-h(y)-\langle\nabla h(y),x-y\rangle.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Canonical Bregman geometries are generator–domain–divergence triples drawn from standard families: positive-definite quadratics, negative entropy, the Burg logarithmic barrier, and spectral matrix generators. Each family uses the same first-order divergence construction but has a different effective domain and coordinate geometry.
assumptions_latex: Each generator is proper and convex on its stated domain and differentiable on the domain interior.
In spectral geometry, \(\phi\) is a scalar convex differentiable function on an interval containing the eigenvalues under consideration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The canonical family consists of the displayed triples \((\Omega,h,D_h)\), with \(D_h\) generated by the common first-order formula on the appropriate domain.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Each geometry may be identified by the pair \((\Omega,h)\), since \(D_h\) is determined by \(h\).
Affine perturbations of a generator leave its Bregman divergence unchanged: \(D_{h+\langle a,\cdot\rangle+b}=D_h\).
special_cases_latex: For \(Q=I\), quadratic geometry gives half the squared Euclidean distance.
On the probability simplex, entropic geometry gives the Kullback-Leibler divergence.
For \(h(X)=\operatorname{tr}(X\log X-X)\), spectral geometry gives the matrix relative-entropy divergence.
immediate_consequences_latex: The domain is part of the geometry and cannot be omitted when logarithmic or entropic generators are used.
Different generators may induce distinct directed geometries on the same ambient vector space.
boundary_notes: The list is representative rather than exhaustive.
Nondifferentiable kernels and infinite-dimensional entropy spaces require other formulations.
The matrix generator requires functional calculus and an explicitly specified spectral domain.

notation.meaning: Domain, convex generator, and induced Bregman divergence.
Spectral trace function obtained by applying φ to the eigenvalues of X.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E=\mathbb R^n\), let \(Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) be symmetric positive definite, and define \(\langle x,y\rangle_Q=x^{\mathsf T}Qy\) and \(\|x\|_Q=(x^{\mathsf T}Qx)^{1/2}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Full-domain finite-dimensional quadratic geometry. The Euclidean specialization is obtained with \(Q=I\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The quadratic generator and its Bregman divergence are
\[h_Q(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx,\qquad \nabla h_Q(x)=Qx,\]
\[D_{h_Q}(x,y)=\tfrac12(x-y)^{\mathsf T}Q(x-y)=\tfrac12\|x-y\|_Q^2,\qquad x,y\in\mathbb R^n.\]
The resulting Bregman geometry is symmetric, translation invariant, and generated by the squared norm associated with the inner product \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetric positive-definite matrix Q defines the quadratic generator one half xᵀQx. Its Bregman divergence is one half of the squared Q-norm of x−y. The generator has full domain and gradient map x↦Qx.
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(Q=L^{\mathsf T}L\) with invertible \(L\), then \(D_{h_Q}(x,y)=\tfrac12\|Lx-Ly\|_2^2\).
The mirror map is \(M_{h_Q}(x)=Qx\), with inverse \(M_{h_Q}^{-1}(\eta)=Q^{-1}\eta\).
special_cases_latex: For diagonal \(Q\succ0\), the divergence is a coordinate-weighted squared Euclidean distance.
immediate_consequences_latex: \(\sqrt{2D_{h_Q}(x,y)}=\|x-y\|_Q\) is a metric.
Left and right Bregman projections coincide for this generator.
The gradient coordinate map is a linear bijection of \(\mathbb R^n\).
boundary_notes: Positive semidefinite but singular \(Q\) produces only a seminorm and loses point separation.
The squared norm \(D_{h_Q}\) itself generally fails the triangle inequality even though its square root is a metric.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Negative-entropy Bregman geometry on the probability simplex
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\Delta_n=\{x\in\mathbb R_+^n:\sum_{i=1}^n x_i=1\}\) and \(\Delta_n^{\circ}=\{x\in\mathbb R_{++}^n:\sum_i x_i=1\}\). Adopt \(0\log0=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite probability simplex with the negative Shannon entropy generator. The second divergence argument lies in the relative interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the negative-entropy generator on \(\Delta_n\) by
\[h(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\log x_i.\]
For \(x\in\Delta_n\) and \(y\in\Delta_n^{\circ}\), its Bregman divergence is
\[D_h(x,y)=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\log\frac{x_i}{y_i},\]
with each term having value \(0\) when \(x_i=0\). This is the Kullback-Leibler divergence from \(x\) to \(y\). In ambient positive-orthant coordinates, \(\nabla h(y)_i=1+\log y_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On the probability simplex, negative Shannon entropy generates the Kullback–Leibler divergence. The first argument may lie on the simplex boundary, while the second must have all coordinates positive. Zero coordinates in the first argument contribute zero under the convention 0 log 0=0.
assumptions_latex: \(h(x)=\sum_i x_i\log x_i\) uses the lower-semicontinuous convention \(0\log0=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_h(x,y)=\sum_i x_i\log(x_i/y_i)\geq0\), with equality exactly when \(x=y\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: On the positive orthant before imposing unit mass, the same generator yields \(D_h(x,y)=\sum_i[x_i\log(x_i/y_i)-x_i+y_i]\).
For simplex points, the linear terms cancel because \(\sum_i x_i=\sum_i y_i=1\).
special_cases_latex: For a vertex \(e_j\) and \(y\in\Delta_n^{\circ}\), \(D_h(e_j,y)=-\log y_j\).
For the uniform point \(u_i=1/n\), \(D_h(x,u)=\log n+\sum_i x_i\log x_i\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The divergence becomes infinite under the extended convention if some \(x_i>0\) while \(y_i=0\).
The entropic mirror coordinate is logarithmic componentwise, modulo the affine normal direction of the simplex.
The divergence is generally asymmetric.
boundary_notes: The gradient of the entropy generator is not finite at zero, so the base point must lie in the relative interior.
The formula is classical relative entropy, not the symmetric Jensen-Shannon divergence.
Simplex mirror coordinates are defined only up to adding a common scalar when viewed intrinsically on the affine hull.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Delta_n:=\{x\in\mathbb R_+^n:\sum_{i=1}^n x_i=1\}\) and \(\Delta_n^\circ:=\{x\in\Delta_n:x_i>0\text{ for every }i\}\). Define the ambient negative-entropy function by \[\widetilde h(x):=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\log x_i,\qquad x\in\mathbb R_+^n,\] with \(0\log 0=0\), and let \(h\) be its restriction to \(\Delta_n\). Then \(h\) is continuous and convex on \(\Delta_n\), strictly convex on \(\Delta_n^\circ\), and differentiable relative to the affine hull there. The ambient gradient representative supplied by \(\widetilde h\) satisfies \[(\nabla\widetilde h(x))_i=1+\log x_i\qquad(x\in\Delta_n^\circ).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negative entropy is the restriction to the simplex of the coordinate sum x log x. It is strictly convex and relatively smooth in the simplex interior, where its displayed derivative is the gradient of the ambient positive-orthant extension.

Define \(H:\mathbb R^n	o(-\infty,+\infty]\) by \(H(x)=\sum_i x_i\log x_i\) for \(x\in\Delta_n\) and \(H(x)=+\infty\) otherwise. Then \[H^*(z)=\log\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^n e^{z_i}ight),\qquad (
abla H^*(z))_i= rac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_j e^{z_j}}.\] Moreover, \(H^*(z+c\mathbf1)=H^*(z)+c\) and \(
abla H^*(z+c\mathbf1)=
abla H^*(z)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Failure of Metric Symmetry and Triangle Inequality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp warning that probability-coordinate relative entropy is a divergence rather than a metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(p=(1,0)\), \(q=(1/2,1/2)\), and \(r=(1/4,3/4)\), \[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)=\log2\quad\text{but}\quad D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\|p)=+\infty,\] so symmetry fails. Moreover, \[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|r)=\log4>D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\|r),\] so the triangle inequality fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: KL divergence is generally asymmetric and does not satisfy the triangle inequality.
assumptions_latex: The standard extended-value support convention is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}\) is neither symmetric nor a metric.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-alphabet Gibbs variational formula and its attainment boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(p,q\in\Delta_n\) and \(q_i>0\) for every \(i\), then \[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)=\sup_{a\in\mathbb R^n}\left\{\langle a,p\rangle-\log\left(\sum_{i=1}^n q_i e^{a_i}\right)\right\}.\] If \(p_i>0\) for every \(i\), the maximizers are exactly \(a_i=\log(p_i/q_i)+c\), \(c\in\mathbb R\). If some \(p_i=0\), the supremum is unchanged but has no finite maximizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: KL divergence is the convex dual of weighted log-sum-exp, with a finite maximizing potential exactly when the first distribution has full support.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)=\sup_a\{\langle a,p\rangle-\log\sum_iq_ie^{a_i}\}\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint convexity and stochastic-channel contraction of finite-alphabet relative entropy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For probability vectors \(p^{(r)},q^{(r)}\) and weights \(\alpha_r\ge0\) with \(\sum_r\alpha_r=1\), \[D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\sum_r\alpha_rp^{(r)}\middle\|\sum_r\alpha_rq^{(r)}\right)\le\sum_r\alpha_rD_{\mathrm{KL}}(p^{(r)}\|q^{(r)}).\] If \(K\) is a finite-state stochastic channel, then \[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Kp\|Kq)\le D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: KL divergence is jointly convex and cannot increase when both probability vectors pass through the same stochastic channel.
assumptions_latex: All displayed vectors are finite probability vectors.
\(K\) is a stochastic channel acting on those vectors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Kp\|Kq)\le D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Log-Determinant Bregman Geometry on Positive-Definite Matrices
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathbb S^{n}\) be the real symmetric matrices with trace pairing \(\langle A,B\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(AB)\), and let \(\mathbb S_{++}^{n}\) be the positive-definite cone. Define \(h(X)=-\log\det X=-\operatorname{tr}(\log X)\) on \(\mathbb S_{++}^{n}\) and \(h(X)=+\infty\) otherwise.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional spectral Bregman geometry generated specifically by the negative log-determinant barrier. Broader trace-spectral generators are nearby variants, not part of this definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(X,Y\in\mathbb S_{++}^{n}\), \[\nabla h(Y)=-Y^{-1},\qquad D_h(X,Y):=h(X)-h(Y)-\langle\nabla h(Y),X-Y\rangle.\] The log-determinant spectral matrix divergence is \[D_h(X,Y)=\operatorname{tr}(Y^{-1}X)-\log\det(Y^{-1/2}XY^{-1/2})-n.\] The positive-definite cone equipped with this generator and divergence is the log-determinant spectral matrix Bregman geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The canonical geometry is generated on positive-definite symmetric matrices by the negative logarithm of the determinant. Its divergence is the trace of the relative matrix, minus the logarithm of its determinant, minus the matrix dimension.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{dom}D_h=\mathbb S_{++}^{n}\times\mathbb S_{++}^{n},\qquad D_h(X,Y)=\operatorname{tr}(Y^{-1}X)-\log\det(Y^{-1/2}XY^{-1/2})-n.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[D_h(X,Y)=-\log\det X+\log\det Y+\operatorname{tr}(Y^{-1}(X-Y)).\]
If \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n\) are the eigenvalues of \(Y^{-1/2}XY^{-1/2}\), then \[D_h(X,Y)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\lambda_i-\log\lambda_i-1).\]
special_cases_latex: For diagonal \(X=\operatorname{diag}(x)\) and \(Y=\operatorname{diag}(y)\), the divergence equals the Burg orthant divergence \(\sum_i(x_i/y_i-\log(x_i/y_i)-1)\).
For \(n=1\), the definition reduces to \(D_h(x,y)=x/y-\log(x/y)-1\).
immediate_consequences_latex: \[D_h(X,Y)\geq0,\qquad D_h(X,Y)=0\Longleftrightarrow X=Y.\]
For every invertible \(A\), \(D_h(AXA^{T},AYA^{T})=D_h(X,Y)\).

For a differentiable convex function \(\phi:I\to\mathbb R\), define \[F(X):=\sum_{i=1}^n\phi(\lambda_i(X)),\qquad X\in\Omega_I.\] Then \(F\) is convex, differentiable, and orthogonally invariant. If \[X=U\operatorname{Diag}(\lambda_1(X),\ldots,\lambda_n(X))U^T\] with \(U\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) orthogonal, then \[\nabla F(X)=U\operatorname{Diag}(\phi'(\lambda_1(X)),\ldots,\phi'(\lambda_n(X)))U^T.\] This matrix is independent of the chosen orthonormal eigenbasis, including when eigenvalues are repeated.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Second-Order Formula for a Separable Spectral Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hessian geometry of twice continuously differentiable separable spectral generators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\phi\in C^2(I)\), \(F(X)=\sum_{i=1}^n\phi(\lambda_i(X))\), and \(X=U\operatorname{Diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n)U^T\in\Omega_I\). For \(H\in\mathbb S^n\), set \(\widetilde H=U^THU\). Then \[\nabla^2F(X)[H,H]=\sum_{i=1}^n\phi''(\lambda_i)\widetilde H_{ii}^2+2\sum_{i<j}\phi'^{[1]}(\lambda_i,\lambda_j)\widetilde H_{ij}^2,\] where \[\phi'^{[1]}(s,t)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{\phi'(s)-\phi'(t)}{s-t},&s\ne t,\\\phi''(s),&s=t.\end{cases}\] This value is independent of the eigenbasis selected within repeated-eigenvalue eigenspaces.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the preceding setting, suppose \(0\le m\le L<\infty\) and \[m\le\phi''(t)\le L\qquad(t\in I).\] Then for every \(X\in\Omega_I\) and \(H\in\mathbb S^n\), \[m\|H\|_F^2\le\nabla^2F(X)[H,H]\le L\|H\|_F^2.\] Thus \(F\) is \(m\)-strongly convex when \(m>0\), and \(\nabla F\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz, relative to the Frobenius norm. Conversely, either matrix inequality holding for all \(X\in\Omega_I\) and \(H\in\mathbb S^n\) implies the corresponding scalar bound by taking \(X=tI_n\) and a rank-one diagonal direction.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\ge1\) be an integer. The positive-semidefinite and positive-definite cones in the space \(\mathbb S^n\) of real symmetric \(n\times n\) matrices are \[\mathbb S_+^n:=\{X\in\mathbb S^n:v^TXv\ge0\text{ for every }v\in\mathbb R^n\},\qquad \mathbb S_{++}^n:=\{X\in\mathbb S^n:v^TXv>0\text{ for every }v\in\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}\}.\] Equivalently, \(X\in\mathbb S_{++}^n\) exactly when \(\lambda_{\min}(X)>0\). Moreover, \[\mathbb S_{++}^n=\operatorname{int}(\mathbb S_+^n).\] The set \(\mathbb S_{++}^n\) is an open convex cone and is invariant under congruence by every invertible matrix \(A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a positive integer n, positive-definite real symmetric n by n matrices have strictly positive quadratic forms, equivalently strictly positive eigenvalues, and form the interior of the positive-semidefinite cone.
knowledge_statements.title: Positive-Definite Cone

source_witnesses.locator: 8 Convex Functions p. 139

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Boundary Distance and Inverse Blowup on the Positive-Definite Cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interior-to-boundary geometry of the symmetric positive-definite cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(X\in\mathbb S_{++}^n\), \[\operatorname{dist}_F(X,\operatorname{bdry}\mathbb S_+^n)=\lambda_{\min}(X).\] Moreover, \[\overline{\mathbb S_{++}^n}=\mathbb S_+^n,\qquad \operatorname{bdry}\mathbb S_+^n=\{X\in\mathbb S_+^n:\lambda_{\min}(X)=0\}.\] Consequently, if \(X_k\in\mathbb S_{++}^n\) converges to a singular \(\bar X\in\mathbb S_+^n\), then \(\|X_k^{-1}\|_2=1/\lambda_{\min}(X_k)\to+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The PSD cone is the closure of the positive-definite cone, its boundary consists of singular PSD matrices, and the Frobenius distance from a positive-definite matrix to that boundary is its smallest eigenvalue. Inversion blows up at the boundary.
assumptions_latex: Distance uses the Frobenius norm and inverse size uses the spectral operator norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\overline{\mathbb S_{++}^n}=\mathbb S_+^n\), the boundary is characterized by \(\lambda_{\min}=0\), and inverse norms diverge along positive-definite approaches to it.
knowledge_statements.title: Boundary Distance and Inverse Blowup on the Positive-Definite Cone

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure, Boundary, and Inverse Blowup of the Positive-Definite Cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interior-to-boundary geometry of the symmetric positive-definite cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(X\in\mathbb S_{++}^n\), the Frobenius distance to the boundary of the positive-semidefinite cone is \[\operatorname{dist}_F(X,\operatorname{bdry}\mathbb S_+^n)=\lambda_{\min}(X).\] Moreover, \[\overline{\mathbb S_{++}^n}=\mathbb S_+^n,\qquad \operatorname{bdry}\mathbb S_+^n=\{X\in\mathbb S_+^n:\lambda_{\min}(X)=0\}.\] Consequently, if \(X_k\in\mathbb S_{++}^n\) converges to a singular \(\bar X\in\mathbb S_+^n\), then \(\|X_k^{-1}\|_2=1/\lambda_{\min}(X_k)\to+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The positive-semidefinite cone is the closure of the positive-definite cone, its boundary consists of singular positive-semidefinite matrices, and distance to that boundary equals the smallest eigenvalue. Inversion therefore blows up on approach to a singular boundary point.
assumptions_latex: Distances use the Frobenius norm and inverse norms use the spectral norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\overline{\mathbb S_{++}^n}=\mathbb S_+^n\), \(\operatorname{dist}_F(X,\operatorname{bdry}\mathbb S_+^n)=\lambda_{\min}(X)\), and inverse norms diverge along positive-definite approaches to a singular boundary point.
knowledge_statements.title: Closure, Boundary, and Inverse Blowup of the Positive-Definite Cone

children.title: Eigenvalue-Induced Divergences
children.top_down_role: Matrix divergences organized through eigenvalue-level structure.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unordered Spectra Do Not Determine Divergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of any formula based only on the two separately unordered spectra when their relative eigenvector alignment is unspecified.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(X)=\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(X^2)\), \(X=\operatorname{Diag}(1,0)\), \(Y_1=\operatorname{Diag}(1,0)\), and \(Y_2=\operatorname{Diag}(0,1)\). Although \(Y_1\) and \(Y_2\) have the same unordered eigenvalues, \[D_F(X,Y_1)=0,\qquad D_F(X,Y_2)=\tfrac12\lVert X-Y_2\rVert_F^2=1.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Separate unordered spectra do not determine a spectral Bregman divergence because relative eigenspace alignment matters.
assumptions_latex: The matrices are real symmetric \(2\times2\) matrices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda(Y_1)=\lambda(Y_2)\) as unordered multisets but \(D_F(X,Y_1)\ne D_F(X,Y_2)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Unordered Spectra Do Not Determine Divergence

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Aligned scalar decomposition for commuting symmetric matrices; eigenvalues are paired in a common eigenbasis rather than independently sorted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=U\operatorname{diag}(x_1,\ldots,x_n)U^\top\) and \(Y=U\operatorname{diag}(y_1,\ldots,y_n)U^\top\), where \(x_i,y_i\in I\), and let \(F(X)=\operatorname{tr}f(X)\) for differentiable convex \(f:I\to\mathbb R\). Then \[D_F(X,Y)=\sum_{i=1}^n\bigl(f(x_i)-f(y_i)-f'(y_i)(x_i-y_i)\bigr).\] If \(f\) is strictly convex, this quantity is nonnegative and vanishes exactly when \(X=Y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For commuting symmetric matrices, a trace-spectral Bregman divergence is the sum of scalar divergences between eigenvalues aligned in a common eigenbasis.
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\in\mathbb S^n\) commute and have spectra in an interval \(I\).
Strict convexity is additionally assumed for the stated equality characterization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_F(X,Y)=\sum_i d_f(x_i,y_i)\ge0\), with equality under strict convexity exactly when \(X=Y\).

notation.meaning: scalar Bregman divergence generated by f

knowledge_statements.title: Commuting Eigenvalue Reduction

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bregman divergence generated by the negative log determinant on the positive-definite cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F(X)=-\log\det X\) and \(X,Y\in\mathbb S_{++}^n\), \[D_F(X,Y)=\operatorname{tr}(Y^{-1}X)-\log\det(Y^{-1}X)-n.\] If \(\mu_i>0\) are the eigenvalues of \(Y^{-1/2}XY^{-1/2}\), then \[D_F(X,Y)=\sum_{i=1}^n(\mu_i-\log\mu_i-1)\ge0,\] with equality exactly when \(X=Y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The negative-log-determinant Bregman divergence is a sum of scalar Burg divergences of relative generalized eigenvalues.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_F(X,Y)=\sum_i(\mu_i-\log\mu_i-1)\ge0\), with equality iff \(X=Y\).
knowledge_statements.title: Log-Determinant Matrix Divergence

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matrix Bregman divergence induced by the trace negative-entropy generator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F(X)=\operatorname{tr}(X\log X)\) and \(X,Y\in\mathbb S_{++}^n\), \[D_F(X,Y)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(X(\log X-\log Y)-X+Y\bigr)\ge0,\] with equality exactly when \(X=Y\). If \(\operatorname{tr}X=\operatorname{tr}Y\), this reduces to the Umegaki relative entropy \(\operatorname{tr}(X(\log X-\log Y))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Trace negative entropy generates the nonnegative matrix relative-entropy divergence, reducing to Umegaki relative entropy for equal-trace matrices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_F(X,Y)=\operatorname{tr}(X(\log X-\log Y)-X+Y)\ge0\), with equality iff \(X=Y\).
knowledge_statements.title: Trace-Entropy Matrix Divergence

assumptions_latex: \(f:I\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable and strictly convex on an interval containing their spectra.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[D_F(X,Y)=\sum_{i=1}^n d_f(\lambda_i(X),\lambda_i(Y))\ge 0,\] with equality exactly when \(X=Y\).

notation.meaning: Spectral trace function induced by the scalar generator
Eigenvalues paired in a common eigenbasis

knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the commuting-matrix reduction; noncommuting spectral divergences generally depend on eigenvectors as well.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X=U\operatorname{diag}(x_1,\ldots,x_n)U^\top\) and \(Y=U\operatorname{diag}(y_1,\ldots,y_n)U^\top\), with every \(x_i,y_i\in I\). For \(F(X)=\operatorname{tr}f(X)\), its matrix Bregman divergence is
\[D_F(X,Y)=F(X)-F(Y)-\langle f'(Y),X-Y\rangle_F=\sum_{i=1}^n\bigl(f(x_i)-f(y_i)-f'(y_i)(x_i-y_i)\bigr).\]
Thus the divergence is the sum of scalar eigenvalue divergences. Strict convexity of \(f\) gives \(D_F(X,Y)\ge 0\), and equality holds if and only if \(x_i=y_i\) for every \(i\), equivalently \(X=Y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For commuting symmetric matrices, a trace-spectral Bregman divergence equals the sum of scalar Bregman divergences between correspondingly paired eigenvalues.
knowledge_statements.title: Eigenvalue-Induced Divergences

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The commuting, simultaneously diagonalized representation is mathematically plausible and the representation content kind fits this leaf, but the record supplies no citation supporting the matrix-gradient formula, aligned eigenvalue reduction, and strict equality condition. Source support is required before the formulation can be reliably reviewed.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Spectra Alone Do Not Determine Noncommuting Divergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp failure of an eigenvalue-only pairing formula without a common eigenbasis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(X)=\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(X^2)\) on \(\mathbb S^2\), \(X=\operatorname{Diag}(1,0)\), \(Y_1=\operatorname{Diag}(1,0)\), and \(Y_2=\operatorname{Diag}(0,1)\). The matrices \(Y_1\) and \(Y_2\) have the same unordered eigenvalues, but \[D_F(X,Y_1)=0,\qquad D_F(X,Y_2)=\tfrac12\lVert X-Y_2\rVert_F^2=1.\] Therefore the separate unordered spectra of \(X\) and \(Y\) do not determine a spectral Bregman divergence when eigenvector alignment is unspecified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two reference matrices with identical eigenvalues can give different spectral Bregman divergences because their eigenvectors are aligned differently with the first argument.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda(Y_1)=\lambda(Y_2)\) but \(D_F(X,Y_1)\ne D_F(X,Y_2)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Spectra Alone Do Not Determine Noncommuting Divergence

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matrix Bregman divergence induced by the trace negative-entropy generator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F(X)=\operatorname{tr}(X\log X)\) on \(\mathbb S_{++}^n\), \[D_F(X,Y)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(X(\log X-\log Y)-X+Y\bigr).\] If \(\operatorname{tr}X=\operatorname{tr}Y\), this reduces to the Umegaki relative entropy \(\operatorname{tr}(X(\log X-\log Y))\), which is nonnegative and vanishes exactly when \(X=Y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The trace-entropy Bregman divergence is matrix relative entropy, reducing to Umegaki relative entropy for equal-trace positive-definite matrices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_F(X,Y)=\operatorname{tr}(X(\log X-\log Y)-X+Y)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Quantum Relative-Entropy Divergence

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) is a Legendre function if it is essentially smooth and essentially strictly convex. Essential smoothness means that \(\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\ne\varnothing\), that \(f\) is differentiable throughout \(\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\), and that \(\|\nabla f(x_k)\|\to+\infty\) whenever \(x_k\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\) converges to a boundary point of \(\operatorname{dom}f\). Essential strict convexity means that \(f\) is strictly convex on every convex subset of \(\operatorname{dom}\partial f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper closed convex function is Legendre when it is essentially smooth and essentially strictly convex.
knowledge_statements.title: Legendre Function Class

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine Stability and Failure Boundaries of the Legendre Class
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary invariance properties of finite-dimensional Legendre functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be Legendre. If \(\alpha>0\), \(a\in E^*\), and \(c\in\mathbb R\), then \[g(x)=\alpha f(x)+\langle a,x\rangle+c\] is Legendre and \(\operatorname{dom}g=\operatorname{dom}f\). If \(A:F\to E\) is an affine isomorphism, then \(f\circ A\) is Legendre on \(F\). These restrictions are essential in general: zero scaling destroys essential strict convexity, negative scaling destroys convexity, and a noninjective affine pullback can destroy essential strict convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive scaling, affine perturbation, and invertible affine changes of variables preserve Legendre functions; zero or negative scaling and noninjective pullbacks need not.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) and \(F\) are finite-dimensional real vector spaces.
\(\alpha>0\) and \(A:F\to E\) is an affine isomorphism.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha f+\langle a,\cdot\rangle+c\) and \(f\circ A\) are Legendre, subject to the stated sharp restrictions.
knowledge_statements.title: Affine Stability and Failure Boundaries of the Legendre Class

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine Stability of the Legendre Class
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary invariance properties of finite-dimensional Legendre functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be Legendre. If \(A:F\to E\) is an affine isomorphism, then \(f\circ A\) is Legendre on \(F\). Positivity and invertibility are essential: zero scaling destroys strict convexity, negative scaling generally destroys convexity, and a noninjective affine pullback generally destroys essential strict convexity.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the Legendre-type class, states the boundary of unrestricted Legendre conjugation, and records the injective-subdifferential characterization. The referenced essential-smoothness conditions are not expanded in this extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A pair \((C,f)\) is called a convex function of Legendre type when \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is open and convex and \(f\) is strictly convex on \(C\) and satisfies conditions \((a),(b)\), and \((c)\) (or \((c')\)) from the referenced definition of essential smoothness. The Legendre transformation gives a symmetric one-to-one correspondence on this class. In contrast, the Legendre conjugate of a general differentiable convex function need not be differentiable or convex, so its iterated Legendre conjugate need not be defined. Moreover, if \(\bar f\) is closed, proper, and convex and \(C=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}\bar f)\), then \(\partial\bar f\) is one-to-one if and only if \((C,\bar f|_C)\) is of Legendre type.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Legendre-type pair consists of an open convex set and a strictly convex function satisfying the cited essential-smoothness conditions. Legendre transformation is a symmetric one-to-one correspondence on this class, whereas unrestricted Legendre conjugation can fail to remain differentiable or convex. For a closed proper convex function, the subdifferential is one-to-one exactly when the function restricted to the interior of its domain is of Legendre type.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is strictly convex on }C\text{ and satisfies the cited conditions }(a),(b),\text{ and }(c)\text{ or }(c')
\bar f\text{ is closed, proper, and convex, with }C=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}\bar f),\text{ for the subdifferential characterization}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (C,f)\text{ is of Legendre type};\quad \text{Legendre transformation is symmetric and one-to-one on this class};\quad \partial\bar f\text{ is one-to-one}\iff(C,\bar f|_C)\text{ is of Legendre type}.

children.top_down_role: Interior differentiability or boundary behavior relevant to Legendre generators.

assumptions_latex: \(f:E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Approaching the domain boundary from its interior forces \(\|\nabla f\|\) to diverge.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is essentially smooth when \(U=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\) is nonempty, \(f\) is differentiable on \(U\), and for every sequence \((x_k)\subset U\) converging to any \(\bar x\in\operatorname{bdry}(\operatorname{dom}f)\),
\[\|\nabla f(x_k)\|\longrightarrow+\infty.\]
Consequently, no finite gradient limit can persist along an interior approach to the boundary. This boundary blow-up is intrinsic: changing to any equivalent norm on the finite-dimensional space leaves the condition unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Essential smoothness requires differentiability in the domain interior and unbounded gradient norm along every interior approach to its boundary.
knowledge_statements.title: Essential Smoothness Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Interior Differentiability Does Not Imply Essential Smoothness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp failure when the boundary-gradient condition is omitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(f:\mathbb R\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) by \[f(x)=\begin{cases}x^2,&x\ge0,\\+\infty,&x<0.\end{cases}\] Then \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, convex, and differentiable on \(\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)=(0,\infty)\), but for \(x_k\downarrow0\), \(f'(x_k)=2x_k\to0\). Thus \(f\) is not essentially smooth.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex function may be differentiable throughout its domain interior but fail essential smoothness because its gradient stays bounded near the boundary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Interior differentiability alone does not imply essential smoothness.
knowledge_statements.title: Interior Differentiability Does Not Imply Essential Smoothness

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel-conjugate characterization of essential smoothness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function on a finite-dimensional real vector space. Then \[f\text{ is essentially smooth}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f^*\text{ is essentially strictly convex}.\] Equivalently, \(f\) is essentially strictly convex if and only if \(f^*\) is essentially smooth.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fenchel conjugation exchanges essential smoothness and essential strict convexity.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex on a finite-dimensional real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is essentially smooth if and only if \(f^*\) is essentially strictly convex.
knowledge_statements.title: Essential Smoothness–Essential Strict Convexity Duality

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subdifferential Domain of an Essentially Smooth Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order boundary consequence of essential smoothness in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, convex, and essentially smooth, and put \(U=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\). Then \[\operatorname{dom}\partial f=U,\qquad \partial f(x)=\{\nabla f(x)\}\quad(x\in U).\] In particular, \(\partial f(x)=\varnothing\) for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\setminus U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an essentially smooth closed convex function, subgradients exist exactly in the domain interior and there equal the ordinary gradient; finite boundary points have no subgradient.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, convex, and essentially smooth.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dom}\partial f=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\), with singleton subdifferentials there and empty subdifferentials at finite boundary points.
