children.title: Curvature Certification Outcomes
children.top_down_role: Distinctions among certified, uncertified, malformed, and genuinely nonconvex expressions.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal V\) be a fixed sound verifier for a typed expression language \(\mathcal E\). Let \(\operatorname{WF}(e)\) denote syntactic and type well-formedness, and let \(\operatorname{Der}(e)\) be the set of curvature certificates derivable by its registered rules.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mutually distinguished outcomes of a fixed syntax-directed verifier. The taxonomy separates successful certification, inconclusive analysis, malformed expressions, metadata failure, and externally established nonconvexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The outcome map \(O:\mathcal E\to\mathcal O\) takes values in \[\mathcal O=\{\mathsf{certified}(\kappa),\mathsf{unknown},\mathsf{malformed},\mathsf{metadata\_failure},\mathsf{nonconvex\_established}\}.\] It is defined by: \(O(e)=\mathsf{malformed}\) when \(\neg\operatorname{WF}(e)\); \(O(e)=\mathsf{metadata\_failure}\) when analysis reaches missing, invalid, or inconsistent required metadata; \(O(e)=\mathsf{certified}(\kappa)\) when a sound certificate of requested curvature \(\kappa\) is derived; \(O(e)=\mathsf{nonconvex\_established}\) only when a separate valid countercertificate establishes failure of the requested curvature; and \(O(e)=\mathsf{unknown}\) otherwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The verifier distinguishes a derived curvature certificate from an inconclusive result, a malformed expression, a metadata failure, and a separately established failure of the requested curvature. In particular, unknown does not mean nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[O(e)=\begin{cases}\mathsf{malformed},&\neg\operatorname{WF}(e),\\\mathsf{metadata\_failure},&\text{required metadata are unusable},\\\mathsf{certified}(\kappa),&\kappa\in\operatorname{Der}(e),\\\mathsf{nonconvex\_established},&\text{a valid countercertificate exists},\\\mathsf{unknown},&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The taxonomy may be represented as a tagged sum so that diagnostic status is not conflated with the curvature lattice.
special_cases_latex: A well-formed convex function outside the grammar can have outcome \(\mathsf{unknown}\).
An atom called with incompatible shapes has outcome \(\mathsf{malformed}\), not \(\mathsf{unknown}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Only \(\mathsf{certified}(\kappa)\) authorizes reliance on the corresponding static certificate.
An unknown outcome carries no negative semantic assertion about the expression's actual curvature.
boundary_notes: The \(\mathsf{nonconvex\_established}\) tag requires evidence stronger than failure of disciplined rules.
Implementations may refine diagnostics but must preserve these semantic distinctions.
This taxonomy does not rank alternative valid certificates.
review_flags: No inspected source defined this five-way outcome taxonomy, especially the countercertificate and metadata-failure distinctions.
knowledge_statements.title: Taxonomy of Static Curvature-Analysis Outcomes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports this five-way taxonomy. The outcome precedence is not fully specified when more than one condition applies, particularly metadata failure versus an otherwise derivable certificate.

children.title: Certified Curvature Outcomes
children.top_down_role: Expressions recognized by the disciplined grammar.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear-Time Certificate Checking under Constant-Time Local Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural checking cost, excluding arithmetic bit complexity and derivation of semantic side conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a curvature certificate be a rooted tree with \(N\) bounded-arity nodes and height \(h\). If registered metadata lookup and every recorded local-premise check take \(O(1)\) time, then a depth-first bottom-up checker runs in \(O(N)\) time and uses \(O(h)\) auxiliary traversal space when child states may be discarded after checking their parent. Costs for deriving or independently verifying range, domain, and arithmetic predicates must be added separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With bounded arity and constant-time local checks, a curvature derivation tree is verifiable in linear time and depth-proportional auxiliary space; semantic side-condition costs are additional.
assumptions_latex: \text{The certificate is a rooted tree with }N\text{ bounded-arity nodes and height }h.
\text{Metadata lookup and every recorded local-premise check cost }O(1).
\text{A depth-first checker may discard child states after checking their parent.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_{\mathrm{check}}(N)=O(N),\qquad S_{\mathrm{aux}}=O(h).
review_flags: The bound excludes arithmetic bit complexity, metadata-oracle cost, certificate storage, and independent derivation of semantic side conditions.
knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Time Certificate Checking under Constant-Time Local Access

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Soundness of a Completed Curvature Derivation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic guarantee furnished by a locally valid disciplined-curvature derivation tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose every primitive metadata assertion and every inference rule in a disciplined curvature grammar is semantically sound on its recorded domain. If a finite derivation tree for expression \(e\) passes every local premise check and assigns root label \(\kappa\in\{\mathrm{constant},\mathrm{affine},\mathrm{convex},\mathrm{concave}\}\), then \(e\) has curvature \(\kappa\) on the inferred domain \(D_e\). The converse is not asserted: failure to construct such a tree does not imply that \(e\) lacks the curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A locally valid derivation from sound metadata proves the reported root curvature, but absence of a derivation does not disprove that curvature.
assumptions_latex: \text{All primitive metadata assertions and inference rules are sound on their recorded domains.}
\text{The derivation tree for }e\text{ is finite and locally valid.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Derive}(e,\kappa,D_e)\Rightarrow e\text{ has curvature }\kappa\text{ on }D_e.
knowledge_statements.title: Soundness of a Completed Curvature Derivation

assumptions_latex: A fixed disciplined grammar supplies sound atom metadata and sound composition rules.
The expression has a finite syntax tree whose leaves have known curvature.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A completed derivation tree is a checkable certificate that the root expression has the reported curvature on its inferred domain.

notation.meaning: Certified curvature label of the expression.

review_flags: A canonical DCP source is required to support the recursive certification taxonomy.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Syntax-directed curvature certificates produced by a sound disciplined grammar.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A certified curvature outcome for \(e\) is a label \(\kappa(e)\in\{\mathrm{constant},\mathrm{affine},\mathrm{convex},\mathrm{concave}\}\) together with a finite derivation tree. Each leaf records a valid primitive label, and each internal node records an atom, certified child labels, required sign or range facts, applicable monotonicity metadata, and the composition rule yielding the parent label. The certificate also records \(D_e\). It is valid when every local premise is checkable and every rule application is sound on \(D_e\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A certified outcome consists of a curvature label and a finite, locally checkable derivation using valid atom, sign, range, domain, and composition metadata.
knowledge_statements.title: Certified Curvature Outcomes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate content kind is appropriate for the stated derivation-tree object, but no source supports this exact certificate structure or outcome taxonomy.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(e\) be a well-formed expression, \(\Gamma_e\) its inferred domain predicate, and \(\kappa\in\{\mathsf{constant},\mathsf{affine},\mathsf{convex},\mathsf{concave}\}\). Let \(C_e=\{x:\Gamma_e(x)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive result of a fixed sound disciplined grammar. Certification is relative to the expression tree, metadata environment, inferred domain, and requested curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A certified curvature outcome for \(e\) is a finite derivation object \(\Pi_e\) whose leaves are valid leaf or atom metadata and whose internal steps are registered sound propagation rules, with root judgment \[\Pi_e:\quad \Gamma_e\vdash e:\kappa.\] Validity requires \(C_e\) to be an admissible convex domain and requires the function denoted by \(e\) to have curvature \(\kappa\) on \(C_e\). The reported outcome is the tuple \(\mathsf{certified}(e,,_e,_e)\), not merely the label \(\kappa\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An expression has a certified outcome when a finite derivation, built only from valid metadata and sound propagation rules, concludes a curvature judgment on the inferred convex domain. The outcome records the expression, curvature, domain predicate, and certificate object.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[O(e)=\mathsf{certified}(e,\kappa,\Gamma_e,\Pi_e)\Longrightarrow e\text{ has curvature \(\kappa\) on }C_e=\{x:\Gamma_e(x)\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: A certificate can equivalently be stored as the annotated expression tree whose root label is \(\kappa\).
special_cases_latex: An affine certificate simultaneously entails valid convex and concave interpretations.
A constant expression may use the most specific label \(\mathsf{constant}\) while also satisfying affine, convex, and concave curvature.
immediate_consequences_latex: The certificate can be checked without rediscovering the expression's curvature.
The certified domain is part of the result and cannot be silently enlarged.
boundary_notes: Certification is sufficient, not complete.
A certificate relative to one metadata registry need not remain valid after metadata changes.
The definition does not imply that a canonical conic representation exists.
review_flags: No inspected source directly defined certified outcomes as the stated derivation tuple.
knowledge_statements.title: Certified Curvature Outcome

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports the derivation-object definition. The displayed reported tuple \(\mathsf{certified}(e,,_e,_e)\) is corrupted and does not match the four-component tuple stated in the plain text and conclusion.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear-Time Certificate Checking under Constant-Time Metadata Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural checking cost, excluding arithmetic bit complexity and metadata-oracle cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a curvature certificate contain \(N\) syntax-tree nodes. If each node has bounded arity, registered metadata lookup and each local rule check take \(O(1)\) time, and referenced sign, range, and domain facts are supplied in directly checkable form, then a bottom-up certificate checker runs in \(O(N)\) time and uses \(O(h)\) traversal space, where \(h\) is the tree height. Without these access assumptions, the cost of proving range, domain, or arithmetic predicates must be added separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With bounded arity and constant-time metadata and premise checks, a curvature derivation is verifiable in time linear in its tree size; expensive semantic side conditions are excluded and must be counted separately.
assumptions_latex: \text{The certificate has }N\text{ bounded-arity nodes and height }h.
\text{Metadata lookup and every recorded local-premise check cost }O(1).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_{\mathrm{check}}(N)=O(N),\qquad S_{\mathrm{check}}=O(h).
review_flags: Bound excludes bit complexity and the cost of independently deriving semantic side conditions.
knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Time Certificate Checking under Constant-Time Metadata Access

children.title: Unknown-Curvature Outcomes
children.top_down_role: Expressions whose curvature is not certified by the selected grammar.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epistemic meaning of an unknown result from a fixed syntax-directed curvature verifier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed grammar \(\mathcal G\), expression representation, and metadata database, the outcome \(\kappa(e)=\mathrm{unknown}\) means that no available derivation assigns a definite root label such as constant, affine, convex, or concave. It is not a certificate that the represented function violates convexity or concavity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unknown means that the selected verifier cannot derive a definite curvature label, not that the represented function is nonconvex or nonconcave.
assumptions_latex: The verifier's grammar, expression representation, and metadata database are fixed.
The verifier is sound but need not be complete.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\kappa(e)=\mathrm{unknown}\not\Rightarrow e\text{ is nonconvex or nonconcave}.

notation.meaning: Curvature outcome returned for expression e

review_flags: The set and names of definite labels vary by verifier.
knowledge_statements.title: Unknown-Curvature Outcomes

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unknown Curvature Relative to a Disciplined Grammar
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Fix a metadata environment \(M\), a sound rule set \(G\), a well-formed expression \(e\), and a requested curvature class \(\kappa\). Write \(M,G\vdash e:\kappa\) when the grammar derives the requested certificate.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epistemic failure of a selected certification grammar, not a semantic assertion that the represented function is nonconvex or nonconcave.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The outcome for \(e\) is unknown curvature relative to \((M,G,\kappa)\) when \[\operatorname{WF}(e),\qquad M\text{ is usable along the analyzed tree},\qquad M,G\nvdash e:\kappa,\] and no accepted countercertificate establishes failure of curvature \(\kappa\). The tagged result is \[O_{M,G,}(e)=\mathsf{unknown}.\] Thus unknown records the absence of a derivation within the selected grammar while leaving the expression's actual curvature undecided.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unknown curvature means that a well-formed expression could not be certified by the selected metadata and rules, and no valid countercertificate establishes that the requested curvature fails. It is an inconclusive grammar-relative outcome.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[O_{M,G,\kappa}(e)=\mathsf{unknown}\not\Longrightarrow e\text{ fails to have curvature \(\kappa\)}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Unknown is the residual well-formed outcome after excluding successful derivation, malformed syntax, metadata failure, and established semantic failure.
special_cases_latex: A convex function written in a form not recognized by \(G\) can be unknown.
An expression may be unknown for convexity but certified for quasiconvexity under a different grammar.
immediate_consequences_latex: Rewriting the expression or enriching metadata may change an unknown outcome into a certified one.
Rejecting an optimization model solely because of an unknown tag is a policy decision, not a proof of nonconvexity.
boundary_notes: Unknown must not be labeled nonconvex.
Missing mandatory metadata belongs to the metadata-failure category when that distinction is available.
The outcome is relative to the requested curvature and the fixed grammar version.

notation.meaning: No derivation of the requested curvature exists in the selected system.

review_flags: No inspected source directly supported this grammar-relative unknown-outcome definition.
knowledge_statements.title: Unknown Curvature Relative to a Disciplined Grammar

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports this grammar-relative definition. The main statement writes \(O_{M,G,}(e)\), omitting \(\kappa\), while the conclusion uses \(O_{M,G,\kappa}(e)\).

children.title: Metadata-Inference Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Lost or invalid certificates caused by insufficient or inconsistent metadata.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: At an atom node \(v=a(v_1,,v_k)\), let \(S_i\) be the inferred child states and let \(M_a\) be the registered atom metadata. The transfer operation is a partial map \(F_a(M_a;S_1,,S_k)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local boundary at which structural propagation cannot produce a sound state because required metadata are absent, ill-typed, inconsistent, or inapplicable. This is distinct from a sound but inconclusive unknown-curvature result.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The metadata-inference failure boundary is the set \[\mathcal B_M:=\{(a,S_1,,S_k):F_a(M_a;S_1,,S_k)\text{ is undefined because }M_a\text{ is missing, inconsistent, ill-typed, or invalid on the inferred ranges}\}.\] An expression has a metadata-inference failure when its postorder traversal first reaches a node whose local configuration lies in \(\mathcal B_M\). No curvature certificate may be propagated through that node unless conservative replacement metadata yield a separately sound transfer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The failure boundary consists of atom-and-child-state configurations for which the metadata transfer operation is undefined because necessary declarations are missing, inconsistent, ill-typed, or invalid on the inferred ranges. Analysis cannot soundly pass that node without valid replacement metadata.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[(a,S_1,\ldots,S_k)\in\mathcal B_M\Longrightarrow F_a(M_a;S_1,\ldots,S_k)\text{ supplies no curvature certificate}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The boundary is the complement of the domain of the partial transfer map: \(\mathcal B_M=(\mathcal A\times\mathcal S^k)\setminus\operatorname{dom}F\), restricted to well-typed node configurations.
special_cases_latex: An atom with no curvature declaration lies on the boundary when curvature propagation requires that declaration.
Conflicting claims that an atom is both strictly increasing and strictly decreasing on the same nonconstant interval constitute inconsistent metadata.
A child range outside every declared metadata cell makes the regional transfer inapplicable.
immediate_consequences_latex: Ancestors of a failed node cannot receive certificates that depend on the missing state.
A diagnostic can identify the first failing node and the missing metadata component.
boundary_notes: A defined transfer returning \(\mathsf{unknown}\) is not itself metadata failure.
An expression can be mathematically well-defined even when its analyzer metadata fail.
The boundary depends on the metadata registry and abstract-state precision.

notation.meaning: Partial metadata transfer operation for atom \(a\).

review_flags: The exact partial-transfer failure boundary is a proposed formalization without inspected source support.
knowledge_statements.title: Boundary of Metadata-Driven Inference

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports the proposed partial-transfer boundary. Several argument lists contain malformed double commas, and the complement formulation introduces \(\mathcal A\), \(\mathcal S\), and a global map \(F\) without defining them consistently.

children.title: Domain-Inference Failures
children.top_down_role: Certificate loss caused by missing or invalid domain information.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure to establish the argument-domain or rule-validity inclusion required by a composition certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(e(z)=f(g_1(z),\ldots,g_m(z))\), let \(D_f\) be the declared domain of \(f\), and let \(R\subseteq D_f\) be a region on which a candidate rule is valid. A domain-inference failure occurs when the verifier cannot certify \((g_1(z),\ldots,g_m(z))\in R\) throughout the analyzed domain. The rule must then be withheld, even when the inclusion is mathematically true but unavailable to the verifier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A domain-inference failure is the inability to prove the argument-domain inclusion required by an atom or composition rule; it does not establish that the inclusion is false.
assumptions_latex: The verifier applies only rules whose domain and validity premises have been certified.
The range information used by the verifier is sound but may be incomplete.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nvdash (g_1(z),\ldots,g_m(z))\in R\) implies that the rule requiring this inclusion is unavailable.

notation.meaning: Declared domain of the outer atom
Region on which a candidate rule is valid

review_flags: Abstract verifier model; particular domain-propagation mechanisms are implementation dependent.
knowledge_statements.title: Domain-Inference Failure Boundary

assumptions_latex: A composition \(e(z)=f(g_1(z),\ldots,g_m(z))\) is submitted to the verifier.
Applying an available rule requires certification that the argument tuple belongs to a region \(R\subseteq D_f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Failure to derive the required domain inclusion blocks that rule and may force an unknown outcome, even if the inclusion is mathematically true.

notation.meaning: Metadata validity region required by a rule.

review_flags: No supplied locator addresses domain-inference failure in disciplined curvature verification.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certification failure caused by an unproved atom-domain inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A domain-inference failure occurs when the verifier cannot derive \[(g_1(z),\ldots,g_m(z))\in R\subseteq D_f\] for every \(z\) in the current feasible domain, although a candidate composition rule requires this inclusion. The rule must then be withheld because the outer atom may be undefined or its metadata may be invalid outside \(R\). This is an inference failure rather than evidence that the mathematical inclusion is false. Adding explicit constraints or stronger range propagation can change the outcome without changing the represented function on its feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Domain inference fails when a required argument-to-domain inclusion cannot be certified, so the corresponding composition rule cannot be applied.
knowledge_statements.title: Domain-Inference Failures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary content kind fits the node, but the claimed inference behavior and remediation mechanisms are verifier-specific and uncited.

children.title: Sign-Inference Failures
children.top_down_role: Certificate loss caused by unresolved or invalid sign information.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure to establish a sign regime required by conditional curvature or monotonicity metadata.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a candidate rule is valid only when the argument tuple belongs to a sign regime \(S\), and the verifier has sound inferred ranges \(R_i\) for arguments \(g_i\). A sign-inference failure occurs when \(R_1\times\cdots\times R_m\nsubseteq S\). The sign-conditioned rule must then be withheld, even if a stronger analysis would establish the required sign property.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sign inference fails when sound inferred ranges do not establish the sign regime required by a conditional rule.
assumptions_latex: The candidate rule has an explicit sign premise \((g_1,\ldots,g_m)\in S\).
Each inferred range \(R_i\) soundly over-approximates the attainable values of \(g_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: R_1\times\cdots\times R_m\nsubseteq S\Rightarrow\text{the sign-conditioned rule is unavailable}.

notation.meaning: Sign regime required by the candidate rule
Sound inferred range of argument i

review_flags: Range domains and sign lattices vary across verifier implementations.
knowledge_statements.title: Sign-Inference Failure Boundary

assumptions_latex: A composition rule requires a sign regime \(S\) for one or more arguments.
The verifier's sign analysis returns an over-approximation of each argument's possible values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If the inferred ranges do not imply membership in \(S\), sign-conditioned metadata cannot be invoked and curvature certification may fail.
review_flags: No supplied locator addresses sign-analysis failure in disciplined curvature verification.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certification failure caused by an unproved argument-sign condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A sign-inference failure occurs when a rule requires \((g_1(z),\ldots,g_m(z))\in S\) throughout the feasible domain, but the inferred ranges \(R_i\) do not establish that inclusion. For example, metadata restricted to \(g_i(z)\geq0\) is unavailable when \(R_i\) contains both negative and nonnegative values. The verifier must not select the restricted metadata merely because the true expression may satisfy the sign condition. Stronger constraints, range analysis, or an equivalent representation may permit certification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sign inference fails when inferred argument ranges do not prove the sign regime required by conditional curvature or monotonicity metadata.
knowledge_statements.title: Sign-Inference Failures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement matches the sign-inference failure container, but the range-analysis and conditional-metadata behavior require an authoritative source.

children.title: Insufficient Metadata
children.top_down_role: Uncertified expressions arising from metadata that is too weak for structural verification.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Missing, but noncontradictory, premises for every candidate structural rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal R\) be the candidate rules at a syntax node, let \(P(r)\) be the certified premises required by \(r\), and let \(M\) be the available certified facts. Metadata are insufficient at the node when \(P(r)\nsubseteq M\) for every \(r\in\mathcal R\), while the available facts remain consistent. No candidate rule can then derive a definite curvature label.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metadata are insufficient when every candidate rule lacks at least one required certified fact, without the metadata being contradictory.
assumptions_latex: Candidate rules and their premise sets are fixed.
Only certified facts in \(M\) may discharge rule premises.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigl(\forall r\in\mathcal R,\ P(r)\nsubseteq M\bigr)\Rightarrow\) no candidate rule is applicable.

notation.meaning: Candidate rules at the syntax node
Certified premises required by rule r

review_flags: The exact premise vocabulary is verifier dependent.
knowledge_statements.title: Insufficient Metadata

children.title: Inconsistent Metadata
children.top_down_role: Malformed verification states arising from conflicting structural metadata.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Contradictory declarations and propagated consequences in an abstract structural verifier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M(G)\) be the metadata constraints asserted or soundly propagated on an expression graph \(G\), and let \(\mathcal A(G)\) be the set of attribute assignments satisfying them. The metadata are inconsistent exactly when \(\mathcal A(G)=\varnothing\). In that state no curvature certificate may soundly be derived from the metadata; the state must be rejected or reported as inconsistent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metadata are inconsistent exactly when no assignment satisfies all declarations and sound propagation constraints; certification from that state is invalid.
assumptions_latex: Every propagation constraint included in \(M(G)\) is sound under the verifier's declared semantics.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal A(G)=\varnothing\Rightarrow\) no sound metadata-based curvature label is available.
review_flags: Constraint vocabulary and consistency-checking procedure are implementation dependent.
knowledge_statements.title: Inconsistent Metadata

children.title: Equivalent-Rewriting Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Different certification outcomes for mathematically equivalent expression structures.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation-dependent outcomes of a fixed, sound but incomplete syntax-directed curvature verifier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be a fixed syntax-directed curvature verifier. Equivalent-rewriting sensitivity occurs when \(\llbracket e_1\rrbracket=\llbracket e_2\rrbracket\) on their common domain but \(V(e_1)\ne V(e_2)\). For example, \(\sqrt{x^2+1}=\lVert(x,1)\rVert_2\); a verifier that recognizes the norm representation but cannot apply its composition rules to the square-root representation certifies only the latter.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mathematically equivalent expression trees can receive different outcomes from a sound but incomplete syntax-directed verifier; the square-root and norm forms give a standard conditional witness.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is sound, syntax-directed, and uses a fixed atom library and rule set.
Expression equality is evaluated on the common effective domain.
For the stated witness, \(V\) recognizes the norm form but lacks an applicable rule for the square-root form.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\llbracket e_1\rrbracket=\llbracket e_2\rrbracket\not\Rightarrow V(e_1)=V(e_2)\).

notation.meaning: Function represented by expression tree e

review_flags: Verifier behavior in the example is explicitly conditional on its atom library and rules.
knowledge_statements.title: Equivalent-Rewriting Sensitivity

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\llbracket e\rrbracket\) denote the extended-valued function represented by expression \(e\), and let \(O_G(e)\) be the outcome of a fixed syntax-directed grammar \(G\). Define semantic equivalence by \(e_1\equiv e_2\) when their domains and values agree.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sensitivity of a structural verifier to syntactic representation. Equivalence includes equality of effective domains, not merely equality on points where both formulas happen to be finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A grammar \(G\) is equivalent-rewriting sensitive on a pair \((e_1,e_2)\) when \[e_1\equiv e_2\quad\text{and}\quad O_G(e_1)\neq O_G(e_2).\] In particular, certification sensitivity occurs when \(e_1\equiv e_2\), one expression has outcome \(\mathsf{certified}(\kappa)\), and the other has outcome \(\mathsf{unknown}\) or metadata failure. The sensitivity set is \[\operatorname{Sens}(G)=\{(e_1,e_2):e_1\equiv e_2, O_G(e_1)
eq O_G(e_2)\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equivalent-rewriting sensitivity occurs when two expressions represent exactly the same extended-valued function, including the same domain, but a fixed structural grammar assigns them different certification outcomes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[(e_1,e_2)\in\operatorname{Sens}(G)\Longleftrightarrow \llbracket e_1\rrbracket=\llbracket e_2\rrbracket\text{ and }O_G(e_1)\neq O_G(e_2).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The grammar is rewriting invariant on a class \(\mathcal C\) exactly when \(\operatorname{Sens}(G)\cap(\mathcal C\times\mathcal C)=\varnothing\).
special_cases_latex: Associative regrouping can change an expression tree while preserving the represented function.
Introducing an auxiliary affine expression can expose a recognized composition without changing the projected function.
Two formulas equal only on a strict subset of their domains are not equivalent under this definition.
immediate_consequences_latex: Certification is a property of the expression representation together with the grammar, not solely of the denoted function.
A semantics-preserving normalizer can reduce sensitivity if it maps equivalent expressions to a common recognized form.
boundary_notes: Different diagnostics with the same certified curvature and domain need not count as materially different outcomes if the outcome map intentionally quotients diagnostics.
Semantic equivalence may itself be difficult to decide.
Rewriting must preserve implicit domains to qualify.

notation.meaning: Set of equivalent expression pairs with different outcomes.

review_flags: No inspected source directly formalized rewriting sensitivity using equality of extended-valued semantics and outcome inequality.
knowledge_statements.title: Certification Sensitivity Under Equivalent Rewriting

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically coherent and distinct, but no source supports the precise equality-of-extended-semantics and outcome-inequality formalization.

children.title: Certification-to-Compilation Boundary
children.top_down_role: The boundary between curvature verification in this chapter and graph reduction or conic canonicalization elsewhere.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Interface Between Curvature Certification and Canonical Compilation
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal V(e)=(\kappa_e,\Gamma_e,R_e,\Pi_e)\) be a successful static certificate. Let \(\mathcal C\) be a partial compiler mapping certified expressions or optimization models to a target graph, cone program, or other canonical representation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separation of semantic verification from representational reduction. Certification supplies admissibility facts; compilation additionally requires implementation-specific graph or cone representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The certification-to-compilation boundary is the interface type \[\mathsf{Cert}(e)=(e,\kappa_e,\Gamma_e,R_e,\Pi_e),\] together with the precondition \[\mathcal C(\mathsf{Cert}(e))\text{ is defined only if every atom in \(e\) has a target-compatible reduction and all generated domain obligations are representable}.\] Certification guarantees the asserted curvature and domain semantics but does not assert that \(\mathcal C\) is defined. Compilation correctness, when compilation succeeds, requires semantic equivalence between the source expression on \(\Gamma_e\) and the projection or value function of the generated target representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The boundary passes a certified expression, its curvature, domain, range, and certificate to a separate compiler. Certification alone does not guarantee compilability: every atom must also have a target-compatible reduction, and all domain obligations must be representable. Successful compilation must preserve the certified semantics.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{Certified}(e)\centernot\Longrightarrow e\in\operatorname{dom}\mathcal C,\qquad e\in\operatorname{dom}\mathcal C\Longrightarrow \llbracket\mathcal C(e)\rrbracket\equiv\llbracket e\rrbracket\text{ on }\Gamma_e.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The boundary may be viewed as two partial maps: \(\mathcal E\xrightarrow{\mathcal V}\mathsf{Cert}\xrightarrow{\mathcal C}\mathsf{Target}\).
special_cases_latex: A certified affine expression usually has a direct affine target representation.
A certified convex atom without a registered graph implementation is valid analytically but not compilable by that compiler.
An implicit domain condition may require additional target constraints during compilation.
immediate_consequences_latex: Curvature errors and missing-reduction errors are distinct diagnostics.
A new target reduction can make an already certified atom compilable without changing its curvature metadata.
boundary_notes: This definition does not prescribe a particular target cone or solver.
Compiler correctness is a separate obligation from verifier soundness.
Approximate or inexact reductions require an extended interface carrying approximation guarantees.

notation.meaning: Certificate package exported by static verification.

review_flags: No inspected local source directly specified the verifier/compiler interface and semantic-preservation contract.
knowledge_statements.title: Interface Between Curvature Certification and Canonical Compilation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports the proposed verifier/compiler interface. The conclusion asserts semantic equivalence whenever compilation is defined, but this follows only under an explicit compiler-correctness assumption, which is not included in the formal hypotheses.

children.title: Graph-Implementation Interface
children.top_down_role: Navigation from certified atoms to epigraph or hypograph implementations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact conversion between convex and concave graph templates by value negation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any extended-real function \(f\), \[(x,t)\in\operatorname{hypo}f\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(x,-t)\in\operatorname{epi}(-f).\] Consequently, an exact epigraph implementation of the convex function \(-f\) induces an exact hypograph implementation of the concave function \(f\) by negating the value coordinate, and conversely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A concave atom's hypograph implementation is an epigraph implementation of its negative after negating the value variable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{hypo}f=\{(x,t):(x,-t)\in\operatorname{epi}(-f)\}.
knowledge_statements.title: Epigraph–Hypograph Sign Conversion

assumptions_latex: Each certified atom has a registered exact conic or standard-form graph template.
The template's cone and affine maps are supported by the target compiler.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A certified atom can be compiled exactly through its registered epigraph or hypograph representation; curvature certification alone does not supply such a representation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact interface from certified atoms to registered standard-form graph templates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a certified convex atom \(f\), a graph implementation is data \(A,B,c,K\) satisfying \[\operatorname{epi} f=\{(x,t):\exists z,\;Ax+Bt+cz\in K\},\] with dimensions adjusted so that the displayed affine conic constraint is well defined. For a certified concave atom, the corresponding template represents \(\operatorname{hypo} f\). Compilation replaces an occurrence of the atom by an auxiliary value variable, auxiliary variables \(z\), and the registered graph constraints. Exactness requires equality with the epigraph or hypograph, not merely a relaxation. A curvature certificate without a registered template establishes shape but does not itself authorize compilation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compilation replaces a certified atom by an exact registered epigraph or hypograph formulation using auxiliary variables and supported standard-form constraints.
knowledge_statements.title: Graph-Implementation Interface

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind correctly fits the graph-implementation interface. However, the exact compilation claim lacks a supporting source, and the conic template uses ambiguous notation \(cz\) for an affine map of potentially vector-valued \(z\). A source-backed, dimensionally explicit template is required.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \[f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\},\qquad g:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\},\qquad K_i\subseteq\mathbb R^{q_i}\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\] where \(f\) is convex, \(g\) is concave, and each \(K_i\) is a designated closed convex cone. Auxiliary variables range over \(u\in\mathbb R^p\), and \(A_i,a_i,B_i,b_i\) have compatible finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional, exact lifted conic implementations are covered. The definition treats the epigraph of a convex atom and the hypograph of a concave atom; it does not assert that every convex or concave function possesses an implementation over a chosen cone catalogue.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[\operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,t):f(x)\le t\},\qquad \operatorname{hypo}g=\{(x,t):t\le g(x)\}.\] A convex graph-implementation interface for \(f\) is finite data \(\mathcal I_f=(p,m,(K_i,A_i,a_i,B_i,b_i)_{i=1}^m)\) satisfying \[\forall(x,t)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R:\quad f(x)\le t\iff \exists u\in\mathbb R^p\ \forall i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}:\ A_ix+a_it+B_iu-b_i\in K_i.\] A concave graph-implementation interface for \(g\) is such data satisfying \[\forall(x,t)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R:\quad t\le g(x)\iff \exists u\in\mathbb R^p\ \forall i:\ A_ix+a_it+B_iu-b_i\in K_i.\] Thus the interface converts an accepted epigraph or hypograph comparison into a lifted conic system whose projection onto \((x,t)\) is exactly the comparison set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A graph-implementation interface for a convex function is a finite lifted conic description whose feasible points project exactly onto the function's epigraph. For every input and bound, the epigraph inequality holds if and only if some auxiliary vector satisfies every emitted cone constraint. For a concave function, the analogous interface projects onto its hypograph. Exact equality after projection is required; merely producing a relaxation or an approximation is not a graph implementation in this sense.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{epi}f=\pi_{x,t}\{(x,t,u):A_ix+a_it+B_iu-b_i\in K_i\ \forall i\}\] for the convex interface, with \(\operatorname{epi}f\) replaced by \(\operatorname{hypo}g\) for the concave interface.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[f(x)\le t\iff (x,t)\in\pi_{x,t}(Q_f),\qquad Q_f:=\{(x,t,u):A_ix+a_it+B_iu-b_i\in K_i\ \forall i\}.\]
The hypograph interface for \(g\) is equivalently an epigraph interface for the convex function \(-g\), after replacing \(t\) by \(-t\).
special_cases_latex: If every \(K_i\) is a Lorentz cone, the interface is a conic-quadratic representation of the epigraph or hypograph.
If the lifted system is one linear matrix inequality over a positive-semidefinite cone, the convex interface is a semidefinite representation of \(f\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Fixing \(t=\alpha\) in a convex interface yields an exact lifted representation of the sublevel set \(\{x:f(x)\le\alpha\}\).

Replacing a nonlinear objective \(f(x)\) by an epigraph variable gives \(\inf_{x\in X}f(x)=\inf\{t:x\in X,\ (x,t)\in\operatorname{epi}f\}\); an available interface turns the epigraph constraint into its lifted conic system.
boundary_notes: The ordinary equality graph \(\{(x,t):t=f(x)\}\) is generally not convex; “graph implementation” here refers to the convex epigraph or concave hypograph comparison used by a compiler.
Approximate outer or inner representations do not satisfy the defining biconditional and require a separate approximation contract.
Representability alone does not bound the size of the lifted system or the cost of constructing and solving it.

notation.meaning: Coordinate projection retaining the original variables \((x,t)\).
Auxiliary variables introduced by the implementation.

children.title: Convexity–Representability–Tractability Gap
children.top_down_role: Distinction between mathematical convexity, available standard-form representations, and computational accessibility.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A concrete convex-but-unrepresentable boundary for finite linear-inequality lifts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal L_{\mathrm{poly}}\) permit only finite systems of linear equalities and inequalities with finitely many auxiliary variables. The function \(f(x)=\|x\|_2\) on \(\mathbb R^2\) is convex, but its epigraph is not polyhedral. Because a linear image or projection of a polyhedron is polyhedral, \(f\) has no exact graph representation in \(\mathcal L_{\mathrm{poly}}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Euclidean norm is convex but cannot be represented exactly by a finite lifted linear-inequality graph formulation, because its epigraph is nonpolyhedral.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal L_{\mathrm{poly}}\text{ permits finite linear equalities and inequalities and finite-dimensional auxiliary variables}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C(f)\text{ holds but }R_{\mathcal L_{\mathrm{poly}}}(f)\text{ fails}.
knowledge_statements.title: Convexity beyond Polyhedral Graph Libraries

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dependence of representability and tractability claims on their declared interfaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose every template and construction admitted by \(\mathcal L_1\) is also admitted unchanged by \(\mathcal L_2\). Then exact representability in \(\mathcal L_1\) implies exact representability in \(\mathcal L_2\), while the converse need not hold. An exact representation yields a polynomial-time reduction only when its construction time and encoded size are polynomial and the target problem admits the asserted resource bound under the same data and accuracy model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conservatively larger graph library preserves existing representations, while tractability transfers only when construction, representation size, and target-solver complexity are controlled in one encoding model.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal L_2\text{ conservatively contains every template and construction of }\mathcal L_1
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: R_{\mathcal L_1}(f)\Rightarrow R_{\mathcal L_2}(f),\quad\text{while tractability transfer additionally requires polynomial construction, size, and target-solver bounds}.

notation.meaning: Exact representability of f using library L.

review_flags: Complexity conclusions are conditional on the declared encoding, accuracy criterion, and computational model.
knowledge_statements.title: Library and Encoding Relativity

assumptions_latex: Representability refers to an available finite exact formulation in a specified standard-form library.
Tractability refers to computational accessibility under a stated input encoding, accuracy criterion, and algorithmic model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Neither \(C(f)\Rightarrow R_{\mathcal L}(f)\) nor \(R_{\mathcal L}(f)\Rightarrow T_{\mathcal M}(f)\) holds without additional assumptions on the library, representation size, data access, and computational model.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates semantic convexity, library-relative representation, and model-relative computational tractability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a function \(f\), the predicates \(C(f)\), \(R_{\mathcal L}(f)\), and \(T_{\mathcal M}(f)\) describe distinct properties. Convexity \(C(f)\) is a semantic inequality on the domain of \(f\). Representability \(R_{\mathcal L}(f)\) requires an available finite exact graph formulation using a chosen library \(\mathcal L\). Tractability \(T_{\mathcal M}(f)\) requires an algorithm with a specified resource bound in model \(\mathcal M\). In general, convexity need not yield a formulation in \(\mathcal L\), and possession of a formulation need not yield tractability when its size, conditioning, data encoding, cone oracles, or accuracy requirements are uncontrolled.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convexity, availability of an exact standard-form representation, and computational tractability are distinct; neither transition follows without library and complexity assumptions.
knowledge_statements.title: Convexity–Representability–Tractability Gap

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary kind is appropriate for this gap container, and the distinctions are conceptually sound. The two non-implication claims are nontrivial and depend on precise definitions of the representation library and computational model, but no supporting citation or sourced counterexample is provided.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal P=\{P_d:d\in\mathcal D\}\) be an encoded family of finite-dimensional minimization problems \[P_d:\quad \inf_{x\in X_d} f_d(x),\] let \(|d|\) denote input size, and fix a catalogue \(\mathfrak K\) of standard closed convex cones together with an explicit encoding of affine conic systems. Accuracy is measured by \(\epsilon>0\) in a fixed computational model.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition separates a semantic property of each optimization problem, a syntactic lifting property relative to a specified cone catalogue, and an algorithmic property of the encoded family. Tractability means worst-case polynomial solvability in the declared model, not merely favorable observed performance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define three predicates. First, \[\mathrm C(\mathcal P)\iff \forall d\in\mathcal D:\ X_d\text{ is convex and }f_d\text{ is convex on }X_d.\] Second, \(\mathrm R_{\mathfrak K}(\mathcal P)\) holds when an exact conic formulation can be constructed from \(d\) with encoding length polynomial in \(|d|\): there are auxiliary variables \(u\), a cone \(K_d\) that is a finite product of cones from \(\mathfrak K\), and affine data such that every objective and feasibility comparison used by \(P_d\) is equivalent to a projection of \[A_dx+B_du+c_dt-b_d\in K_d.\] Third, \[\mathrm T(\mathcal P)\iff \exists\mathcal A\ \exists q\text{ polynomial}\ \forall d\ \forall\epsilon>0:\ \mathcal A(d,\epsilon)\text{ returns a prescribed }\epsilon\text{-solution within }q(|d|,\operatorname{Digits}(d,\epsilon))\text{ operations}.\] The convexity–representability–tractability gap is the failure of either bridge \(\mathrm C\Rightarrow\mathrm R_{\mathfrak K}\) or \(\mathrm R_{\mathfrak K}\Rightarrow\mathrm T\) under the stated catalogue, encoding, accuracy, and computational model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an encoded family of optimization problems, convexity means that every feasible set and objective has the required convex geometry. Representability means that each instance can be compiled exactly into a polynomial-size lifted affine conic system over a declared catalogue of standard cones. Tractability means that one algorithm returns the prescribed approximate solution for every instance with worst-case running time polynomial in the input size and requested accuracy digits. A convexity-to-representability gap occurs when convex geometry does not supply such an available exact formulation. A representability-to-tractability gap occurs when a formulation does not meet the additional size, construction, encoding, regularity, or algorithmic conditions needed for a polynomial-time guarantee.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathrm{Gap}_{\mathfrak K}(\mathcal P):=\bigl(\mathrm C(\mathcal P)\wedge\neg\mathrm R_{\mathfrak K}(\mathcal P)\bigr)\ \vee\ \bigl(\mathrm R_{\mathfrak K}(\mathcal P)\wedge\neg\mathrm T(\mathcal P)\bigr),\] with every predicate interpreted relative to the declared encoding and computational model.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The distinction may be recorded as the implication chain \[\text{convex geometry}\ \not\Rightarrow\ \text{available polynomial-size standard-cone lift}\ \not\Rightarrow\ \text{polynomial-time solvability without further hypotheses}.\]

At the instance level, exact representability is the projection identity \[X_d=\pi_x\{(x,u):A_dx+B_du-b_d\in K_d\};\] at the family level, \(\mathrm R_{\mathfrak K}\) additionally requires uniformly polynomial construction and encoding size.
special_cases_latex: For \(\mathfrak K\) consisting of nonnegative orthants, Lorentz cones, or positive-semidefinite cones, \(\mathrm R_{\mathfrak K}\) specializes respectively to polynomial-size LP, conic-quadratic, or semidefinite representability.
A convex function may satisfy \(\mathrm C\) while lacking a representation in a restricted catalogue; representability is therefore catalogue-relative.
immediate_consequences_latex: A curvature certificate establishes only \(\mathrm C(\mathcal P)\); it is not by itself a conic formulation or a complexity certificate.

An exact finite lift establishes instance-level representability but does not establish \(\mathrm T(\mathcal P)\) unless its construction and size, the cone-processing method, the accuracy convention, and the required regularity or boundedness data satisfy the family-level complexity assumptions.
boundary_notes: The predicate \(\neg\mathrm R_{\mathfrak K}\) is relative to the chosen cone catalogue and encoding; enlarging the catalogue can change its truth value.

Practical speed and polynomial worst-case tractability are different notions. A polynomial method may be impractical, while a method without a polynomial worst-case bound may perform well empirically.
The definition concerns exact reformulations. Approximate relaxations, discretizations, and oracle-only descriptions require separate approximation guarantees.

notation.meaning: Convexity predicate for the problem family.
Uniform exact polynomial-size representability over cone catalogue \(\mathfrak K\).
Polynomial solvability under the fixed accuracy and computation model.
Encoding-dependent measure of the requested accuracy and relevant data magnitude.
